en: The Mahāyāna Yoga Vajra-nature Ocean Mañjuśrī Thousand Arms and Thousand Bowls Great King of Teachings, Scroll One.
Thus have I heard. At one time, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni was at the abode of Maheśvara.
In the palace of the Heavenly King, within the Vimala-maṇi-ratna hall,
the Tathāgata sat upon a throne of a hundred precious maṇi-jewels together with the Tathāgata Vairocana.
In the Lotus Treasury Assembly within the Ocean of Vajra-nature,
he preached this sutra together with immeasurable Great Brahma Kings and others.
And he spoke it together with a multitude of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, as numerous as atoms,
concerning the Vairocana Tathāgata’s ocean of the nature of the dharma-realm, the secret Vajradhātu Lotus-womb Treasury World-ocean.
Within it was the Great Sage Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva,
manifesting a golden-hued body from which emerged a thousand arms, a thousand hands, and a thousand alms bowls.
Within the bowl, a thousand Śākyamunis appeared;
from those thousand Śākyamunis, there further appeared a hundred trillion manifested Śākyamunis.
At that time, the World-Honored One Śākyamuni...
At that time, from amidst the great assembly and upon the throne of a hundred jewels,
he addressed the sixteen great beings, bodhisattvas such as Samantabhadra.
And all the great bodhisattva-mahāsattvas,
listen attentively, listen attentively!
Now I shall explain how, through the empowerment of the holy power of the Tathāgata Vairocana in the past,
all bodhisattvas within the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu) were enabled to cultivate and realize the samādhi of Mañjuśrī’s secret vajra-mind.
May all bodhisattvas and all sentient beings attain their own wisdom,
enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, and be awakened through its revelation and realization.
At that time, Vairocana Tathāgata—
Then he addressed the Muni, the World-Honored One, and the thousand Śākyas—the thousands, hundreds, and billions of emanated Śākyas—saying:
"I have, since ancient times, practiced the teachings of the Vajra Secret Bodhi Dharma."
This Great Sage Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva Mahāsattva was my former teacher.
I shall now relate the causes and conditions concerning that teacher of the past and long ago.
I consider the nature of purity to be named Vairocana;
it serves as the root of bodhi for all sentient beings, being the adamantine nature.
I am thus the fundamental original self-nature.
Because it is the seed of the noble Vajra-wisdom,
at that time, after the Tathāgata Śākyamuni had finished preaching this sutra,
[it was] the pure mind of the former Tathāgata Vairocana.
The great sage Mañjuśrī, the thousand-armed Bodhisattva, appeared in a golden body,
manifesting the secret ocean-like Dharma-treasury of the empowerment of practice,
so that all sentient beings might enter this King of Yoga Mahāyāna Sūtras.
He proclaimed the *Vairocanābhisambodhi-tathāgataguhyaka-gambhīra-dharmanaya-sūtra*, the *Samyaksaṃbodhi*.
The World-Honored One taught this sūtra as the profound and wondrous Dharma, the *Vajraguhyasāgara-kośa-mahāyāna-yoga-vajrabodhi-samādhi-sūtra*.
At that time, when the Tathāgata Vairocana spoke this teaching on the secret samādhi of the Great Sage Mañjuśrī,
it was for the sake of all sentient beings.
From the time he first aroused the aspiration on the causal ground,
he led sentient beings and cultivated the practice until achieving unsurpassed bodhi.
Now, I shall explain the thirty branches of the Three Mysteries and the three types of bodhi of Mañjuśrī, the Vajra of the Noble Nature of the Five Wisdom Honored Ones of the Buddha.
May all bodhisattvas and all sentient beings cultivate and enter swift and rapid awakening to profound penetration,
and realize entry into the Buddha-mind and the adamantine sacred power.
Because it is the Tathāgata-samādhi of the noble nature of bodhi,
all those who have previously attained buddhahood have fully cultivated this most supreme Mahāyāna, extraordinary teaching of the Dharma.
One shall swiftly attain the fruit of Buddhahood and Bodhi.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One proceeded to explain the fundamental root and essential meaning of the sutra.
At that time, Śākyamuni Tathāgata—

He himself spoke of a time long ago, in the past, incalculable as the number of atoms, equal to space, extending to the end of the dharma-realm—beyond description, beyond description—in ages of such vast antiquity.
This is the teaching on the *samādhi* method of the thirty branches of the Triple Secret Vajra Bodhi,

which subsumes all dharmas within the Five-Crested Vajradhātu, and the *samādhi* method of the Great Maṇḍala of the Consecration of the Venerable Five Wisdoms, practiced by all Buddhas and Tathāgatas when they were Bodhisattvas on the causal ground.
Then, at that time, the Tathāgata Vairocana entrusted Mañjuśrī,
commanding him to transmit [this teaching] and serve as the preeminent teacher for all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
Through contemplative observation, one swiftly realizes and enters the profound and penetrating wisdom-contemplation;
one enters the heart of all Buddhas and realizes the nature of the ocean of the pure, noble wisdom-dharmadhātu of Vairocana’s dharma-body and wisdom-body.
At that time, Vairocana Tathāgata brought forth the five wisdoms of enlightenment,
the supreme dhāraṇīs of all phenomena, and all samādhis;
these constitute the fundamental secret with its five gates in total.
This compendium of all dharmas, the Mahāyāna Sūtra,
is the secret dharma teaching of the profound ultimate truth that accords with the *samyak-saṃbodhi* of all Buddhas.
How should one practice its sequential stages?
By relying on the explanation of the Noble One’s intent and seeking to cultivate the practice of contemplative observation,
one enters this dharma-gate.
First, the World-Honored One, the Muni, taught that entering the contemplation of the letter A signifies the meaning of primordial quiescence and non-arising.
This was spoken by Vairocana Tathāgata when,
in the past, he had become a thousand Śākyamunis, each of whom manifested a hundred billion emanation-Śākyamunis upon attaining enlightenment;
at that time, while this Buddha was on the causal ground as a bodhisattva.
The Tathāgata taught this contemplation of the syllable A for the purpose of cultivating entry into the fundamental gate of purity and non-arising. Second,
the Muni, the World-Honored One, taught the contemplation of the syllable RA for the purpose of entering the meaning of original emptiness and freedom from defilement.
This was spoken by the Tathāgata Akṣobhya;
it was spoken by the fearless, transcendent, and sovereign Buddha who, in the past, subdued hundreds of thousands of millions of māra-folk.
This was at the time when this Buddha attained enlightenment.
When this Buddha was practicing as a bodhisattva on the causal ground,
the Tathāgata taught him this contemplation of the syllable RA.
Third, the entry into the immovable gate of the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) through cultivation:

the World-Honored One, the Muni, taught the contemplation of the syllable *PA*, which signifies the meaning of the fundamental reality being unstained, unattached, and free from defilement; this was spoken by Ratnasambhava Tathāgata.
This was spoken by the Buddha Universal Fulfillment, Constant Sufficiency, and Sovereignty, who in the past subdued the root of greed in hundreds of thousands of millions of beings.
This occurred at the time when that Buddha attained enlightenment.
When this Buddha was practicing as a bodhisattva on the stage of causes,
the Tathāgata taught him this contemplation on the syllable *pa*,
whereby he entered the gate of the equality of the true suchness (*tathatā*) of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
Fourth, the Muni, the World-Honored One, taught the meaning of the sublime practice of entering the contemplation of the letter *A* as primordially pure;
this was spoken by the Tathāgata Avalokiteśvararāja for the sake of subduing the root of hatred throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of past eons.
Spoken by the Buddha Amitāyus-vīrya-vaśitā.
At the time this Buddha attained the Way,
while he was practicing as a bodhisattva on the causal ground:
The Tathāgata taught this contemplation on the syllable *va*,
which is the gateway to the Pure Land through the principle of entering sublime contemplation.
Fifth, the Muni, the World-Honored One, taught the contemplation on the syllable *na*, the meaning of which is that all things are fundamentally empty and devoid of intrinsic nature.
This was spoken by the Tathāgata Amoghasiddhi;
it was originally taught by the Buddha Durjayajñānālokendrarāja, who in the past subjugated the root of delusion for hundreds of thousands of billions of beings.
At the time this Buddha attained enlightenment— when he was practicing as a Bodhisattva on the causal ground—
the Tathāgata taught him this contemplation on the syllable *Na*.
By cultivating it, he entered and accomplished the gate of liberation of Vajra-Bodhi.
At that time, having thus explained the sequence of the Dharma teachings of these five Tathāgatas and having taught the contemplation of the five Buddhas, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni—
This is the teaching on the gate of liberation through the bodhi of noble wisdom— the five vajras and five peaks that are the root of the bodhi of all Buddhas—
and the place entered by all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and worthy sages.
It is the place where all bodhisattvas at the stage of initial resolve and all sentient beings cultivate and realize contemplative practices to achieve Buddhahood;
it is the realm of all Great Brahmās, Śakras, and the Four Heavenly Kings.
It is the place where the various śrāvakas and the fourfold assembly of disciples,
as well as sons and daughters of good family, train and achieve unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi).
The Buddha addressed the great assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas:
"If there are bodhisattvas who have first resolved their minds toward enlightenment,
as well as all members of the fourfold assembly— sons and daughters of good family— and others."
If one should resolve upon bodhicitta,
the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī shall make this vow:
"I possess ten inexhaustible, profound, and great vows of all Buddhas."
All bodhisattvas and all sentient beings who enter into my vow are the sons of the World-Honored Buddhas,
and they are also my parents.
What do you think? I have a prior vow and great aspiration.
Relying upon my ten kinds of great aspirations, I first [dedicate them] for the sake of my parents, brothers, sisters, wives, children, and kinsmen.
May they attain the fulfillment of the retributive fruits of wealth and nobility;
may brothers be friends and sisters be respectful, possessing a compassionate heart that refrains from killing;
and may they be permitted to study the Mahāyāna, reciting and chanting the honored sutras.
May I convert all classes of beings and lead them to Bodhi.
May I also serve as their preceptor, sub-preceptor, teacher, ācārya, fellow student, or companion;
may they receive my Dharma teachings and learn from me the rules of decorum.
He took me under his guidance, instructing me to generate supreme aspirations,
dedicate [merit] to the Mahāyāna, and train for bodhi until gradually attaining the Buddha-way.
Thereafter, I served as a minister, official, and high-ranking administrator, managing secular affairs on behalf of others.
Each and every one of them is upright and pure, possessing loyalty and filial piety toward their country; they all share a karmic affinity for turning toward Bodhi.
May they encounter the Triple Gem and be inspired to resolve upon the mind of Bodhi.
What are called the ten inexhaustible, profound, and great vows?

First, the Great Vow: "If there are any sentient beings born within the three realms, whether they arise through their own karma or the karma of others, or are transformed according to conditions, may I become the sovereign of the four dhyānas and the five pure abodes."
The master of the eight meditative concentrations and the four dhyānas;
the Brahma King, lord of the six heavens of the desire realm;
Śakra, lord of all the devas.
Lord of the four heavens and the four wheels;
lord of all gods and dragon kings;
lord of the eight classes of spirits and ghosts.
Lord protector of the Buddha-dharma;
lord of the monasteries and palaces;
lord of the four great world-sustainers.
Lord of the adamantine and firm;
Lord of the benevolent deities who protect the land;
Lord of great nations and small nations.
Lord of the kings scattered like grains of millet;
commander-in-chief of all armies;
sovereign who governs all that is protected.
May all beings of the four modes of birth— whether aquatic or terrestrial, born from womb, egg, moisture, or transformation—
and all sentient creatures of the nine categories of moving life,
together take birth in the three periods of time and aspire for the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
May those who have not yet heard my name hear it;
and having heard my name, may all sentient beings within my Dharma fully resolve to attain bodhicitta.
They dedicate [their merit] toward the Mahāyāna to cultivate the unsurpassed path.
If there are sentient beings who, as worldly physicians with the medicine of the Dharma,
provide healing for all ailments.
He was skilled in calculating chronologies and mathematics, as well as in arts, crafts, and games.
He was proficient in secular classics, literary composition, song, and praise.
Through discourse and playful engagement, he guided others toward liberation.
Adapting to various types of beings and engaging with them through shared activities, one guides worldly beings,
causing them to awaken the correct view of bodhicitta and receiving it correctly;
thus, those who share a karmic affinity with me may enter the Buddha-way.
Second, regarding great vows: if there are sentient beings who slander me or harbor anger toward me.
They inflict punishment, harm, and kill me;
such people constantly harbor resentment toward myself and others,
unable to achieve liberation from it.
May we share a common affinity so that they may resolve to attain bodhicitta.
Third, as for my great vow: if there are sentient beings who cherish and hold my body dear, [may they likewise generate the aspiration for enlightenment].
With lustful minds, they see me and seek to obtain me;
upon my body and upon the bodies of others,
they extensively practice flattery, crookedness, false views, and perversions.

Furthermore, regarding those who have committed pure or impure deeds, as well as all manner of evil and unwholesome acts, I vow that they shall all share in this same object of focus and be inspired to give rise to the bodhicitta.
Fourth, as for the great vow: if there are sentient beings...
They treat me with contempt and harbor doubts toward me;
they oppress me unjustly and deceive me.
They slander the Triple Gem and harbor hatred and envy toward the virtuous and worthy.
Those who have bullied me throughout my lives always give rise to unwholesome states;
yet those with whom I share a karmic connection cause me to resolve upon the mind of Bodhi.
Fifth, regarding great vows: if there are sentient beings...
They despise me, slight me, feel shame before me, and feel remorse toward me;
they honor me, yet do not honor me;
they obstruct me, yet do not obstruct me.
Using me or not using me;
taking me or not taking me;
seeking me or not seeking me.
They want me and do not want me;
they follow me and do not follow me;
they see me and do not see me.
May all beings together share this affinity with me, causing them to resolve upon the mind of enlightenment.
Sixth, regarding great vows: if there are sentient beings...
They constantly take the lives of others,
acting as butchers, executioners, hunters, or fishermen;
with hostile intent toward one another's lives, they kill and harm each other.
There is no severance of the cycle as they repay one another life after life;
their murderous intent remains fierce and they feel no remorse for their transgressions,
selling meat for wealth to sustain their own lives.
One with such a mind will forever lose the human body;
there shall be no separation from the retribution of their actions.
Thus, one should cause them to give rise to the bodhicitta.
If others take my wealth and goods from me,
I give them wealth and goods;
or if they bestow wealth and goods upon me, I likewise bestow wealth and goods.
Regarding the wealth and possessions one has acquired, as well as those not yet acquired, may all those with whom I have a karmic connection be inspired to resolve upon Bodhicitta.
Seventh, as for great vows: if there are sentient beings...
Whether it be making offerings to me or making offerings to others;
or whether it be constructing temples, monastic residences,
monasteries, Buddha-stūpas, meditation halls, or forest hermitages in solitary and quiet places.
Whether it be all merits created by oneself or created by others,
or the creation of images of Bodhisattvas and Buddhas,
or causing others to practice giving and establish meritorious blessings.
Dedicating it throughout the entire realm of phenomena toward the enlightenment of all Buddhas,
may all sentient beings equally partake of this merit;
as well as others, one's own friends, companions, teachers, and disciples.
Practicing asceticism, restraining the body, and abstaining from food;
observing precepts or violating them; performing practices or not performing them;
and being instructed and exhorted by one's upādhyāya and ācārya.
May those who listen to my teachings, those who receive my instructions, those who follow the teachings of others,
those who practice together with me, those who share the same karma, and all those with whom I have a karmic connection,
be inspired to resolve upon Bodhicitta.
Eighth, as for the great vow: if there are sentient beings who have extensively committed various transgressions and fall into the hells with no prospect of escape,
undergoing all manner of suffering and affliction throughout immeasurable kalpas;
Emerging from hell, they are reborn into the five destinies.
First, as animals, they return to their former lives,
bearing burdens as camels, donkeys, pigs, dogs, oxen, sheep, elephants, horses, slaves, servants, or attendants.
I repay the karmic debts of others, even at the cost of my own life multiplied over kalpas;
I return what was stolen to its owners without ceasing.
Throughout the five realms of existence, I manifest in forms according to the needs of those to be transformed.
They are constantly born into the same world as others to teach and transform people;
sometimes they manifest as the poorest, most afflicted, blind, deaf, mute,
or lowliest beggars among the multitude of all sentient beings.
Sharing the same kind, the same conditions, the same tasks,
and the same conduct, they are led by their common karma to enter the Buddha-way.
Having a shared affinity with me, they are inspired to give rise to the bodhicitta.
Ninth, regarding the great vow: if there are sentient beings who,
being unrestrained in body and mind, are arrogant and conceited,
they thereby defile and mire the Buddha-dharma within my teaching.
Teachers and disciples lack shame and dread of blame;
they misappropriate the funds of the Sangha and the Buddha, as well as the property of Bodhisattvas,
and engage in killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct.
They engage in lying, frivolous speech, harsh words, and double-tongued slander;
they incite strife and act with unrestrained indulgence in greed and anger;
they do not distinguish between the virtuous and the good, but plunder the wealth of others.
They reject and conceal [the truth], deceive others, and fail to distinguish between good and evil.
They extensively commit the ten non-virtuous actions and all manner of transgressions.
Upon death, they fall into the Avīci Hell and enter the various hells.
Emerging from hell, they cycle through the six realms of existence;
entering the ocean of birth and death and the various evil destinies,
may those with whom I share a common affinity, karma, and path likewise be so.
I shall transform and manifest according to conditions to rescue them and cause them to attain liberation.
May those who share a karmic affinity with me resolve to attain Bodhicitta and seek the Unsurpassed Way.
Tenth, regarding great vows: if there are sentient beings who should encounter my Dharma...
Whether they have a karmic connection with me or no connection with me,
if they share my great vow, they are one with my own body and no different from me.
I practice the four immeasurables, with a mind equal to space.
May they extensively deliver sentient beings without ceasing,
and may they reach Bodhi and ascend the path of perfect enlightenment.
By the power of his noble nature and vows, the Great Sage Mañjuśrī—
Neither entering the triple world nor emerging from the triple world,
the mind is like space, eternally abiding within the Tathāgata’s ocean of pure nature, the treasury of suchness, and dwelling securely within the dharma-realm.
It pervades the essential nature of the consciousness of all sentient beings. Mañjuśrī said:
"I have a great vow; by the power of my noble nature..."
To empower sentient beings so that their karmic defilements are extinguished,
and to enable them to attain the sublime fruit of Bodhi— the state of all Buddhas—
these are known as the ten great vows of a bodhisattva.
When Mañjuśrī had thus made these vast vows,
the trichiliocosm shook in six ways,
and the heavens rained down māndārava flowers that filled the entirety of space.
At that time, the entire assembly beheld those flowers and simultaneously praised the Great Being Mañjuśrī,
exclaiming that his noble power and mastery were inconceivable and ineffable.
At that time, the entire great assembly rejoiced, accepted it with faith, and practiced accordingly.
Then, the World-Honored One Śākyamuni descended from the realm of Maheśvara to the world of Jambudvīpa.
In the kingdom of Śrāvastī, at the Jetavana Monastery,
within the great maṇḍala and amidst the great assembly,
there were ten billion bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
There were seven billion assemblies of Arhats who have attained the four fruits;
six billion assemblies of all the great Brahma kings and devas;
and five billion assemblies of Śakras and all the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Furthermore, there were forty-six billion assemblies of the Four Heavenly Kings;
thirty-five hundred thousand assemblies of the four great wheel-turning kings;
and two hundred and four thousand assemblies of asuras, nāgas, spirits, the eight classes of ghosts and deities, and yakṣas.
Furthermore, there were the deities and spirits of the void, non-celestial wildernesses, and open lands,
numbering one hundred and fifty thousand; there were also the deities of mountains,
peaks, rivers, plains, springs, ponds, streams, seas, forests, trees, grasses, flowers, fruits, and medicinal herbs, as well as all the deities of earth, water, fire, and wind.
There were hundreds of billions of preeminent followers,
as well as sixteen great kings along with the rulers of other minor kingdoms,
and the fourfold assembly of disciples consisting of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās.
Good sons and good daughters, among all sentient beings there are seventy trillion multitudes;
at that time, Śākyamuni Tathāgata was amidst this great assembly.
He sat upon a lion throne made of a hundred jewels and entered a thousandfold adamantine samādhi,
emitting the radiant light of the dharma-realm’s adamantine jewel-flames.
All became golden in color, pervading without exception the oceans of thousands of billions of trichiliocosms.
The World-Honored One then arose from his meditative concentration,
serene and joyful, with a gentle smile.
At that time, within the great assembly,
there were sixteen great beings, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas,
with the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī as their leader.
Rising from his seat, he circumambulated the Buddha three times.
Standing to one side, he knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in reverence toward the Buddha, and addressed the World-Honored One:
"When the Tathāgata was dwelling in samādhi, his countenance was serene and his expression was joyful."
The great assembly had long been unaware of what causes and conditions the Tathāgata would proclaim,
nor what teachings he would expound to extensively deliver all sentient beings.
The Buddha then addressed Mañjuśrī and the sixteen great bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and others.
I shall bring to liberation all infinite sentient beings throughout the entire dharma-realm, who are as vast as space;
I shall reveal the worlds of the past, future, and present,
and all the lands within the trichiliocosm.
The entire assembly of bodhisattvas;
the entire assembly of śrāvakas;
and the entire assembly of the Great Brahmā devas.
All the eight classes of nāgas and spirits;
all the hosts of devas, ghosts, and spirits;
and all the hosts of Śakra and the Heaven of the Thirty-three.
The assembly of the four heavenly wheel-turning kings;
all the disciples of the fourfold assembly;
and sons and daughters of good family, etc.
The Tathāgata said, "I shall now, together with the great assembly,
speak of Mañjuśrī’s past causes and conditions from long ago,
along with those of sixteen great beings, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas."

From the very beginning, he has taught all bodhisattvas and all sentient beings the dharma-instruction for the thirty-limbed samādhi of the Tathāgata’s yoga-vajra bodhicitta, the gateway of the three secrets.
This is the gate of contemplation on the *tathatā* of the adamantine bodhi of all Buddhas, which, when cultivated, leads to entry, realization, and awakening.
The World-Honored One said: "I shall now clearly expound the grounds of the past causes of the sixteen great beings, the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, such as Mañjuśrī."
By the power of the merit and the holy nature of the three secrets of the supreme Vajra Bodhi, through the practice of the secret samādhi of the maṇḍala of all the Buddhas and Tathāgatas,
he intends to cause all Bodhisattvas to...
Having cultivated and realized entry into the vajra-samādhi,
the Buddha addressed the entire assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas,
as well as the śrāvakas, bhikṣus, and the fourfold assembly of disciples.
In this way, Mañjuśrī, one practices the method of the vajra-samādhi of all the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas;
it is beyond comparison, unspeakable, unspeakably unspeakable, and inconceivable.
The assembly of great bodhisattvas said:
"Now, World-Honored One, regarding the vajra-samādhi which you have spoken of as being beyond all measure,
how many kinds of dharmas does it possess?"
The Tathāgata has stated that there are ten kinds of dharmas. What are these ten?
First, suppose that in this world the kalpa-fire were to arise.
It burned the trichiliocosm;
for seven days the fire blazed intensely, its fierce flames extremely hot,
penetrating through the world-system to its infinite reaches.
The Tathāgata dwells therein, established in the vajra-samādhi;
without exerting merit or the powers of mastery,
he is spontaneously cool, serene, and at peace.
It is equal, pure, and characterized by permanence, bliss, self, and purity;
therefore, the dharma of samādhi is profoundly deep and extraordinary.
Excellent, excellent! It is beyond all comparison.
Second, when the Tathāgata faces a fiercely blazing flame and dwells within a great fire,
he remains in the vajra-samādhi, walking, sitting, or standing.
In all his movements and abidings, he is without obstruction.
The Tathāgata’s body is dignified, exalted, and golden in its majestic power;
its radiance is so extraordinary that it eclipses the gates of all evil realms.
Being free from all impurities and entirely pure,
the samādhi of the Tathāgata thus possesses a most rare and extraordinary quality.
Third, even if there were a world like the aforementioned one, ablaze with a great conflagration,
the Tathāgata would enter the Vajra-samādhi therein and cause the Jambudvīpa world to become vast, magnificent, and pure.
It is like the palace of the sovereign god Śakra;
through the Tathāgata’s power of mastery, it attains complete coolness.
This signifies that the World-Honored One abides in samādhi.
This is an exceedingly rare and extraordinary teaching.
Fourth, when the fires of the three realms blaze forth and the great earth is entirely engulfed in a pervasive, intense conflagration,
the Tathāgata dwells therein while abiding in the Vajra-samādhi.
Spontaneously, there appeared flowing springs and bathing pools,
with exquisite flowers, soft grasses, and delicate, lush greenery;
their touch was as supple and pure as that of *kācalindika* cloth.
The fragrant incense was beyond compare;
the Tathāgata dwelt therein with sovereign ease,
manifesting a most rare and extraordinary power of spiritual transformation.
Fifth, as described above, the great fire from above penetrates below,
and the fire from below penetrates above;
everything is completely ablaze.
While the Tathāgata dwelt therein in the Vajra-samādhi,
there spontaneously appeared eight kinds of water of merit,
which filled a cool and refreshing bathing pool to bathe the Tathāgata.
What are the eight?
First, the mind attains happiness as if entering meditative absorption.
Second, pliancy.
Third, it is soft and smooth.
Fourth, its nature is clear, empty, and pure.
Fifth, it is free from all impurities and turbidity.
Sixth, it is clear, limpid, and transparent.
Seventh, one always drinks with peace and well-being.
Eighth, one drinks much without suffering harm.
To eliminate afflictions and attain eternal bliss and purity is the most rare and extraordinary teaching of the Tathāgata’s holy power.
Sixth, when the great fires of the world blaze fiercely, neither ceasing nor subsiding;
The Tathāgata dwells therein in the Vajra-samādhi;
sitting and reclining in tranquil meditation, he is naturally blissful.
A harmonious, light ease, like a cool breeze, wafts over the Buddha’s body.
It is like bathing the body and mind in pure water;
it brings nature into harmony, providing peace, security, joy, and tranquility beyond all comparison—like a person in extreme heat encountering a great tree.
The thick shade and cool breezes blow upon the body, bringing joy and satisfaction.
This samādhi of peace and bliss possesses the incomparable and inconceivable power of the sages;
it is entirely pure, the holy nature of the Tathāgata, a most rare and extraordinary dharma.
Seventh, even if the great trichiliocosm were ablaze with a raging fire,
the Tathāgata would abide within it in the vajra-samādhi; from there,
a cool pond would spontaneously emerge, and a great lotus flower would arise.
It has immeasurable flowers as its retinue;
these flowers are fragrant, pure, and unsurpassed.
Their radiance shines forth like the great solar disc, with a brilliance beyond compare.
The Tathāgata within it is beyond all analogy;
those who behold him are gladdened, filled with joy, and awakened.
His progress toward bodhi cannot be fully described.
This is the most rare and extraordinary teaching of the Tathāgata.
Eighth, above there is a great fire that reaches down to Jambudvīpa;
it fills the space, blazing intensely with a brilliant and radiant flame.
The Tathāgata dwells therein, abiding in the Vajra-samādhi;
sitting with sovereign ease, he enters into samādhi,
his bliss beyond measure, equal to space.
Spontaneously appeared a great fragrant garden producing exquisite, fresh fruits,
as well as five kinds of extraordinary flowers:
the *utpala* and the *puṇḍarīka*.
There were *pāṇḍumṛdā* flowers, *kubjaka* flowers, and great *mandārava* flowers;
they shone with five colors, fragrant, pure, and brilliant,
of various kinds and exquisite beauty beyond measure.
Those who see it will rejoice and spontaneously realize it;
the third dhyāna brings inexhaustible satisfaction and bliss.
This is the exceedingly rare and extraordinary Dharma of the Tathāgata.
Ninth, even if hundreds of thousands of worlds were filled with blazing, intensely raging, and boundless great fires,
the Tathāgata would abide within them in the Vajra-samādhi,
sitting, standing, walking, or staying, remaining in meditative absorption and fixed concentration.
The divine power of the Lord Maheśvara is peerless; by his spiritual might,
he spontaneously manifests hundreds of thousands of Buddhas and hundreds of thousands of inconceivable pure lands.
The noble nature of the Tathāgata causes all bodhisattvas to behold his manifested spiritual powers,
so that they may cultivate entry into the ultimate nirvāṇa of bodhi—
the vajra-buddha-ground of permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
This is the Tathāgata’s mastery of supernatural powers, a most rare and extraordinary dharma. Tenth:
even if the fires of the kalpa at the end of infinite eons were to blaze with fierce and violent flames.
Without ceasing, the flames blazed fiercely;
within them, the Tathāgata entered this vajra-samādhi,
and spontaneously the Tathāgata manifested the Anavatapta Great Lake.
From within that pond, a great lotus flower emerged,
adorned with the wondrous colors of a hundred jewels reflecting one another;
its radiance was like the sun, beyond worldly analogy, and ineffable.
That great lotus flower pervades the trichiliocosm;
there is no part of the entire dharma-realm that it does not encompass.
The flower blazes brilliantly, emitting great rays of light and colors equal to the void.

Suddenly, a voice spoke, saying: "The Tathāgata’s original great vow is to cause countless great bodhisattvas and all sentient beings to fully realize and enter the Vairocana Dharmakośa of True Suchness— the ocean of pure nature, the vajra-samādhi."
To swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect,
and complete enlightenment is the exceedingly rare and extraordinary dharma of the Tathāgata’s adamantine great wisdom;
therefore, the World-Honored One has spoken thus.
There are ten kinds of vajra-samādhis,
profound and sublime dharmas that are beyond measure and beyond analogy.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the entire great assembly of all the great bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
It should be known that all such Tathāgatas possess these various,
extraordinary, most rare, marvelous, and sublime dharmas;
these are the dharmas of all Buddhas, the Tathāgatas.
In previous lives, he practiced the secret thirty-fold dharma-teaching of the Vajra-samādhi for the sake of the three types of awakening;
through the power of the unsurpassed fruit and the great wisdom of noble insight, he accomplished all the Buddha-dharma teachings of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"May all sentient beings fully awaken and attain perfect enlightenment.
For this reason, the Tathāgata spoke these words to Mañjuśrī:
"Thus, you should yourself proclaim this Buddha-vajra-samādhi for the sake of all sentient beings.
Mañjuśrī then withdrew from the presence of the Holy One.
Not daring to speak of the holy teaching himself before the Tathāgata, at that time the World-Honored One accepted Mañjuśrī’s self-proclamation and addressed him, saying:
"Mañjuśrī, in the past..."
For the sake of all sentient beings throughout the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*),
one should cause them to give rise to the mind of unexcelled, perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
How does one practice and maintain the Tathāgata’s Vajra Samādhi?
This teaching is most rare and extraordinary;
it cannot be compared, cannot be fully described, and cannot be measured.
Then, at that time, the World-Honored One spoke again to Mañjuśrī:
You should, within this great assembly, personally proclaim to all the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and to all sentient beings your own original causes,
great vows, noble practices, and the meritorious adornments of your buddha-field and pure land.
When all the great bodhisattvas have attained awakening,
may they hear this profound, wondrous Dharma and its supreme meaning from you.
Mañjuśrī again addressed the Tathāgata, saying to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One, with your great compassion, look down upon me and grant me your pity;
if you permit me to speak, I shall do so."
The World-Honored One replied, "I shall grant your request.
At that time, Mañjuśrī, in the presence of the Tathāgata and before the great assembly,
entered the samādhi of the Vajra-samādhi.

With unimpeded divine vision, they clearly perceive all the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, great Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, and all worthy sages throughout the unspeakably unspeakable number of Buddha-fields and worlds, as numerous as the atoms in the trichiliocosm, in the ten directions.
In this way, all these Buddhas and Bodhisattvas have been fully transformed and delivered by Mañjuśrī to attain Buddhahood,
enabling them to realize *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

At that time, the great assembly of all bodhisattvas and all sentient beings likewise simultaneously beheld the manifestation of Mañjuśrī’s holy virtue in transforming and saving, appearing as all the Buddhas.
At that time, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni addressed the great assembly, saying:
"It was not I who exhorted you to resolve upon Bodhicitta;
it was entirely due to the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī."
In the past, they exhorted others to resolve upon Bodhicitta,
causing them all to attain fulfillment and achieve Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, such that they all became Buddhas. At that time,
the great assembly praised them with one voice, saying:
They praised the Great Sage Mañjuśrī,
who has long planted the roots of virtue to guide all sentient beings;
the great assembly deeply revered Mañjuśrī’s inconceivable and incomparable nature.
Furthermore, at another time, Mañjuśrī was among the great assembly.
He again prostrated himself and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"I have a great vow; I further pray that the Tathāgata will grant me his empowerment."
Now, before the World-Honored One,
without rising from my seat, I shall use an emanation body to pervade Buddha-lands as numerous as the atoms within the worlds of the ten directions.
For the sake of all sentient beings and all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas,
he expounded the teaching on the samādhi of the gate of the three secrets of the Tathāgata’s Mahāyāna Yoga-Vajra.
I now manifest before the great assembly,
so that all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and all sentient beings may practice and enter this yoga-vajra-samādhi.
Those who have realized unsurpassed,
perfect enlightenment shall all fulfill their vows to attain Buddhahood in the future.
At that time, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva...
Within the assembly of the Tathāgata,
he manifests supernatural powers to extensively deliver the multitudes of beings throughout the dharma-realm of other directions,
in accordance with the truth and non-falsity of his previously made vows.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Siṃhavikrāntagāminigarjitasvara rose from his seat in the midst of the assembly,
prostrated before the World-Honored One, and knelt with his right knee on the ground.
With palms joined in reverence toward the Buddha,
he addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"Mañjuśrī’s universal vow for the future."
When all bodhisattvas and all sentient beings attain Buddhahood,
Mañjuśrī, you shall likewise come to become a Buddha;
what will be the name of that Buddha?
May all sentient beings attain the fruit of Buddhahood.
Mañjuśrī, what is the name of the title by which you become a Buddha?
What is your epithet?
Then the Bodhisattva Siṃhavikrāmin, standing before the Tathāgata,
addressed Mañjuśrī:
"O Benevolent One, for the sake of this great assembly..."
Regarding those who speak of the names of the Buddhas to be realized in the future, what do you think, Mañjuśrī-vāg-siṃha Bodhisattva?
"Cease, cease! There is no need to speak."
I now dare not, in the presence of the Tathāgata,
speak for myself regarding the name by which I shall become a Buddha in the future.
Mañjuśrī has spoken repeatedly, yet I still dare not speak of it myself.
At that time, the Tathāgata addressed the great assembly of all bodhisattvas and all sentient beings,
saying to the Bodhisattva Siṃhavikrama:
"Good son, I now declare before this great assembly that Mañjuśrī shall,
throughout immeasurable kalpas to come, guide and lead all sentient beings."
In the future, when he attains Buddhahood,
he shall be named the Tathāgata Samantadarśin;
likewise, all sentient beings shall also attain Buddhahood in the future.
Their names are also identical to those of that Buddha.

Why is this? Because the Tathāgata Samantadarśin possesses his own power of aspiration, which universally causes sentient beings, as numerous as the atoms of the ten directions, [to attain enlightenment].
Those who call my name shall obtain universal vision;
once they have obtained this vision,
they will do so without the need for further effort.
When the defilements of sin are naturally and certainly extinguished,
one shall then attain universal Buddhahood,
receiving the name Tathāgata Samantadarśin.
Therefore, all good sons, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, should vow to have deep faith and not harbor any doubts.
If you are free from doubt, you will receive the assistance and protection of all the Buddhas of the ten directions.
He stroked his crown with his hand, and as he cultivated and realized bodhi,
the Tathāgata then addressed the Bodhisattva Siṃhavikrāmin:
"If there be any sentient beings..."
It is impossible that anyone would not believe these words;
such a person has recently emerged from hell.
In previous lives, they must have been born with the bodies of those who are blind, deaf, or mute.
For what reason? Because from lifetime to lifetime they shall not behold a Buddha;
they will constantly fall into the hells or take birth as animals, cycling through the four realms of existence without rest.
Such a person cannot be instructed nor can they be taught with loyalty.
At that time, the entire great assembly heard the Tathāgata speak of the benefits of the Tathāgata Samantadarśin’s attainment of Buddhahood.
The merit of all sentient beings is perfected and their power of fortune is exceedingly great.
The great assembly felt profound shame and remorse;
with sincere faith, they yearned for and accepted what the World-Honored One had spoken.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī again addressed the World-Honored One before the great assembly, saying:
"I have now made a vow from the very beginning."
Whether I am in the world or have entered parinirvāṇa,
if there are sentient beings or any bodhisattvas who invoke the name of the Tathāgata Samantadarśin, [they shall all attain supreme perfect enlightenment].
Furthermore, for those who recollect my name,
all grave offenses as well as the slandering of the Vaipulya sutras shall be completely extinguished;
even the offenses of icchantikas, without exception, shall all be utterly eradicated.
All shall surely attain Buddhahood.
What Mañjuśrī has spoken is indeed not false;
the entire great assembly all believe and accept it.
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha once more, saying:
"Now I have yet another great vow:
when I practice for enlightenment together with all sentient beings,"
Within my buddha-field, as for all bodhisattvas and all sentient beings who are born into my world,
at the time of their initial birth,
they shall have the four requisites of clothing, food and drink, and bedding.
Whatever was required emerged from his hands as soon as it was thought of;
having thus produced these garments, food, drink, and bedding, he took them.
First, one should make offerings to all the Buddhas, Tathāgatas, and Bodhisattvas;
only thereafter should one enjoy it oneself.
At that time, Mañjuśrī had finished recounting his own original vows.
All bodhisattvas and all sentient beings will give rise to profound and sincere faith;
they shall then believe, accept, take refuge in, and practice it.
Therefore, O Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Siṃhavikrāntaghoṣa, [you should do so].
I further and most earnestly entreat the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, to speak:
in the future age of the final dharma,
by what should one act and how should one practice?
The World-Honored One addressed Siṃhavikrama:
"I shall analyze and explain this for you.
Son of good family, in a future age..."
At the time when the Dharma of the Buddha is about to perish during the final kalpa of Jambudvīpa,
if there are any bodhisattvas or any sentient beings who,
from the beginning, have made offerings of the seven precious treasures, food, drink, banners, and canopies;
If one were to perform various kinds of offerings for a thousand kalpas to the stupas,
temples, relics, and images of the Buddhas throughout worlds as numerous as the atoms in seven koṭis of Ganges Rivers in the ten directions;
If there are bodhisattvas and all sentient beings who study the teachings, practices, and vows of the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī,
they shall walk for seven steps.
The measure of the merit and benefits received from this is incalculable,
extraordinary, and beyond compare;
it surpasses the merit of a bodhisattva who makes offerings to the stūpas and temples of seven koṭis of Buddhas.
A hundredth part does not equal it, nor can it be reached even by calculation or analogy. Why is this?
It is because the World-Honored One has manifested this for the sake of the great assembly.
The merit of practicing and learning the conduct and vows of Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva is exceedingly great;
it is most supreme, transcendent, immeasurable, and boundless.
Why is this? Because Mañjuśrī is the Vajra Mother of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas.
Therefore, from the diamond-like Prajñāpāramitā body and mind of Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva,
all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are born;
for this reason, the World-Honored One spoke of all Bodhisattvas.
The merit and power of the blessings and vows from practicing the conduct of Mañjuśrī are exceedingly great;
they surpass the merit of the former bodhisattvas’ offerings. Why is this?
Because those who make offerings to the precious stūpa [attain such merit].
This is what is called the mind with outflows (sāsrava-citta).
Such merits are limited and finite.
However, if a bodhisattva practices and studies the secret teachings on the conduct and vows of Mañjuśrī, [the merit will be immeasurable].
Thus, one cultivates the Tathāgata’s vajra-like, untainted mind, which is infinite and immeasurable.
For this reason, one swiftly transcends to the Buddha-ground and attains the Dharma-body of all Buddhas.
At that time, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni spoke of the past cultivation of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī,
instructing all bodhisattvas and all sentient beings.
They cultivate and study the merit of great vows;
their noble power and noble nature are preeminent and beyond compare.
At that time, the entire assembly of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas...
The disciples of the four assemblies— the sons and daughters of good family—
all rejoiced, believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.
Next, one should speak of all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
By the power of the merit and dharmas realized through the cultivation of noble wisdom,
at that time, Śākyamuni Tathāgata was within the great assembly at the site of practice in the Jeta Grove Monastery.
He addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Siṃhavikrāntagāminigarjitasvara:
"I entrust to you, in the presence of this great assembly of bodhisattva mahāsattvas,
the aforementioned teachings on the Vajra-Bodhi Samādhi of all Buddhas of the three periods of time."
It is entrusted to Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva;
he shall serve as the leader for the sixteen great bodhisattvas and transmit it to all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
And for all sentient beings,
may they realize the empowerment of the Tathāgata’s noble power,
and advance in the cultivation of the samādhi of the true nature of reality (dharmatā) of the Vajra Three Mysteries of all Tathāgatas, according to the sūtra teachings.
Furthermore, regarding those who cultivate the contemplation of the noble nature of the Tathāgata,
Siṃhavikrāmin asked:
"What is called the Sūtra Teaching on the Samādhi of the Real Characteristic and the Dharma-nature?"
"What is meant by 'contemplating the noble nature of the Tathāgata'?
Then Siṃhavikrama and all the bodhisattvas together prostrated themselves before the Tathāgata and addressed the World-Honored One."
Please analyze and explain this for us;
so that we bodhisattvas and all sentient beings throughout the ages from remote antiquity may rely upon the Tathāgata’s teachings.
Those who advance in the study and uphold the teachings of the *Sarvabuddha-āryajñāna-dharmatā-yoga-vajra-guhya-samādhi-sūtra*,
as well as those who practice the contemplation of the noble nature (*ārya-dhātu*) of the Tathāgata.
The Buddha addressed Siṃhavikrama and the others:
"This sutra is the root of all Mahāyāna sūtras of all Buddhas; it is the teaching of the Samādhi of the Secret Dharma-nature of all scriptures."
"You should uphold this and practice it with diligence.
At that time, the Tathāgata, together with the entire great assembly and all the bodhisattvas,
having spoken this sūtra— the secret Dharma-nature sūtra which is the root of all sūtras— concluded his teaching.
At that moment, all worlds and Jambudvīpa suddenly became vast,
magnificent, pure, and transformed into the color of gold.
In the sky, the fragrance of a hundred precious sandalwoods wafted forth.
Fragrant breezes blew through the trees and flocks of birds sang in harmony,
all producing sounds like the chanting of *brahman* hymns;
at that time, such auspicious signs appeared.
"Extraordinary and marvelous, never before seen in the world of Buddhas," the World-Honored One then addressed Siṃhavikrama and the others:
"You should uphold this teaching of the sūtra as spoken by the Tathāgata."
The entire great assembly, including Siṃhavikrānta and all the bodhisattvas,
felt inconceivable awe and remorse, wondering:
"How shall we uphold and practice this sutra exactly as it has been taught?"
At that time, the World-Honored One then taught this fundamental scripture of the Mahāyāna—
the Yoga Secret Vajra Samādhi of all Buddhas— for the sake of Siṃhavikrama and all the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
Regarding the tenets and essence of this sūtra,
there are two gates in total.
How are the tenets and essence of this sūtra explained?
There are two gates: first, taking the pure real mark (*śuddha-lakṣaṇa*) as the thesis;
second, taking the *tathatā*-dharmadhātu as the essence.
What is meant by taking the pure real mark as the thesis?
The fundamental root of this discourse on the sūtra has three aspects.
First, the intrinsic nature of Vairocana’s dharmakāya is fundamentally pure;
its central tenet is the emergence of all phenomena from the vajra-samādhi.
Second is the *saṃbhogakāya* of Vairocana,
which takes as its primary principle the power of the vows and practices of the noble nature of Samantabhadra.
Third is the manifestation of the thousand Śākyamunis, wherein the hundreds of thousands of millions of Śākyamunis manifest the body of noble wisdom.
The primary thesis is that the body of Mañjuśrī flows forth to act as the mother of Prajñā;
this shall be explained in due order.
Second, how is the essence of this sūtra described?
The Tathāgata has the true suchness (tathatā) of the dharma-realm as its essence.
What do you think? There are five fundamental holy bodies:
first, the essence is the vajra-nature of holy wisdom, which is the pure self-nature of the original source.
Second, its essence is the vajra of bodhicitta, the great perfect nature-mirror that is immovable.
Third, its essence is the vajra-dharmadhātu of equality.
Fourth, its essence is the vajra of the noble power of wisdom and activity, which observes the principle according to its true nature.
Fifth, it is accomplished as the essence of the vajra-wisdom sword of the noble nature of bodhi,
as described above.
All bodhisattvas should therefore cultivate and study this with sincere resolve to swiftly realize the stage of Buddhahood.
Therefore, having explained the essential nature of the Tathāgata, one must now consider:
what is called the Tathāgata’s contemplation of all noble natures?
If a bodhisattva practices this contemplation of all noble natures of the Tathāgata, [how should they do so?]
The World-Honored One has taught that all bodhisattvas and all sentient beings face ten kinds of great obstacles that bind the body and mind.
If one can cultivate and maintain the contemplation of the noble nature, [these obstacles will be overcome].
First, one must recognize that the essential nature of the mind-ground is bound by ignorance;
if this is not recognized, the nature of the mind will be obscured and covered,
such that the eye of noble wisdom cannot open.
As for the nature of these fetters,
they are extremely subtle obstacles.
Prior to [attaining] Bodhi, one should first recognize the ten kinds of mental fetters.
Regarding those whose bodies and minds are obstructed by great difficulties,
how may they attain penetration and advance toward the cultivation of unsurpassed bodhi?
If a bodhisattva currently practices contemplative cultivation:
One must receive the Dharma from a master ācārya and definitively resolve the ten kinds of fetters that bind body and mind,
thereby swiftly attaining the noble nature and awakening to bodhi.
One should then cultivate and attain the power of the Tathāgata’s noble wisdom and noble nature,
observing and penetrating until one realizes the Bodhi-vajra liberation and the Dharmakāya of the Tathāgata.
What are called the ten kinds of fetters?
First, due to an innate nature of stinginess and envy,
their minds are constantly ensnared, fettered, and obscured,
causing their minds to hold wrong views and preventing them from attaining right awakening.
This is called the obstruction of entanglement.
Second, there is the obstruction caused by being shrouded by the shadows of ignorance;
the eye of wisdom is difficult to open because it is covered and obscured by delusive confusion.
This is called the hindrance of entanglement.
Third is the confusion and delusion of afflictions— namely greed, hatred, and false views—
which cause one to be fixated on various things and unable to believe in what is correct.
Falling into the pit of ignorance and being deeply attached to the worldly net is called "entanglement and obstruction.
Fourth, the swift current of craving for the five desires flows constantly.
The afflictions and hindrances delude the mind, their defilements heavy and binding;
one is swept away by ignorance without any prospect of respite.
This is called the obstruction of entanglement.
Fifth, the Mara of sensory flavors continues through the succession of death without ceasing;
struck by the arrow of perversion, one meets an untimely end in the prime of life.
This is called the obstacle of entanglement.
Sixth, one is scorched by the dense smoke of anger and resentment;
the eye of the mind is thereby obscured and obstructed.
This is called the obstacle of entanglement.
Seventh, they are constantly scorched by the blazing fire of craving;
with the hearts of tigers and wolves, they lunge and snatch from all four directions.
This is called being bound by body and mind and obstructed by ignorance.
Eighth, drinking the intoxicating wine that stupefies evil Māras, their minds are overwhelmed;
consuming the poisonous medicine of transgressions, they are deluded and run about wildly.
This is called being bound and obstructed in body and mind.
Ninth, being constantly obstructed by the afflictions of the five hindrances,
one’s mind of right wisdom is shrouded and difficult to liberate;
this is called being bound in fetters and unable to attain awakening.
Tenth, there is the great river of the ocean of suffering,
where the six realms and four modes of birth revolve through the five destinies without interruption;
with stinginess and greed dwelling in the mind, one constantly suffers from famine.
They pass from birth into death and fall into the hells without end.
This is called being bound and unable to attain liberation.
Therefore, these are the ten kinds of entanglements.
Obscuring the body and mind, it creates obstacles that hinder practice,
preventing one from realizing the fruit of Bodhi and Buddhahood.
Thus, this teaching [is intended for] all Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas and all sentient beings.
One cultivates the contemplation of the noble nature of the Tathāgata’s bodhi.
How does one realize this contemplation of the noble nature?
The Bodhisattva, with sincere resolve, practices the three natures and three non-natures of the mind-ground.
Having removed the obscurations of delusion and the ten envelopments that shroud and conceal [the mind], one attains liberation.
The Tathāgata shall now fully explain the cultivation and realization [of this].
There are three general meanings for opening up the ground of the mind (cittabhūmi).
First, the three natures and the three absences of nature;
second, the arising of wisdom is the function of insight;
third, when the mind moves, the mind’s eye sees.
What are the three meanings?
First, regarding the nature of the thoroughly imagined (parikalpita-svabhāva):
when subtle awakening-wisdom arises within the nature of pure consciousness, this is the function of wisdom (prajñā).

When the function of wisdom illuminates the quiescence of the thoroughly imagined nature, then the function of knowledge is the realization of the quiescent illumination; the function of wisdom is thus quiescent extinction.
How, then, can the thoroughly imagined nature be extinguished?
If awakening-wisdom is characterized by non-arising, it is called realization;
when the function of wisdom is quiescent, then the nature of the parikalpita (imagined) is extinguished and purified.
How, then, does one realize the paratantra (dependent) and pariniṣpanna (perfected) natures?
Regarding the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*):
the mind arises entirely in dependence upon form.
Regarding the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*): [it is the absence of duality].
There is nothing upon which it relies; the nature of mind has no point of attachment.
Contemplating with true insight, the nature of mind is translucent and pure;
it is quiescent and unmoving, its nature like lapis lazuli.
When the internal and external are luminously pure, this is called seeing the nature of reality as immovable.
When the mind realizes tranquility, it is called the three natures and the three non-natures.
If a bodhisattva practices and realizes this, [they attain liberation].
One attains the three natures of the Tathāgata.
For the noble-natured practitioner who contemplates these, the ten kinds of fetters are removed and they are spontaneously liberated;
thus, they swiftly reach the primordial source, the intrinsically pure bodhi and nirvāṇa.
Therefore, this entire great assembly—
including all the great bodhisattva-mahāsattvas,
the fourfold disciples, and the sons and daughters of good family— [should listen].
Having heard what the Buddha had spoken, they were filled with joy and leaped for gladness, attaining what they had never experienced before; they accepted it with faith and practiced accordingly.
*The Mahāyāna Yoga Sūtra of the Ocean of Vajra-Nature Mañjuśrī with a Thousand Arms and a Thousand Bowls, the Great King of Teachings*, Fascicle One.
*The Mahāyāna Yoga Sūtra of the Ocean of Vajra-Nature Mañjuśrī with a Thousand...*
The Sūtra of the Great King of Teachings, the Thousand-Bowl Arm, Scroll Two.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master and Śramaṇa Amoghavajra of Daxingshan Temple, by Imperial Decree.

Chapter Two: The Supreme Chapter on the Manifestation of All Buddhas and the Realization and Cultivation of Vajra Bodhi. Second, the second chapter explaining the manifestation of all Buddhas and the realization and cultivation of Vajra Bodhi: At that time, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni...
He addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying:
"I now entreat all the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas,
to empower all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas through their holy power."
One should cultivate the samādhi-vision of the dharma of the three secrets and the three types of awakening of all Tathāgatas,
causing the minds of all bodhisattvas to become equal to the nature of space and like the dharma-dhātu.
To extensively deliver sentient beings and inexhaustible living creatures;
and furthermore, to cause the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī,
together with all bodhisattvas and all sentient beings, [to attain this].
Acting as a leader,
the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī then addressed the World-Honored One and the assembly of bodhisattvas, saying:
If there are any bodhisattvas or any sentient beings who aspire to seek unsurpassed enlightenment and practice all dharmas of the true Buddha-vajra-sacred-nature samādhi, [they shall attain it].
All phenomena are precisely the minds of all sentient beings;
they constitute the Dharma-treasury within the mental ground of sentient beings,
wherein exists the seed-nature of afflictions.
That the nature of afflictions is itself the nature of bodhi means that the fundamental nature within the minds of sentient beings is truly pure,
empty, and unattainable.
Therefore, the mind of sentient beings is the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom; this is the locus of that wisdom.
Bodhisattvas direct their aspiration toward the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom and apply diligent effort to contemplate and illuminate it.
When the nature of mind awakens to and realizes cessation,
one immediately attains the awakening of the mirror-like clarity of the mind.
Through this crystalline purity, one penetrates emptiness and thus realizes the wisdom of equality within the mind.
One who realizes the wisdom of equality thoroughly awakens to and penetrates the fact that the nature and fundamental essence are truly empty;
they realize and enter the mind within emptiness.
When the nature of each and every mind is realized as the ground of the essence of suchness,
it is called "entering the wisdom of suchness," which is the realization of the *pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna* (wisdom of wondrous observation).
One attains the pure noble wisdom of suchness-nature;
one obtains the vajra wisdom of all-accomplishing action;
and one realizes the nature of bodhi, thereby perfecting noble wisdom.
Therefore, this is called the profound penetrating wisdom of the four types of bodhi-knowledge.
Entering the vajra-samādhi of the heart-mind of all Buddhas and corresponding with noble wisdom is called the thirty branches of mudrās and seals of the yoga of the three mysteries.
Through the empowerment of the ten branches of the samādhi of body-secret,
one purifies the body-faculty and realizes the noble power of the wisdom of the body-nature.
When the ten branches of samādhi of the oral secret empowerment are sustained and the wisdom of contemplative insight is purified in the mind,
then through the empowerment of the holy power, the ten branches of samādhi of the mental secret empowerment become tranquil.
Then the ground of the secret intention is purified;
it is the true purity of suchness.
It is the seal of the realization of nature, the samādhi of non-empty noble wisdom, the diamond-like concentration (vajropama-samādhi), and the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body.
Because those who accomplish such secret teachings cause all the great bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and all sentient beings to study and train in these instructions,
entering into yoga and practicing the Buddha’s vajra-samādhi— the dharma-teaching of the three mysteries of enlightenment.
Because they had entered the samādhi of the dharma-realm and the boundless samādhi of the ocean of the noble nature,
at that time, among the great assembly of bodhisattvas,
there were only sixteen great beings, the Great Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas.
Together with the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī,
they shared the same vows and practices to cultivate and realize the Mahāyāna Yoga Vajra Three Mysteries Bodhi Samādhi, along with all others,
such as the Bodhisattvas of the Ten Stages of Faith and Bhadrapāla.

The assembly of śrāvakas, such as Śāriputra and others, do not share the same mind as Mañjuśrī, which is equal to the nature of space and as vast as the dharmadhātu in its universal deliverance of sentient beings; this distinguishes them from the various bodhisattvas and śrāvakas.
With a narrow mind and limited wisdom, their aspirations were inferior;
only after eighty billion *koṭi-nayuta* hundreds of thousands of *kalpas* had passed did they begin to fulfill the five *pāramitās* while practicing the bodhisattva path.
At that time, Mañjuśrī, together with sixteen great beings, benevolent bodhisattvas mahāsattvas,
made vast and magnificent vows three times before the Tathāgata and the great assembly.
May we, together with the sixteen virtuous ones, the Great Being Bodhisattva Samantabhadra and the rest,
have minds equal to space, universally delivering sentient beings as extensively as the realm of space.
Furthermore, may all sentient beings [attain liberation].
May I share in my own inexhaustible great vows;
I shall rescue them without ceasing.
Furthermore, I have a great vow: may it be shared by us Bodhisattvas, as well as our bodies and minds.
Pervading the dharma-realm like the great void, it is without obstruction.

With his wisdom-body and reward-body, he constantly vows to manifest before the nine classes of sentient beings within the six realms and four modes of birth—those born from wombs, eggs, moisture, or transformation.
I constantly manifest this body before all sentient beings.
May they see my form so that their obstacles are immediately extinguished,
and may I cause all sentient beings to give rise to the bodhicitta.
Turning toward the Mahāyāna Yoga Secret [Mantra],
one cultivates bodhicitta and swiftly transcends to the stage of Buddhahood.
For this reason, O Lion-Valiant Bodhisattva, [it is taught].
Prostrating before the Tathāgata, he addressed the World-Honored One:
"As the Tathāgata has previously declared, you have caused Mañjuśrī,
along with all bodhisattvas and all sentient beings, to become supreme leaders who guide others in the cultivation of unsurpassed bodhi."
"How does one practice the Vajra-samādhi visualization of the three gates of secret mantra yoga?
At that time, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva [taught] for the sake of Siṃha Bodhisattva and the other sixteen great beings."
Regarding the sequential practice of the Tathāgata’s secret accomplishment of the contemplation of all vajra-bodhi:
how does one perform the empowerment of the contemplation of bodhi through the practice of the sixteen great beings?
How may one also come to see and hear the sixteen bodhisattvas, such as Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra,
as well as the secret transmission and empowerment of the primordial, adamantine, and most excellent names and the practice of bodhicitta?
Through the cultivation and study of all bodhisattvas, sentient beings, and living creatures, they shall all attain buddhahood.
What is the original sequence of these names?
Why is it that by hearing and beholding the sublime names of these sixteen bodhisattvas, [such results are attained]?
How are the sixteen great beings, the bodhisattvas, named?
First is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Samantabhadra of the eastern direction,
whose name is Vajrapāṇi.
I prostrate to the Tathāgata Vairocana for the sake of all sentient beings.
May he empower all sentient beings, causing them to enter the samādhi of all Vajrasattvas.
Because it is wondrously firm and stable, one realizes and enters the adamantine true nature of the pure *dharmakāya* of all Tathāgatas,
thereby transforming ethical discipline, meditative concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation.
He forms the Vajradharmacakra,
benefiting all sentient beings and causing all Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas to cultivate and enter the contemplation of the Buddha-mind.
Second is the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva King of Non-Emptiness,
known as Vajra-Akarṣaṇa (Vajra Hook Summoner),
who has entered samādhi of his own accord.
Having realized the heart-mind of Vairocana Buddha,
he brought forth the Great Hook-summoning Seal of all Tathāgatas,
and invoked all Tathāgatas to manifest their supernormal powers.
From the form of the great vajra hook,
there appear the bodhisattva mahāsattvas who empower all worlds.
They cause all bodhisattvas to cultivate and enter the *tathatā* (suchness) contemplation of the *dharmakāya-bodhi* of as many Buddhas and Tathāgatas as there are atoms in the dust.
Third is the Mahāsattva Mahābodhisattva Māra.
Known by the name Vajracāpa,
he entered samādhi and realized the heart-mind of Vairocana Buddha.
Abiding in the supreme siddhi of the Tathāgata’s great, pure karma of Māra,
one accomplishes the Vajra-Bodhi-Arrow and swiftly enters the noble nature and noble power of the Tathāgata.
He empowered the nature and wisdom of the bodies and minds of all bodhisattvas,
removed all obstacles, and entered the contemplation of the reality-nature of swift vajra-bodhi.
Fourth is the Great Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Supreme Joy King, named Vajraprītipāla.
Having entered samādhi,
he realized entry into the heart-mind of Vairocana Buddha,
becoming one and the same essence with him.
Emanating forms of the *pramuditā-pāramitā* as numerous as motes of dust,
they empower all bodhisattvas,
who enter the wisdom of the contemplation of emptiness— the selfless essence of the Vajrabodhisattva.
Fifth is the foremost Great Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva of the South, the Empty Space Treasury (Ākāśagarbha),
whose name is Vajragarbharāja;
he has himself entered into samādhi.
He realizes entry into the Vairocana Buddha-mind, the nature of the Vajra-treasury;
he brings forth the precious treasury of the space-dharmadhātu of all Tathāgatas,
giving birth to the form of the sublime vajra-jewel.
Emanating the light of samādhi from all Buddhas and Tathāgatas as numerous as atoms,
it empowers all Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas,
causing them to enter and cultivate the dharma-contemplation of emptiness within the Vajra-Bodhicitta-cakra Samādhi.
Sixth was the Great Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva of Great Majestic Virtue and Radiance,
whose name was Vajraprabha;
he entered samādhi of his own accord.
He entered the heart of Vairocana Buddha,
emerged from the samādhi of the Vajra Sun-Disk of all Tathāgatas,
and empowered all Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
They cause them to enter and cultivate the Buddha-samādhi of the Three Mysteries of Vajra,
whereby they attain the realization of the single-nature contemplation of the solar-wheel Bodhi.
Seventh is the Great Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Ratnaketu-maṇi.
Named Vajradhvaja,
he entered samādhi and realized the heart-mind of Vairocana Buddha.
He brought forth the holy power of the Vajra Secret Dharma Treasury of all Tathāgatas and empowered all Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas,
causing them to enter the Samādhi of the Vajra Supreme Banner Treasure Treasury.
To cause all bodhisattvas to realize the mindless contemplation of the Buddha-nature within the nirvana of the Immovable Ground;
eighth, [to cause] the great bodhisattva-mahāsattvas to be constantly joyful.
Named Vajraprītijñāna,
he entered samādhi and realized the heart-mind of Vairocana Buddha.
Manifesting a joyful expression with a vajra smile,
he empowered all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas,
causing them to cultivate and realize the samādhi of entering the true nature of the vajra joy of all tathāgatas.
He causes all bodhisattvas to realize and enter the contemplation of the vajra-reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi), which is the purity of the nature of delight.
Ninth is the Great Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, the foremost king in the western direction.
Named Vajranetra,
from the moment he entered samādhi,
he realized the self-nature pure body of the heart-mind of Vairocana Buddha.
There emerge from it as many Buddhas, Tathāgatas, as there are atoms;
they cause all sentient beings to abide in samādhi, becoming of one and the same essence.
Equal in measure to the dharma-realm and pervading all of space,
it arises as a great lotus in the form of a vajra-jewel, like the empty dharma-realm.
From that vajra-lotus form...
He gave rise to the noble power of mastery over the supernormal knowledge of the samādhi of the holy wisdom of the vajra-nature of all Tathāgatas,
and empowered all the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas within all buddha-fields as numerous as atoms.
[He taught] the contemplation of the pure land through the compassionate mind of all Buddhas and the sovereign spiritual power that causes entry into the nature of the noble ones.
Tenth was the Great Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī,
titled King of Consecration (*Abhiṣeka-rāja*) and Vajra Wisdom (*Vajraprajñā*).
Since entering the Śūraṅgama Samādhi,
he has realized entry into the Buddha-mind of Vairocana Tathāgata,
becoming one and the same essence with him.
The sovereign nature of the Noble Ones gives birth to as many prajñāpāramitā wisdoms as there are atoms;
it produces the form of the prajñā sword of vajra-wisdom, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River.
He realized the entry into the single nature of the vajra wisdom-sword of all Tathāgatas,
and empowered the great Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas in as many Buddha-fields as there are atoms.
One cultivates entry into the vajra-samādhi of all Tathāgatas;
realizing the sword of vajra-wisdom, one brandishes it to strike away and extinguish the afflictions and karmic obstructions of all sentient beings,
thereby bringing all sentient beings to fulfillment.
They cultivate and realize the contemplation of unsurpassed, perfect,
and complete enlightenment. Eleventh is the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Great Being Wondrous Wisdom Dharma-Wheel,
whose name is Vajramaṇḍala.
Having entered the Samādhi of the Wheel of the Dharma-nature,
he realized and entered the Samādhi of the Ocean of the Dharma-nature of the Mind-Wheel of Vairocana Buddha;
he became one with the Samādhi of the Vajra Realm of the Dharmadhātu and the Wisdom-Wheel of the Single Essence of the Vajra-Sage Nature of all Tathāgatas.
There emerged from [the heart] as many Tathāgatas as there are atoms in all Buddha-fields;
they empowered all Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas,
causing them to enter the great maṇḍala and receive empowerment.
One realizes the noble nature associated with the samādhi of the three secrets of yoga, attaining equal supernormal powers and mastery through noble strength;
one cultivates and realizes the contemplation of the dharmatā-dharmacakra-samādhi.
Twelfth is the Noble Great Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Nameless Intent;
his name is Vajra Holy Speech, who has personally entered the Samādhi of the Signlessness of All-Lettered Prajñā.
One realizes entry into the Vairocana Buddha-mind, the vajra-dharmatā,
becoming one body with it,
and emerges from the state of the secret samādhi-recitation of all Tathāgatas.
He gives birth to the vajra-dharmatā-bodies of Tathāgatas as numerous as all atoms,
and empowers all the great Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas,
causing them to exert themselves.
They cultivate and realize the samādhi of the three mysteries and enter the contemplation of the dharmakāya, the buddha-nature, and the holy nature of the dharma-realm.
Thirteenth is the Great Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Viśvakarman, the foremost of the north.
He was named Vajraviśvakarmadharmacakrapravartana-rāja. Having entered samādhi, he realized and entered the heart of all Tathāgatas—
the Vairocana Buddha-mind— and the treasury of the bodhi-dharma of all Buddhas, which is utterly pure, free from affliction (māra), and profoundly tranquil.
Born in Buddha-fields as numerous as atoms of dust,
all the World-Honored Tathāgatas of Karma are collectively the true suchness Dharma-treasury of the ocean-like nature of all Buddhas, Vairocana Tathāgata.
He gives birth to all Vajrasattvas and Viśvakarmas,
accomplishing the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* of all Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas,
and causing all Bodhisattvas to contemplate their own nature within the ground of the mind.
He cultivated and realized the contemplation of the Vajrayoga Samādhi of Perfect Penetration into All Vajras— the mirror of the wisdom of all Buddhas and the three secrets—
and was the fourteenth, the Great Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Difficult-to-Vanquish Vigor Power.
Named the Empowerment of the Swift Power of Vajra Compassion,
he himself entered the samādhi of the ground of vajra-wisdom and realized the heart-mind of Vairocana Buddha.
Abiding in the samādhi of the nature of the three mysteries of the Tathāgata’s great adamantine secret traces, he became one body with the ocean of the nature of the Buddha’s firm armor;
from this, there emerged hundreds of thousands of forms of great adamantine armor.
Abiding within the palm of the Buddha’s hand,
from the form of the Vajra Armor arise all the buddha-fields,
as numerous as the atoms of all worlds, wherein the Tathāgatas protect all ritual protocols, rules, and vast activities.
Possessing the same sovereign power of the spiritual transformations of all Tathāgatas,
they empower all Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas,
enabling them to attain the path of practice through the diligence of invincible, holy power.

Fifteenth is the Great Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Sarvamārapramardaka, who swiftly realizes and rapidly enters the contemplation of the essential nature of the Tathāgata’s adamantine armor and perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Named Vajra-pratāpa,
he entered samādhi and realized the Buddha-mind of Vairocana Tathāgata, becoming one body and one nature with it.
The weapon of the great adamantine fangs emerges in the form of a vajra and rests within the palm of the Buddha;
from that adamantine fang-form, it proceeds.
One gives birth to the vajra-bodies of Tathāgatas as numerous as the atoms in all Buddha-worlds;
one performs all acts of subjugation and wrathful activity,
serving as the supernatural power and holy might of all Buddhas.
He empowers all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas,
establishing them within the world-system with the weapon of the adamantine fangs,
and subduing all celestial māras through his fierce wrath and terror.
And all the māras of innate afflictions,
so that all bodhisattvas may attain non-obstruction and cultivate the realization of the Tathāgata’s samādhi.
He causes entry into the swift vajra-contemplation of the three secrets of the self-nature of noble wisdom.
Sixteenth is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajramuṣṭidharmadhātumahārāja.
He is named Vajradhātu-dṛḍhapada.
Having entered the samādhi of the moon-disc, the heart, the pure self-nature, and the mirror of wisdom,
he enters the bodhi-stage of the Tathāgata-vajrasattva, the mind of all Buddhas.
All Tathāgatas from as many Buddha-fields as there are atoms in all Buddha-worlds empower all Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas,
causing them to cultivate and realize entry into the samādhi of the wisdom of universal equality.
Having realized the meaning of all dharmas, profound as vajra,
one accomplishes awakening and swiftly transcends into the nature of the wisdom-mirror of the Dharmakāya of all Tathāgatas, Vairocana.
Then one will see one's own body as identical in form to that of the Tathāgata,
realize entry into the nature of the Vajradhātu,
and achieve the five eyes of the Buddha who is the Dharma-wisdom body of all Tathāgatas.
At that time, the sixteen great beings, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas,
each spoke of their respective gateways of contemplation— the vajra-siddhi of all the Buddhas and Tathāgatas—
by which they accomplished anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
May all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and all sentient beings cultivate and realize the entry into the thirty-limbed samādhi of the Vajra Bodhicitta Contemplation, the gateway to the three secrets of yoga.
At that time, the world of Jambudvīpa suddenly became vast, expansive, and pure;
