Causing them to practice the bodhisattva path and guide sentient beings,
so that they may transport one another across [to liberation] and attain the fruit of Buddhahood;
then, suddenly and at that very moment, from within this assembly...
The five great virtuous beings, mahāpuruṣas,
emerged and approached the presence of the Buddha; having prostrated themselves with their heads at the feet of the World-Honored One,
they then uttered these words in a loud voice at that time.
Relying upon this Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva,
I am able to give rise to great vows and great practices to extensively deliver sentient beings;
my mind is like space, never ceasing.
Then, at that time, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī addressed them, saying:
"Great Beings, sons of good family,
you five benevolent great men."
You are able to set forth with me, practicing in accordance with our shared vows;
your minds are equal to space and the dharma-realm, inexhaustible,
and you are able to give rise to the practice of vast, extensive, and great vows.
"You who rescue and deliver all sentient beings and attain perfect enlightenment—
you are truly my son;
for I share the same mind as you, who possess the five virtues."
"To extensively deliver all sentient beings until the end of the future.
The five benevolent great men replied:
"We five benevolent ones share the same vow as Mañjuśrī."
Mañjuśrī then established the names for these five virtuous great beings;
at that time, there were five great virtuous beings.
One enters into awakening by means of these names.
What are the names established for the five benevolent Great Beings?

First is named Vairocana; second is named Akṣobhya; third is named Ratnasaṃbhava; fourth is named Avalokiteśvararāja; and fifth is named Amoghasiddhi. Thus, the names of the five benevolent Great Beings have been established.
At that time, the five benevolent ones were assigned to the five directions, each dwelling in a separate location.
In the world-system of the Samādhi of the Vajra-nature Ocean,
they guide sentient beings and transform the common people.
Therefore, it is thus.
Furthermore, the five benevolent ones again addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying:
"O Great Being, O Benevolent One, explain all dharmas to me, and explain my own mind."
"There is the fundamental purity of the self-nature of *tathatā*.
Regarding these two kinds of phenomena—whether they exist or do not exist—the Great Being, the virtuous Mañjuśrī, replied: 'They both exist and do not exist.'"
What are the two dharmas that are both existent and non-existent?
Regarding the first "both existent," there are again two kinds of meanings.
What are the two kinds of objects?
First is the grasping at a self, and second is the grasping at phenomena.
Regarding those who grasp at phenomena as a self:
The two meanings of attachment to a self and attachment to phenomena constitute obstacles and hindrances within that very self and those very phenomena.
Thus, regarding their emotional nature (*cittatā*),
the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), and all locations,
it is because the nature of wisdom (*prajñā*) cannot function with clarity and mastery.
Second, there are two meanings: the absence of attachment to a self and the absence of attachment to phenomena.
If a bodhisattva does not cling to these two—self and phenomena—then they will attain unimpeded penetration regarding both self and phenomena.
That is to say, because there is no imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva),
one attains the nature of wisdom that is luminously penetrating and characterized by sovereign function.
Regarding the second "also non-existent," there are again two meanings.
What are these two?
First, the suchness of mind;
second, the fundamental self-nature purity of the mind.
What is the first? It is the mind-as-suchness (*tathatā*).
To grasp suchness as having the characteristics of the conditioned is itself the fundamental root of clinging to a self-nature.
Because its intrinsic nature is defiled, it cannot attain purity;
because it possesses obstructions and hindrances in all places,
it gives rise to the afflictions of greed, hatred, and delusion.
Because the nature of the self is subject to suffering through the spontaneous bondage of arising and ceasing everywhere,
how is it that the second [point]— the mind— has a fundamental nature that is intrinsically pure,
naturally quiescent from the beginning, unobstructed, and unimpeded?
This is because True Suchness (*tathatā*), being unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), pervades all places and is identical to emptiness with the fundamental nature of innate purity (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*).
Therefore, its nature is equal to True Suchness and fundamentally pure.
Because the noble nature is empty of intrinsic identity,
it is neither bound nor liberated, being ultimately pure;
because its essential nature is quiescent.
Therefore, these five benevolent ones were great beings.
Upon hearing the teaching of the unsurpassed, perfectly true, and wondrous Dharma of Bodhi, their hearts were filled with great joy;
they immediately rose and prostrated themselves in worship.
Bowing their heads at the feet of the Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva,
those five virtuous men once again addressed the Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva with further questions.
O Benevolent One, please explain further for me the nature of my own mind and that of the Great Being,
the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī.
"And is it not the case that the mental nature and wondrous wisdom of all sentient beings are of one and the same nature?
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī replied:
My mind-nature, yours, that of the five benevolent ones,
and that of all sentient beings are equal and of one substance, without any distinction;
they are as pure as lapis lazuli, transparent and luminous both within and without.
There is neither increase nor decrease; all are equally pure.
Therefore, son of good family, you should believe this with earnest attention.
I now speak this again with emphasis for you and these five virtuous men.
"Therefore, your mental natures, wisdoms,
and those of all sentient beings are no different from mine.
Furthermore, the Great Being Mañjuśrī spoke to the five benevolent ones:
The Buddha said: "My mind has no master and my body has no location;
this is called the Mahāvajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā.
It is because the nature of body and mind is fully endowed with all dharmas."
It is also identical to the Tathāgata’s wisdom-body and dharma-body.
Why? Because the body and its nature are of one essence without distinction, eternally abiding in the *śūraṅgama-samādhi* and the samādhi of intrinsic nature.
Its nature is pure and transparently clear;
therefore, the Tathāgata says:
"Good son, it is also thus."
"O you five benevolent great beings, since you have established these names for yourselves,
how do you understand their meanings as they are explained according to those names?
First, the great being named Vairocana."
The perfection of the wisdom of the purity of body and mind is bodhi.
Second, the Great Being is named Akṣobhya;
his body and mind are immovable in nature and without marks.
The Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom and the Bodhi of Perfect Penetration are these.
Third, the Great Being is named Ratnasambhava;
the Wisdom of Equality and the Bodhi of the Single Tranquility and Single Nature are these.
Fourth is the Great Being named Avalokiteśvararāja.
His body and mind are pure, his wisdom is that of wondrous discernment, and his noble insight penetrates adamantine bodhi. This is he.
Fifth is the Great Being named Amoghasiddhi. His body,
mind, wisdom, and measure are equal to space, and his form is identical to the Dharma-realm.
The noble nature, noble wisdom, the all-accomplishing gnosis,
sovereign supernormal powers, the attainment of siddhi, and all aspects of awakening and liberation—
these are they. At that time, the Tathāgata spoke these words:
Just as the five benevolent great beings possess the nature of wisdom,
they must rely upon the Great Being, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, and his diamond-like *prajñā* wisdom to serve as the sovereign of body and mind,
thereby accomplishing the sacred wisdom-nature of all phenomena.
They are able to bring the body and mind of the five benevolent great men to maturity;
with the nature of wisdom perfectly luminous and the Dharma fully accomplished,
they are then able to realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Therefore, the Great Being Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī is able to bring to maturity the five benevolent great men and the five wisdom-vajra Prajñāpāramitās.
Because it is the vajra-bodhi of the nature of the five wisdoms common to all Buddhas.
At that time, Mañjuśrī again addressed the Tathāgata, saying:
"The nature of the holy wisdom of the body and mind of the great Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas is of one and the same essence."
Likewise, he is of one essence with the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas,
whose pure wisdom of body and mind is of a single substance;
he is also of one essence with the devas and the Great Brahmā Kings, whose pure wisdom of body and mind is of a single substance.
Likewise, the bodies and minds of the eight classes of dragon deities and all sentient beings are identical in their nature of pure wisdom;
this wisdom is pure and without distinction.
It is just like rock crystal, which is transparent and luminous both inside and out without any difference;
it is primordially pure, the true suchness of self-nature,
tranquil, unconditioned, and characterized by non-attainment.
Therefore, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni addressed the Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī, saying:
"Excellent, excellent! Because you have skillfully expounded and skillfully understood the dharmas of the vajra-samādhi of all Buddhas, you are now a truly auspicious Great Being."
They bring all sentient beings to the realization of unsurpassed bodhi,
and they themselves, like all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas,
also attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, the great assembly addressed Mañjuśrī, saying:
"By practicing what teachings and by studying what meanings of the Dharma?"
The Great Being Mañjuśrī bowed his head to the Tathāgata and said:
“I now constantly practice the Mahāyāna Yoga Great Teaching, the Secret Vajra Samādhi Contemplation consisting of thirty branches.”
Furthermore, all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas,
and Mahāsattvas likewise study and practice according to this teaching,
thereby achieving accomplishment and realizing *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The Great Being Mañjuśrī said:
"If there should be all the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and the fourfold assembly,
as well as sons and daughters of good family,"
In the future final age, during the period of the Semblance Dharma,
those who encounter this Great Yoga Teaching— the secret samādhi method of the gateway of the three mysteries—
possess merit that is immeasurable and incalculable.
It is beyond the reach of calculation or analogy.
Such a person must have planted various roots of goodness under immeasurable Buddhas in past lives in order to encounter this teaching.
"May they swiftly realize unsurpassed bodhi.
What kind of person may encounter this teaching on the yoga of the secret samādhi?
The Great Being Mañjuśrī replied:
In the future final age,
if there are bodhisattvas and the fourfold assembly, or any sons and daughters of good family,
who are able to eliminate the notion of a self, the notion of a person, the notion of a sentient being, and the notion of a life-span.
Those who are able to endure the world with a mind of loyalty, filial piety,
and humility shall encounter this Yoga Vajra Secret Samādhi Dharma Teaching.
Such persons are capable of relinquishing body and life in their quest for Bodhi.
The sinful karma of these beings from previous lives shall be extinguished;
by gradually practicing and training, they shall attain Buddhahood.
Why, then, would sentient beings not encounter [this teaching]?
They shall not see the Buddha nor hear the True Dharma.
This is because there may be ignorant sentient beings in the world,
or those whose karmic obstacles from past lives are profound.
Or perhaps in the past, throughout former lifetimes,
they have extensively committed the ten evil deeds and the five heinous crimes;
or they have slandered the Buddha, slandered the Dharma, or slandered the Sangha.
Such sentient beings possess three kinds of heavy obstructions;
consequently, they are unable to encounter this teaching on the samādhi of the true Dharma of all Buddhas.
What are these three kinds of heavy obstructions?
The first layer of hindrance is the arrogance of self-conceit;
being obscured by false views and attachments, one is unable to humble oneself to serve all Buddhas,
Bodhisattvas, teachers, monks, and parents, nor to study the wondrous and profound Dharma.
The second category of hindrances consists of envying the virtuous and being jealous of the capable;
asserting one's own correctness while criticizing the faults of others;
relying on power, harboring greed and anger, and being fond of seeking fame and profit rather than applying oneself diligently.
Furthermore, they will be unable to learn the True Dharma of the Tathāgata.
The third heavy obstacle consists of excessive greed, excessive desire, indolence, sleep, lethargy, restlessness,
and frequent violation of the precepts due to a lack of diligent effort.
Such a person does not recognize cause and effect and does not respect teachers and elders.
They do not perceive what is wholesome and virtuous, nor do they guard the path of karma.
Therefore, such a person is coarse and wicked.
Throughout life after life, it is difficult to encounter the True Dharma;
even when face-to-face with it, one may fail to meet a Great Spiritual Friend (kalyāṇamitra).
Having extensively created evil karma, one falls at death into the Avīci hell and other hells.
Such persons shall not encounter this True Dharma of the Three Mysteries,
the yoga-secret samādhi teachings.
At that time, within the great assembly...
There was a great assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas,
a great assembly of śrāvakas,
and a great assembly of devas.
There are great assemblies of nāga spirits,
great assemblies of ghosts and deities,
as well as the fourfold assembly, including sons and daughters of good family.
Together they entreated the Tathāgata and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"We, this assembly, further beseech the Tathāgata to once again speak of the Great Being Mañjuśrī."
In the past, he practiced the profound teachings of the Mahāyāna,
the dharma-instructions on the samādhi of the three secrets of the Vajra,
and the supernatural powers, sovereign mastery, holy virtues, and spiritual might.
Never having heard it before and never having seen it before,
we, this assembly, shall likewise follow the Great Being Mañjuśrī in extensively making great vows and aspiring to study the Mahāyāna Yoga Secret Teachings of the Three Mysteries.
Therefore, the great assembly simultaneously requested the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata,
to speak for our sake regarding the profound and wondrous conduct and the extraordinary, holy nature of Mañjuśrī.
At that time, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni was in the Jeta Grove Monastery at Śrāvastī amidst a great assembly; there,
the Tathāgata entered the Vajra-samādhi for the sake of the multitude.
Arising from samādhi, he expounded the Tathāgata’s Dharma teachings for the three periods of a single lifetime and manifested the Great Being Mañjuśrī,
who had formerly practiced the bodhicitta of the three secrets.
Possessing supreme, holy power and mastery over supernatural faculties,
at that time the Tathāgata Śākyamuni addressed the great assembly, saying:
"I shall now act for your sake."
Having extensively analyzed and explained the Tathāgata’s teachings of a single lifetime and the Dharma of the three periods,
he was finally able to behold the noble virtue and power of Mañjuśrī,
who performed great supernatural feats to bear witness to these teachings.
He guides all classes of beings, causing them all to take refuge and follow;
he practices the contemplation of the secret holy nature of the thirty branches of the Mahāyāna Yoga Great Teaching and the Samādhi of the Three Mysteries of Vajra.
At that time, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni taught the doctrine of the three periods during his own lifetime;
therefore, during the first period, he taught the doctrine of existence, the śrāvaka discipline, and the vinaya.
Initially, there was the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna), which delivers the five classes of beings, all sentient beings,
and those who have attained the four fruits among the four types of noble ones.
In the second period, the Tathāgata taught the doctrine of emptiness to shatter the pervasive conceptualizations of sentient beings who cling to the existence of signs.
He delivers the fourfold assembly of śrāvaka disciples,
as well as all those on the three stages of worthiness prior to the bhūmis who practice for enlightenment,
causing them to return to emptiness and signlessness.
Because one does not grasp at nor cling to the practice of the Middle Vehicle,
it is therefore called taking refuge in the teaching of emptiness.
During the third period, the Tathāgata expounded the secret dharma-teaching that is neither empty nor existent.
It shatters the attachment to existence and the attachment to emptiness—
the delusive teachings within both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna—
and it shatters the attachment to existence and the attachment to non-existence.
One should refute those who cling to existence so as not to cause them to become attached to existence;
one should refute the Bodhisattvas' clinging to non-existence so as not to cause them to become attached to emptiness.
Why is this? Because it is through such practice that Bodhisattvas cultivate and realize [the truth].

To those who contemplate the sacred nature of the Dharma-realm, the ocean of the nature of the Tathāgata-dharmakāya, the treasury of the True Suchness of the Vajra-samādhi in thirty branches of the three mysteries of the Great Vehicle’s Yoga Mahāyāna teachings.
Because that which is unconditioned, signless, neither existent nor non-existent, is called the "Non-empty Secret Liberation Bodhi.

Therefore, the Tathāgata has clearly expounded this Great Being Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva’s Yoga Great Teaching: the Dharma-nature, the Three Mysteries, Noble Wisdom, Samādhi, and the Contemplation of the Noble Nature.
To all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who extensively deliver sentient beings,
to the fourfold assembly of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas,
and to the hosts of devas, nāgas, ghosts, spirits, and yakṣas.
May all sons and daughters of good family cause [their merit] to be dedicated toward the Mahāyāna,
the practice of entering the yoga of the Great Teaching, the samādhi of the three types of awakening, and the noble nature of contemplation.
In order that they may swiftly reach the source— the true suchness of self-nature, the fundamental nature of nirvana, and unsurpassed, perfect,
and complete enlightenment— at that time, the great assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas...
When the time for the *pravāraṇā* ceremony and the conclusion of the summer retreat arrived,
the Tathāgata addressed the Great Being, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying:
During the first three months of the summer retreat, you were invited to attend the *pravāraṇā* ceremony; however,
at the time of your departure, you went to teach in the Dragon Palace and have not returned since,
so the summer retreat has concluded without your presence for the *pravāraṇā*.
When the time drew near, Mañjuśrī did not arrive.
Kāśyapa thought to himself: "If he does not come when the later period arrives to attend the Dharma assembly for the *pravāraṇā* and the conclusion of the summer retreat, he shall be expelled."
When the great assembly, including Kāśyapa and others, was shrouded in doubt as to why the time had come yet they did not arrive,
Mahākāśyapa and the others thought to themselves:
"It is not fitting for Mañjuśrī alone to enter the assembly."
"If they should arrive later, they must certainly be expelled.
Mahākāśyapa and the others then addressed the Buddha, saying,
"The time for the Dharma service has arrived."
The Tathāgata said to Mahākāśyapa:
"When the time approaches, you should perform the pravāraṇā ceremony as a dharma-activity.
The karmadāna should then strike the ghaṇṭā within the assembly."
Once the sound of the gong has ceased,
the Great Being Mañjuśrī shall arrive together with the sound of the gong at the same moment. Thus,
the monastic assembly shall not be deficient in the ritual for the *pravāraṇā* (invitation to admonish) and the conclusion of the summer retreat.
He also severed the doubts of the assembly of śrāvakas and achieved mastery.
At that time, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni saw that the Dharma proceedings within this assembly were nearing their conclusion.
At that time, the Tathāgata, secretly augmenting his spiritual power with holy intent,
revealed and instructed the Great Being Mañjuśrī so that he might receive it as a sacred secret.
Mañjuśrī understood the holy intent of the World-Honored One.
Then, within the assembly for the *pravāraṇā* ceremony,
he shall manifest the power of his supernatural faculties and holy virtue;
at that moment, he will appear with a body sixteen feet tall, of the color of purple-polished gold.
He sat upon a seat of a hundred-jeweled lotus within the ocean of the vajra-nature of the dharmadhātu.
Upon the body of Mañjuśrī were arrayed various necklaces of a hundred jewels and exquisite celestial garments of wondrous gems.
The crown and back are surrounded by a halo, and the crown has five topknots.
Upon his head is a crown of seven precious jewels,
upon which he bears the five Tathāgatas.
On the body of the Bodhisattva appear two hundred and twenty-two great mudrās of his hands;
he has a thousand arms and a thousand hands,
each of which holds a bowl of vaidūrya.
Within each almsbowl, there was a manifested Buddha;
thus, a thousand Śākyamunis appeared simultaneously.
At that time, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni addressed them, saying:
Mahākāśyapa, you should observe this:
look closely at the lapis lazuli bowl in the hand of the Great Being, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī;
what kind of signs are there within it?
Mahākāśyapa then rose from his seat,
prostrated himself with his head at the feet of the World-Honored One,
and departed. Mahākāśyapa then stood before Mañjuśrī.
Having finished paying homage with his head at [the Buddha's] feet,
he looked into the bowl and saw within it ten billion trichiliocosms.
There are ten billion formless realms, ten billion form realms, and ten billion six desire realms.
There are ten billion Mount Sumerus, ten billion sets of four continents,
ten billion Jambudvīpas in the south, and ten billion Sahā worlds.
Ten billion Śākyamuni Tathāgatas;
ten billion thousand-armed and thousand-bowl Mañjuśrī Bodhisattvas;
and ten billion Kāśyapas.
Within the Mañjuṣībhadra vessel are ten billion worlds.
Within these worlds are ten billion Mahākāśyapas,
each of whom questions Mañjuśrī before him regarding the meaning of the Mahāyāna Dharma.
Furthermore, there were ten billion Golden Pure Lands of Mount Pañcaśīrṣa;
within each, he likewise saw ten billion Mañjuśrīs,
accompanied by assemblies of hundreds of billions of bodhisattvas.
Surrounded by them,
he then appeared, emitting a great radiance to transform and deliver the common people, rescuing and gathering in all beings.
Furthermore, he saw that the assembly of ten billion Mahākāśyapas was caught in a great web of doubt,
and they sought refuge and repented their transgressions before the Great Sage Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva.
The followers of Kāśyapa spoke:
"We are people of the Hīnayāna, possessing but small wisdom and small capacity;
we have fallen into the net of doubt, and we pray that our transgressions may be extinguished."
At that time, Mahākāśyapa and the śrāvakas,
in the presence of the Tathāgata and the Great Being Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva,
immediately made vows to widely propagate their great aspirations.
First, in accordance with the instructions of the Great Being, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī,
one should practice the contemplation of the holy nature of samādhi within the yoga of the three secrets, dedicated toward the Mahāyāna aspiration for study.
At that time, Mahākāśyapa and his assembly prostrated themselves before the Tathāgata,
touching their heads to the ground to pay homage at the feet of the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, I pray that the World-Honored One will accept my intention;
for us followers of the Hīnayāna,
I pray that you grant us the opportunity to confess our transgressions and doubts, and bestow upon us the prophecy of the Mahāyāna.
Then, within that assembly,
at that time, Śākyamuni Tathāgata was together with Mahākāśyapa and his retinue.
Having performed repentance and received the prediction of enlightenment, they were inspired to set their minds upon the Mahāyāna.
After Kāśyapa and the others had made their vows, the Tathāgata addressed them, saying: "In a future age..."
Encountering immeasurable and innumerable Buddhas, Tathāgatas,
one gradually cultivates and studies the yoga of the three secrets, the vajra-bodhicitta, and the sacred nature of liberation; thereby,
one shall attain the fruit of Buddhahood and realize *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Therefore, at that time, all the bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, the fourfold assembly,
and the great multitude collectively beheld the noble nature of the Great Being Mañjuśrī’s sovereign spiritual power and its unimpeded nature.
To sever all the great doubts of Kāśyapa and the others,
you should study the Mahāyāna so as to swiftly transcend to the stage of Buddhahood.
For this reason, the assembly of Kāśyapa and the rest together made the great vow.
Furthermore, may we, in every lifetime, encounter all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones,
and gradually train in and study the three mysteries of Mahāyāna Yoga,
until we attain the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of Buddhahood.
At that time, Śākyamuni Tathāgata,
for the sake of the śrāvaka assembly headed by Mahākāśyapa,

taught the ten kinds of non-transgressions of the bodhisattva path, the nature of liberation, and the holy power and mastery that transcend the three realms of existence through the cultivation of the Mahāyāna.
The desire realm lacks meditative concentration and is not free from defilement;
in the two higher realms above it, one does not abide in the four dhyānas nor rely upon the four formless attainments.
Those who cultivate this secret samādhi of the Tathāgata do so within the three realms of existence and in Jambudvīpa.
Therefore, the stage of training for a bodhisattva enables one to maintain the pure conduct (*brahmacarya*).
If one studies the Vajra Secret Samādhi,
one will swiftly attain profound penetration of the Buddha-mind and transcend the three periods of time.
Within samādhi, one is not defiled by the desire realm, does not abide in the four dhyānas, and does not realize the four formless attainments.
This is called non-attachment to the three realms of existence; it is termed "transcending the world."
Therefore, the assembly of śrāvakas headed by Mahākāśyapa together prostrate themselves before the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, saying:
"We pray only that the World-Honored One will now act for our sake."
We proclaim the Great Vehicle’s teaching on the Tathāgata’s precepts for upholding the three secrets, which are not to transgress the ten grave prohibitions.
We, the śrāvakas, shall dedicate ourselves entirely toward practicing and entering the secret of the Tathāgata’s Vajra Bodhi— the three secrets of Mahāyāna Yoga.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the assembly of Mahākāśyapa, expounding upon the non-violation of the ten major precepts:
"Listen attentively, listen attentively! I shall now analyze and explain them for you."
The Buddha told Kāśyapa: "It is like a person of the Hīnayāna who upholds the ten grave precepts of the Śrāvaka;
if they commit any of the ten grave transgressions against the code of discipline, each and every one of those offenses arises from the karma of body, speech, and mind."
Within the realm of appearances, to err regarding phenomena is to fail to perceive the mind.
The nature of the mind is quiescent and its self-nature is pure;
yet, because one perceives appearances and clings to them, there is leakage regarding phenomena.
This is called the grave transgression of the Hīnayāna.
It consists of the conceptualization of grasping at views that give rise to offenses through adherence to fixed dharmas;
being defiled by attachment to mental conceptions, one is unable to relinquish them.
Therefore, one should not give rise to [the thought of] being born in heaven or falling into hell.
This is called the Vinaya-piṭaka of the Śrāvaka-vehicle concerning the loss of dharmas as phenomena.
Thus it is for a Mahāyāna Bodhisattva who upholds the ten major grave precepts.
That is not so. For instance,
when a bodhisattva upholds the precepts,
they constantly cultivate the mental states of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity within the Mahāyāna.
To rescue and protect all sentient beings while illuminating the nature of the mind as tranquil and non-arising;
to clarify the mind and perceive the nature as ultimately pure—
this is called the true nature.
It is without defilement, without attachment, without grasping, and without abandoning;
therefore, it is called the tenfold Great Vehicle.
The Bodhisattva’s great precepts are likewise thus.
At that time, the assembly of Śrāvakas, including Mahākāśyapa and the others,
upon seeing the Tathāgata preach the Dharma of the ten major precepts of the Mahāyāna,
felt a sense of reverent shame and turned their aspirations toward the Mahāyāna.
We only pray that the Tathāgata will instruct us by naming them;
our assembly will develop deep faith and acceptance, and we shall personally uphold them.
What are the ten levels of pure prohibitions of the Mahāyāna?
It is named "not transgressing" and "not violating," the true nature of which is quiescence.
Within the ten grave precepts, how can the Mahāyāna be both transgressive and non-transgressive?
First, regarding all mental phenomena of the Tathāgata:
The vajra-nature is primordially pure and ultimately quiescent.
If a bodhisattva, within the nature of the Mahāyāna,
is able to uphold the ten grave precepts, [they shall attain this state].
Awakening to the true purity of the mind and clearly perceiving that the nature of the mind is undefiled and unattached,
the Bodhisattva who is thus able to uphold the ten grave precepts is called one who possesses the indestructible Vinaya.
Second, regarding all mental phenomena (*cittadharma*) of the Tathāgata:
the self-nature of the obstacles to the self is ultimately unattainable and primordially undefiled.
A bodhisattva who upholds the weighty precepts [should understand this].
The nature of precepts is like empty space; one does not perceive the mind-nature, which is vividly tranquil.
When a bodhisattva upholds the weighty precepts, they realize and see that the essence of the mind and the nature of the self are empty and non-existent.
Therefore, it is called the essence that transcends all characteristics of existence.
This is what is called the faultless Vinaya.
Third, it is the entirety of the Tathāgata’s mental phenomena.
The afflictions and delusive thoughts are fundamentally pure.
For a bodhisattva who upholds the weighty precepts,
there is in reality nothing to be attained within the nature of pure consciousness.
The Bodhisattva maintains the precepts with a mind that finds nothing real;
they perceive neither signs nor perversions,
neither bodhi nor true nature.
It is called the Vinaya of the Supreme True Nature.
Fourth, regarding the suchness and the limit of reality of all mental phenomena of the Tathāgata:
within that limit of reality, one perceives neither the upholding of precepts nor the breaking of precepts.
When a bodhisattva upholds the grave precepts,
they should demonstrate that one ought to contemplate the mind-ground;
seeing the nature of the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), the nature of the mind is luminously pure.
Not perceiving the nature of precepts, nor the defilements of various views regarding the observance of precepts,
it is therefore called the purity of the mind-nature;
it is the thorough penetration of the noble nature, the *tathatā* (suchness), and the *vinaya*.
Fifth, because all mental phenomena, bodhi, and the noble nature of the Tathāgata neither come nor go,
he is named "Tathāgata.
A bodhisattva should uphold the weighty precepts.
One attains the vision of the Tathāgata’s true mind-nature.
This true nature is equal to the dharma-realm;
it is characterized by neither coming nor going, and is unconditioned.
A bodhisattva who is able to uphold the pure precepts of the Tathāgata perceives that the Buddha-nature is equal to space and without distinction.
For this reason, it is called the holy nature of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body Bodhi.
This is truly called the inconceivable *vinaya*.
Sixth, all the dharmas of the Tathāgata’s mind-nature are fundamentally non-abiding,
fundamentally placeless, and fundamentally unattached.
When a bodhisattva upholds the ten grave precepts,
within non-abiding they do not perceive the nature of transgressing these ten grave precepts.
When the bodhisattva maintains these precepts, [they abide thus].
Within the unattached mind-nature, which is vast and pervasive throughout the dharma-realm,
it extends universally through all things like pure lapis lazuli, transparent both within and without;
this is called the purity of the vinaya of the nature of selflessness.
Seventh, all mental phenomena of the Tathāgata are equal to the limit of space because they are free from all marks; thus,
a bodhisattva is able to uphold the grave precepts.
Within the void of the mind, one does not perceive any characteristic of violating the precepts;
within the nature of the precepts, one realizes the purity of the nature of the Dharma-eye.
This is called the Vinaya of the Dharma-eye that purifies all six consciousnesses.
Eighth, regarding all mental phenomena of the Tathāgata:
these dharmas are fundamentally unborn and are now without cessation.
When a Bodhisattva is able to uphold the weighty precepts, [he realizes this].
One perceives and maintains the precepts within the nature of non-arising.
With each thought, the sacred nature is quiescent and pure;
through non-arising and non-ceasing, one realizes the stage of Buddhahood.
One shall swiftly achieve unsurpassed bodhi;
this is called the Vinaya of the Equality of the Three Times. Ninth:
All mental phenomena of the Tathāgata are the true wisdom of the suchness (tathatā) of all Buddhas;
he does not perceive any characteristics in any phenomena.
Why is this? Because the fundamental nature of the minds of sentient beings is originally suchness (tathatā).
If, within the nature of suchness, one perceives the observance of precepts, this is called "having signs" (sanimitta).
A bodhisattva cannot attain liberation if they perceive the observance of precepts; rather,
they must not grasp at or become attached to any signs whatsoever.
This is called the stainless liberation and the pure *vinaya*.
Tenth, all mental phenomena (*citta-dharma*) of the Tathāgata are ultimately signless (*animitta*);
they are free from mental conceptions (*saṃjñā-manasikāra*), pure, and unobstructed.
A bodhisattva who is able to uphold the ten grave precepts does not perceive the existence of precepts nor the non-existence of precepts within the nature of pure morality;
thus they are said to have realized the liberation from all marks of precepts and the fetters of attachment to the Lesser Vehicle.
This is called the ultimate *vinaya*.
Therefore, all Buddhas, Tathāgatas,
and all Bodhisattvas rely upon this Mahāyāna *vinaya*.
By upholding these ten kinds of noble nature— the ten major precepts of signlessness—
one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, being ultimately pure and free from all signs.
At that time, Mahākāśyapa further addressed the great assembly of śrāvakas who had attained the four fruits,
as well as the devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of spirits.
The sons and daughters of good family from the fourfold assembly,
together with the great multitude,
once again entreated the Tathāgata Śākyamuni.
For the sake of the assembly,
he once again expounded in detail: during which eon and at what time in the past did the Great Being, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, [practice]?
Having thus encountered and met with the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones,
who expounded this Great King of Teachings Sūtra on the Samādhi Contemplation of the Thirty Branches of the Three Mysteries Dharma Gate,
at that time Mahākāśyapa and his assembly addressed the Buddha, saying:
"We only pray that the World-Honored One will further proclaim for us, this great assembly,
the past causes and conditions of the Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva.
At that time, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni...
Then he addressed the great assembly headed by Mahākāśyapa, saying:
"I shall explain this to you in detail,
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva."
In the past, during an age long ago, incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas as numerous as the atoms of the sands of the Ganges,
the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī encountered Vairocana of the Five Vajra Peaks.
The five honored ones of the five wisdoms, the five Tathāgatas,
appeared in the world simultaneously. At that time,
there was one Buddha within that assembly named Akṣobhya-vajra-siddhi Tathāgata.
Furthermore, it is said that in a past and remote age,
in the world-system called Wonderful Banner,
there was another Buddha who appeared in the world named Vairocana.
The World-Honored One of Five Wisdoms, the five Tathāgatas, simultaneously appeared in the world and,
abiding in the vajra-dharmadhātu of space,
proclaimed the holy nature of space.
May all sentient beings be established in noble wisdom that accords with the intrinsic nature of original nirvāṇa,
and may they reach the further shore of the true reality of suchness.
Furthermore, within the Vajra-Dharmadhātu, these five Tathāgatas spoke with one voice, together proclaiming the Great Vehicle Yoga:

the contemplation of the sacred nature of the Samādhi of the Thirty Branches of the Secret Gate of the Three Mysteries, which bestows the rank of Vajra Dharma-King; the Vajra Initiation of the Great Teaching of Yoga; the Maṇḍala of the Prajñāpāramitā that subsumes all dharmas; and the sacred nature of the Bodhi-sattva-nature of all Tathāgatas.
With the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī as the leader,
he instructed the fourfold assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, as well as all sentient beings, including sons and daughters of good family.
At that time, he caused the multitude of people to enter this maṇḍala.
He taught them the practice of the Mahāyāna and conferred upon them the thirty branches of the samādhi of the sacred nature of contemplation on the three secrets of Yoga-Vajra-Bodhi.
Having attained the great samādhi of quiescence— the noble vajra-nature of triply enlightened bodhi—
he further exhorts the Bodhisattva to practice with diligent vigor and contemplate the true nature of suchness within the ground of the mind.
They realize the samādhi of the single nature of the dharma-realm— emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—
and attain entry into hundreds of thousands of dhāraṇī-doors, hundreds of thousands of vajra-doors, hundreds of thousands of samādhi-doors,
and hundreds of thousands of liberation-doors, all of which they fully possess.
In the future, they shall attain Buddhahood together as the Tathāgata Samantadarśin. Therefore, at that time in that world,
there will be the Tathāgata Amoghasiddhi.
At that time, in the midst of the great assembly,
he addressed the Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī, saying:
"Since the distant past, you..."
They drew near to the World-Honored Ones and made offerings to all Buddhas throughout the entirety of space, equal to the dharma-realm,
for as many eons as there are atoms within unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields.
Having seen the Buddhas and heard the True Dharma,
at that very moment the Buddha spoke to the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī,
saying: "Good son, you should, together with the great Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas and the fourfold assembly, [proclaim this]."
I ask once more the five wisdom deities, Vairocana and the others,
and the five Tathāgatas of the Five Vajra Summits,
to expound upon the stages of mind-ground realization and cultivation for the assembly of the four classes of Bodhisattvas.
Entering the samādhi of the noble nature of contemplation, which is the gateway to the three secrets of the Vajra Bodhi-yoga of all Tathāgatas:
how should one practice so as to attain the realization of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment?
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī,
receiving the holy command of the Buddha,
served as the leader for the great bodhisattvas and the fourfold assembly.
Together they requested Vairocana and the other five wisdom-honored ones, the five Tathāgatas,
to jointly expound the yoga-secret Vajra Dharma-gate.
How should the great Bodhisattvas and the fourfold assembly practice and realize it?
When one practices, studies, realizes, and enters the noble nature of the Tathāgata’s Mahāyāna Yoga Vajra Samādhi Contemplation of All Dharmas,
at that time, there are the five Tathāgatas of the five wisdoms of Vairocana.

With one voice, they spoke together, addressing the Great Being, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying: "O Son of Good Family, there are all sentient beings, as well as the great Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas and the fourfold assembly of disciples."
Those who have deep faith in this teaching— the yoga of the secret samādhi of Vajrabodhi—
should receive it with earnest attention and must renounce their kingdoms, cities, wives, and children, not sparing even their own bodies or lives.
For those who seek unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment,
they shall attain entry into this holy nature of contemplation:
the secret samādhi of the Tathāgata’s yoga-vajra-bodhi.
Then one shall swiftly attain the fundamental source, the empty and pure vajra-nature of the sacred essence,
and achieve the fruit of Buddhahood, the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
At that time, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni—
Then he himself spoke of how, in the distant past,
the Great Being Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva simultaneously encountered the time when the five Tathāgatas of the Five Vajra Summits and the Five Wisdom Honored Ones appeared in the world.
At that time, among the five World-Honored Ones, Śākyamuni Tathāgata manifested his appearance in the world as a Buddha named Amoghasiddhi Tathāgata,
and spoke to the Great Being Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva.
He bestows the samādhi teaching of the three secrets of the five wisdom-honored ones, the five Tathāgatas, and the vajra bodhicitta,
and transmits it to all sentient beings so that they may practice the path of the bodhisattva.
His conduct is vast and his vows are boundless;
he brings forth all the merit of the great vows of bodhisattvas without ceasing.
At that time, Mañjuśrī...
She has always been the mother of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddha-Tathāgatas in worlds as numerous as the atoms of dust;
she has also always been the leader of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of bodhisattvas, preaching for them the inexhaustible Dharma-gate of unsurpassed Bodhi.
Acting as a teacher for all bodhisattvas,
he teaches and brings all sentient beings to maturity,
causing them to realize the three secrets of enlightenment that transcend the three periods of time.
The Great Being, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, extensively delivers sentient beings;
his mind is equal to space and never ceases its activity,
and his fame is heard throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
He constantly serves as a Dharma teacher amidst assemblies of Buddhas as numerous as the sands of all the Ganges rivers,
even down to every single atom; he is praised by all Tathāgatas and abides in profound wisdom.
One is able to perceive the reality of the suchness of the dharma-nature through true insight;
one penetrates all phenomena— empty and signless— without obstruction,
attaining ultimate liberation through non-apprehension.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, who acts with a single-minded resolve,
has fully accomplished all the practices he undertook.
For this reason, at that time, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni—
Within this great assembly,
I shall now entrust to the Great Being, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, the teachings on the Mahāyāna Yoga Samādhi of the Five Wisdom Honored Ones and the Five Tathāgatas.
He commanded the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī to transmit this teaching.
The World-Honored One declared, "You shall be the foremost in upholding and flourishing this teaching—
the yoga of the three mysteries, the gate of samādhi, and the practice of contemplation."
It is transmitted to the great Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, the fourfold assembly, and other sons and daughters of good family.
If one attains entry into this Yoga gateway of the three secrets—the thirty-limbed Vajra-Bodhi Samādhi-Samāpatti visualization—then [one shall attain realization].
Then one will swiftly transcend [the world] and attain liberation;
realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
and shall surely attain Buddhahood.
At that time, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni addressed Mañjuśrī, saying:
"Good son, you should listen attentively."
I shall now explain this again in detail for you and the great assembly; wait but a moment.
When I speak of the various bodhisattvas, they will naturally have their own realization.
Thus, the Tathāgata spoke concerning the past, long-gone eons.
There was a Buddha named Vipaśyin Tathāgata.
When he appeared in the world, all the bodhisattvas studied this teaching of the Yoga Secret.
Having spoken thus, the Tathāgata [passed away].
Suddenly, there appeared thousands of billions of golden buddha-fields,
and bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges emerged to serve as witnesses.
Therefore, the various great bodhisattvas each spoke of their own teachings on the samādhi of the yoga of the three secrets of the Vajra,
through which they realized unsurpassed enlightenment.
At that time, the great bodhisattvas and others said:
"We have encountered Mañjuśrī,
who has guided us and caused us to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
By practicing the yoga of the Vajra Secret, one attains perfect enlightenment;
therefore, the entire assembly of Bodhisattvas shall appear together to realize this teaching on the gateway of the three secrets of yoga.
At that time, there was a great king of a kingdom in this world named King Pure-Eyed (Vimalanetra).
Within this country, he constantly practiced the True Dharma to transform and govern the people.
During the reign of that king,
he encountered a consecrated great master who expounded this teaching on the samādhi of the three secrets of yoga.
Having heard this teaching,
he immediately resolved to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
At that very moment, the Great King of the Nation, the Devaputra Viśuddhanetra, [did so].
At that time, by imperial decree throughout the land,
all śramaṇas were ordered to establish dharma-assembly halls for the initiation and transmission of the path of the samādhi of these three gates of secret mantra.
He then established a site for the Way (bodhimaṇḍa).
Every year, he spent one hundred days practicing the Way through recitation and meditation.
Within the royal palace, he likewise constructed a site for the Way for the transmission of the Dharma.
Then the Ācārya, the master of the teaching and guide who bestows the Dharma,
shall confer the empowerment upon the Heavenly King.
Thereafter, the King shall practice and study the yoga of the holy teachings of the three secrets, the bodhi-vajra, and the holy nature.
He did not cease his efforts until the end of his life;
thereafter, when the time was ripe, there were spiritual responses:
all Buddhas protected and remembered him, and the myriad nations came to pay their respects.
May the realm be peaceful and tranquil, and may the myriad subjects enjoy peace and happiness.
At that moment, the King shall receive blessings;
thereafter, the Son of Heaven, Pure Eyes, will gradually [attain his goal].
He attained an extended lifespan of over five hundred years.
Through gradual cultivation and study, he realized the five pāramitās;
he accomplished the four wisdoms of bodhi, and his six sense faculties were entirely purified and perfected.
Thereafter, you shall encounter all the Buddhas, Tathāgatas, and draw near to them in every lifetime.
O King, you should make offerings to and serve them so that nothing is in vain;
you shall swiftly attain Buddhahood and realize Bodhi.
At that time, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni addressed the Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva amidst the great assembly,
saying: "Good son, if there are great bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, the fourfold assembly, and others..."
Having generated the great bodhicitta and disregarding one's own body and life,
one should, with the genuine faculty of faith,
act as a seeker of unsurpassed bodhi.
Then one attains entry into this yoga of the Great Teaching, the secret contemplation of the noble nature of the thirty branches of the samādhi of the three secrets of the Vajra.
For this reason, Śākyamuni Tathāgata said:
If there is a bodhisattva who intends to establish a site for the Way,
they should first select an exceptionally superior location.
They should dig a pit one zhang deep, ensuring it is free of all tiles, rubble, bones, stones, charcoal, wood, and any other impure substances.
One who is fit to serve as a site for the Way (bodhimaṇḍa) should turn toward the ground of Great Purity and Adornment,
and therein establish a Vaipulya site for the Way, wherein the Great Maṇḍala is installed for the conferral of empowerment and the transmission of the Dharma.
At that time, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni addressed Mañjuśrī, saying:
"Good son, if there should be sentient beings in every successive life..."
One who, having made vast, expansive, and great vows, is able to construct this maṇḍala, bestow the empowerment, and transmit the Dharma within the samādhi-maṇḍala of the path—
such a person’s merit and virtue are equal in measure to the dharma-realm.
This merit is like space, having no end;
it is immeasurable and incalculable.
At that time, if there should be kings, princes, queens, princesses, palace attendants, or court ladies, and so forth—
One who is able to establish this pure great maṇḍala shall cause the land to be peaceful and the king to enjoy longevity; the queen and consorts shall live long lives,
and the myriad regions shall submit to his transformative influence.
The people will enjoy peace and happiness, and the winds and rains will follow their proper seasons.
Therefore, any high minister who is able to establish this site of practice (bodhimaṇḍa) will enjoy long life and fortune,
and shall always remain pure and auspicious.
Within the nation, loyalty and filial piety will flourish; the country will be secure and the people joyful.
Prosperity and well-being will increase ever further, and blessings shall not go to waste.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī and the other great Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas.
If there are any sentient beings who encounter this teaching on the samādhi of the three mysteries of this yoga, they have,
in the past and throughout immeasurable dust-mote numbers of buddha-fields, [made offerings to the Buddhas].
Having made offerings to countless Buddhas,
one will then encounter this Tathāgata-yoga Great Teaching, the Samādhi of the Holy Nature Contemplation of the Three Secrets,
and likewise encounter and receive instruction from a Dharma-ācārya.
From life to life, may you study these Mahāyāna Yoga teachings;
may you swiftly attain Buddhahood and quickly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Therefore, all the great Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas and the fourfold assembly—
Therefore, you should resolve to seek it with diligent study and vigor, never regressing;
you should have profound faith, indeed, profound faith, and give rise to great vows to practice and learn this teaching.
At that time, the great assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas,
as well as the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas,
and the devas, nāga kings, and the eight classes of spirits, [all assembled].

The fourfold assembly of disciples—sons and daughters of good family—all rejoiced and marveled at this unprecedented Dharma, receiving it with faith and practicing it accordingly. At that time, the great multitude were all filled with joy in their hearts.
Furthermore, he again entreated the Great Being, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī,
to once more address the great assembly before the Tathāgata,
the World-Honored One, and explain what teachings should be practiced during the final dharma period at the end of the kalpa.
Mañjuśrī spoke thus, declining repeatedly:
"In the presence of the Tathāgata, I do not dare to speak for myself.
Furthermore, I pray that the assembly of people will together invite the Tathāgata."

For the sake of the great assembly, please explain for us what teachings you will employ to extensively deliver sentient beings and all bodhisattvas during my future life, in the final age of the Semblance Dharma.
At that time, Śākyamuni Tathāgata addressed Mañjuśrī and the great assembly, saying:
"I shall now expound and analyze this for you."
When the Tathāgata is in the world, he guides and delivers sentient beings;
encountering the World-Honored One brings incomparable merit.
He is called the extraordinary and most supreme field of merit.
The Buddha said to Mañjuśrī,
"Good son, those who possess merit are able to encounter a Tathāgata while he is still in the world."
After the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, those of meager merit will be unable to encounter him.
For this reason, the World-Honored One told Mañjuśrī:
"If there are any sentient beings who receive the Tathāgata’s teaching of the true Dharma, they will regard the Buddha as possessing ten kinds of majestic virtue, inspiring awe and reverence."
One who generates a mind of longing and the thought that such an encounter is difficult to find will, upon receiving the teachings,
certainly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Why is this? Because while the Tathāgata dwells in the world, the karmic power of all sentient beings is supreme;
he is the one who bestows the teachings upon all sentient beings, the bodhisattvas, and the fourfold assembly.
Each and every one of them realized the unsurpassed bodhi of the Buddha-ground and the fruits of the Four Noble Paths of the Bodhisattvas.
If this were after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, it would be truly difficult for those of meager merit to encounter a Buddha.
In the age of the Final Dharma, those who wish to transmit the Tathāgata’s authentic teaching of the Mahāyāna must encounter a great master, a Dharma-ācārya.
Such a person is called one who occupies the seat of the Buddha as a successor and upholds my teaching.
One cultivates the Mahāyāna Yoga Secret Vajra Bodhi; therefore,
one establishes a sublime maṇḍala, and within that maṇḍala,
one installs the image of the Tathāgata as the central deity.
As well as the forms and images of the various tutelary deities and bodhisattvas,
which are exactly like those of the World-Honored One when the Buddha, during his lifetime, bestowed the True Dharma upon them;
for this reason, within the maṇḍala, the ācārya—
To all sentient beings, as well as to the bodhisattvas and those of the Mahāyāna, and the fourfold assembly:
just as when the Buddha was present, they shall receive the teachings according to the Dharma.
Those who enter the yoga of the three secrets, the thirty-limbed vajra-samādhi, and the contemplation of the sacred nature of secret bodhi—
Therefore, if all bodhisattvas and the fourfold assembly of disciples— monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen, as well as sons and daughters of good family—
should receive these teachings with sincere devotion, they shall [attain their goal].
One must by all means persevere for a long time and steadfastly practice the Vajra True Dharma, the secret treasury of the Tathāgata;
for this reason, one is called a disciple of the Tathāgata.
Having received the transmission of the Dharma, one should practice with diligent vigor;
without fail during the six periods of the day, one should perform the path of walking meditation and recitation.
Then, one must transmit the teachings and guide all sentient beings.

Each [of these] is entrusted to an ācārya who possesses deep faith, is well-versed in the Mahāyāna Yoga, and understands the secret teachings on the thirty branches of the three mysteries and the contemplation of samādhi.
Furthermore, one must also guide and lead the fourfold assembly of sentient beings,
causing them to return to the samādhi of the thirty secret gates of Mahāyāna Secret Yoga,
thereby enabling all sentient beings to swiftly reach the original source.
One realizes the path of attaining enlightenment through the single nature of the secret vajra bodhi of the yoga of self-nature purity;
such a person swiftly realizes anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, the great assembly— including all the great bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas,
as well as the fourfold assembly of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and gandharvas, and the bhikṣus,
bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās— [all gathered there].
If an ācārya intends to bestow the Dharma upon those who are training under him,
he must first secretly transmit the essential instructions of the thirty gates of contemplation.
Regarding the contemplation of the Vajra-Bodhi-dharma:
In the "Chapter on the Noble Nature of the Tathāgata" within the *Yogarahasya-samādhi*,
for this reason, the entire assembly of great bodhisattvas and all sentient beings—
One who practices the secret teachings on the contemplative cultivation of the Tathāgata’s noble nature should earnestly request the ācārya three times within the pure precinct of the great maṇḍala.
Regarding the thirty contemplation gates of the three mysteries— the secret seals and oral transmissions based on the teachings—
these must not be disclosed but should be transmitted only in secret.
If one does not rely upon the verbal instructions of the Tathāgata, [the practice will be ineffective].
If one merely proclaims and manifests [the teachings] without obtaining the power of the sages to penetrate secretly and the empowerment of the Buddha's wisdom,
then one will be possessed and obscured by Māras; thus,
the noble practices one cultivates will not lead to the attainment of the Way.
At that time, the great assembly, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, were all filled with joy;
they thirsted for and yearned after it, and with faith and acceptance, they put it into practice.
*The Mahāyāna Yoga Sūtra of the Ocean of Vajra-Nature Mañjuśrī with a Thousand Arms and a Thousand Bowls, King of Great Teachings*, Fascicle Five.
