Whether the bodhisattva abides in the four modes of deportment, [he remains thus].
Advancing in the cultivation of bodhi, there is no passing through it in vain;
one immediately realizes and enters the wisdom-nature of all Three Jewels,
such that the true, quiescent essence is constantly present before one.
Thus they shall be born life after life to encounter the Buddhas, see the Saṅgha, and behold the Dharma;
in every generation they shall diligently train in the majestic deportment of the Buddha,
and constantly enter the noble path of faith, diligence, and wisdom.
It is called the faith that accords with non-belief because it enters the path through the emptiness of conviction;
it does not perceive the four modes of deportment, as it realizes the emptiness of non-arising.
It is without volitional activity, without utility, without sensation, without knowledge, and without wisdom.
Arising from the concentration on emptiness, one enters the dharmas of worldly convention;
yet in the entering and exiting of these two states of dharma, there is no dualistic appearance.
Mind and mind continue in succession, always abiding within the state of empty mind.
Advancing in accordance with Bodhi, one realizes the mind and perceives the nature;
within these two dharmas, one penetrates their lack of mutual distinction.
This is because the fundamental Bodhi of the stage of advancement is identical in its single nature and characteristic to Suchness.
Fifth is the concentrated mind.
When a bodhisattva cultivates all wholesome dharmas,
all that is wholesome arises from the power of concentration.
They attain unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment.
Within all Mahāyāna teachings, these bodhisattvas cultivate the wisdom of enlightenment.
First, one should practice contemplation to clarify the mind and illuminate the nature,
causing the mind to become tranquil and stable so as to realize the purity of the nature.
Within the unconditioned path of the nature, one does not perceive the existence of any dharma.
If a bodhisattva cultivates the bodhi of all buddhas, they will,
through the power of meditative concentration,
extinguish all sins and give rise to the untainted wisdom of the prajñāpāramitā of all dharmas.
By means of the dharmas of the samādhis of the bodhi of all Buddhas,
one enters the Tathāgata’s contemplation of quiescence and realizes the nature of signlessness,
signless wisdom, immeasurable noble practices, immeasurable wisdom-mind, and the samādhi of the noble nature.
All ordinary beings and noble ones,
as well as Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, enter this samādhi of the Buddha-nature and bodhi without exception.
At that time, the Bodhisattva realizes the nature of the essence and becomes conjoined with the state of nobility.
This is all due to the power of the samādhi of noble wisdom regarding the essential nature of all things;
thereby one perceives the subtle self-grasping of the intrinsic nature of the self, the person, the master,
the sentient being, the attachment to the view of self, the agent, and the experiencer.
Among all forms of attachment and bondage,
for one who clings and does not understand,
the very nature of the fetter of views constitutes an obstruction.
Furthermore, it is impossible for all various marks, conditioned causes and conditions,
and the winds that stir the mind to cease without attaining the power of meditative concentration and tranquility.

Therefore, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas and all the Buddhas-Tathāgatas cause all sentient beings to cultivate and enter the meditative concentration of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), emptiness (*śūnyatā*), the emptiness of emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*),

the eight inversions, non-existence, and the dependent origination of provisional tranquility; they observe through the wisdom of contemplation the emptiness of emptiness and the illumination of emptiness.
All illusory transformations are merely provisional combinations that perish moment by moment;
the retributive fruits of the three realms, including sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness,
as well as the very root of the nature of transgression, are all extinguished through the attainment of meditative concentration.
When one realizes the essence of the mind, becomes free from all marks, and clearly perceives the nature,
then all marks are extinguished and correct wisdom arises;
for by attaining the noble nature, one enters into the bodhi of all Buddhas.
Sixth is the mind of wisdom.
The bodhisattva aspires to seek the Buddha-dharma;
with the eye of wisdom within the ground of the mind, they contemplate the original source.
The wisdom of primordial emptiness within the fundamental nature is neither cause nor condition, nor is it without conditions;
it is neither possessed of causes nor devoid of causes.
Within the wisdom of emptiness, the noble power and noble nature of the Middle Way—
knowing this essence is called "mind" (citta);
that which takes this essence as its object is called "consciousness" (vijñāna).
One discerns that all phenomena are merely the convergence of causes and conditions;
this "self" and "person" is merely a provisional designation for a master.
Thus, the bodhisattva regards all sentient beings [in this way].
Extensively practicing wisdom and knowledge to lead others into Bodhi;
sharing the same path as the Way to enter the fruit of Buddhahood;
through the causes and conditions of all practices, entering the state of the noble and leaving behind that of the ordinary.
All ordinary minds are caused to be completely extinguished;
their nature attains purity, becoming identical with the Buddha-way.
If a bodhisattva cultivates tainted merit, [it is likewise so].
Then one will be born among the various devas.
If one cultivates untainted karma (anāsrava-karma),
one will attain entry into the fruit of the unsurpassed path of Bodhi.
Therefore, when a bodhisattva cultivates all wholesome dharmas and realizes the noble wisdom of the Tathāgata,
this is called the functional activity of the essential nature.
If one holds any view of a self,
it is called the power of bondage and liberation through ignorance;
such an obstacle prevents a bodhisattva from cultivating the Tathāgata’s vajra-samādhi.
Through the empowerment of the vajra-spiritual power,
the afflictions of all sentient beings are completely extinguished,
and they attain the realization of bodhi— permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
Therefore, all sentient beings take the habitual tendencies of ignorance and afflictions as the very root of bodhi.
The cultivation of all wholesome dharmas is an afflictive hindrance,
because the essential nature of the function of wisdom is thereby not clarified.
What do you think?
If a bodhisattva practices for anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi,
they should first realize the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*) as the primary holy nature and holy wisdom;
then they should practice the ineffable, practicing the ineffable.
One cultivates the entry into the contemplative wisdom of the vajra-buddha-intelligence of all things.
One enters the Middle Way, the single truth.
Within this, ignorance obstructs wisdom.
Awakening to true purity,
the mind attains clarity.
Within the essential nature and substance of the Bodhisattva’s contemplative observation of the mind-nature, [one realizes this].
When the mind is clarified and purity is perceived, one clearly perceives the nature;
it is neither characterized by form nor devoid of form,
yet it is not non-existent with respect to form.
It neither comes nor goes;
it is neither cause nor condition;
it is not possessed of fault.
It is not non-offense; it is not not regarding offense;
it is not regarding suchness.
It is neither the eight inversions;
it is without arising and without cessation,
illuminated by the blazing flames of the light of wisdom.
Delighting in the transformation of skillful means,
possessing skill in means,
and exercising the sovereign power of supernormal knowledges and the miraculous applications of noble strength.
Because the essence of wisdom functions as the activity of insight;
and because one attains awakening and shall swiftly achieve accomplishment.
Seventh is the mind of aspiration.
The Bodhisattva, with utmost sincerity and without regression, gives rise to vast and great vows;
with a mind of aspiration seeking the mind of aspiration,
they are determined to seek the fruit of the unsurpassed path of Bodhi in the Mahāyāna.
To share the same mind, the same conduct, the same vows, and the same quest as all bodhisattvas and all sentient beings—
this is called the Great Vow and is also called the Great Quest.
By means of causes, conditions, practices, and fruits,
the bodhisattva, throughout eons as numerous as motes of dust,
vows to seek awakening without interruption or cessation.
May the aspiration-mind continue in succession with the aspiration-mind for a hundred kalpas.
To achieve Buddhahood and extinguish transgressions, one seeks great accomplishment;
reaching the ground of the mind, one seeks until arriving at the non-arising, the emptiness of emptiness, where the single aspiration becomes the empty mind.
Contemplating the noble wisdom that enters meditative absorption over many kalpas,
it universally illumines immeasurable moments of mind;
in every moment of mind, one perceives the bonds and aspires to realize the true nature.
When ignorance is extinguished and one is liberated by its very nature,
one then realizes the mind that truly seeks immeasurable sublime conduct; thus,
one reaches the fundamental source, the nature of the mind.
To achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*,
immeasurable merit takes seeking as its foundation.
From the moment a bodhisattva first gives rise to the great vow and seeks the bodhicitta, [this is so].
Within that interval, he extensively practices the bodhisattva path;
when his vows and practices are fulfilled, the fruit of Buddhahood is attained.
Within the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha, the bodhisattva contemplates the single truth.
In the Middle Way, one does not perceive the establishment of any vows;
one constantly enters into quiescence, wherein there are no aggregates or realms.
Regarding all phenomena of the nature of quiescence, one neither sinks nor emerges.
Neither arising nor ceasing, neither seeing nor not-seeing—yet seeing that which is non-seeing.
It is by relying upon wisdom that one enters the nature of suchness (*tathatā*).
This is called the source of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas: the self-nature of suchness, the fundamental true suchness (*mūla-tathatā*), and the pure great vow.
All conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) are named after their essential nature, which is the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) and signless (animitta),
because it is the fundamental source, the essential body, and the noble practice and vow.
Eighth is the protection of the mind.
The Bodhisattva makes vast, extensive, and profound vows,
pledging that throughout the past, future, and present,
they shall be able to protect all the Buddha-dharma without sparing even their own body or life.
The Bodhisattva further, before the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time,
again made vast and great vows,
practicing the holy power and pure conduct of the bodhisattva path.
They all sought the Great Vehicle, the holy teachings of the Tathāgata;
they adorned all pure lands with the merits of the Sangha Jewel, the Dharma Jewel, and the Buddha Jewel;
and they extensively carried out the Buddha-activities of the Three Jewels of the Tathāgata.
Or they may be afflicted by celestial Māras, non-Buddhists, and all kinds of inverted, false views;
or they may be slandered, harmed, or killed by worldly Māras and evil persons,
who disturb their right faith and obstruct the Buddha-dharma.
To eliminate those who destroy the Three Jewels, the True Dharma of the Tathāgata,
and all meritorious qualities,
the Bodhisattva vows to be able to disregard even their own body and life.
With utmost sincerity, they shall uphold and protect the True Dharma of the Tathāgatas,
as well as the meritorious holy teachings of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present.
Bodhisattvas should likewise act for the sake of all sentient beings.
For one who vows to seek unsurpassed bodhi, the Tathāgata first attains Buddhahood for them. Why is this?
Because the mind of a bodhisattva is equal to empty space.
They are protected by the inexhaustible compassion of all Buddhas.

Why is this? Because a bodhisattva is able, together with all sentient beings of the dharma-realm, to contemplate the truth of the path and enter the true suchness of universal correct nature and bodhi.
Constantly abiding in tranquility through the empowerment of the noble ones' power,
one attains the benefit of self and others, extinguishing the karmic retribution for the inherent transgressions of sentient beings,
and also succeeds in eliminating attachment to a self and to persons.
The fetters of attachment to phenomena and views constitute all obstacles;
the Bodhisattva, however, contemplates and penetrates them, entering the mind of non-arising.
He does not perceive any phenomena as being established through the realization of the two truths.
When one contemplates the mind with clarity and stability, the noble nature manifests before one.
By thus guarding the fundamental self-nature which is pure,
within that originally pure nature, there is truly nothing to be perceived.
There is neither sign nor signlessness, and there is nothing to be protected.
Within this unguarded noble nature, there is no action and no reception.
Having reached the state of rightness, one attains the continuity of mind and wisdom.
Mind and wisdom reach the emptiness of non-arising;
one enters and contemplates the path of the wisdom of emptiness, the noble nature, and bodhi.
All are fully realized as entering the principle of the emptiness of emptiness—wherein the mind is conventionally empty, a mere phantom and illusion part by part.
Illusory transformations arise from emptiness and enter the nature of noble wisdom.
One realizes the nature of suchness as being both existent and non-existent;
the dharma-body of the nature of suchness is a provisional emptiness of gathering and dispersing.
It is ungraspable and cannot be protected.
One contemplates the nature of all noble ones and realizes all dharmas;
that one shall likewise attain liberation is for this reason.
Ninth is the mind of joy.
The Bodhisattva constantly abides in joyful bliss and extensively practices the path of goodness toward all sentient beings within the entire realm of phenomena.
They rescue and deliver all sentient beings,
ensuring they always attain peace and happiness; once they have been delivered,
the Bodhisattva constantly gives rise to a heart of joy.
This is called the bodhisattva having realized and attained a joyful mind;
therein, they perceive the Tathāgata’s Dharma-knowledge nature-body for the sake of all sentient beings possessed of consciousness.
Causing their dispositions and natures to resonate with one another so that they enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision;
for this reason, by means of the unconditioned noble nature and sovereign spiritual powers of all Tathāgatas,
worlds are established within the dharmas of sentient beings.
The nature of the noble ones is a provisional synthesis formed through the power of the Path.
It pertains to all conditioned things and the self-karma of sentient beings,
wherein mental dispositions correspond with the harmony of the four great elements.
The consciousnesses of sentient beings interact to form bodies.
Once the Bodhisattva has obtained such a body,
the World-Honored One then causes the Bodhisattva to [realize] the intrinsic nature within this very body and mind.
Clarifying the mind, one enters meditative absorption; illuminating stillness, one perceives the nature.
Through the contemplation of provisional emptiness and quiescence, one neither enters the conditioned nor the unconditioned.
Thus, one realizes the great bliss of nirvana and the intrinsic purity of self-nature.
Without conjunction or dispersion, there is transformation through reception and change through phenomena.

The Bodhisattva realizes the wisdom of emptiness and enters the profound penetration of the Buddha-mind; relying on the path of the emptiness of phenomena, they enter the equality of the dharma-nature and the signless single contemplation. Contemplating that the mind and mental activities are empty, they realize the eloquence of extensive learning and the illumination of wisdom within the nature of the mind.
May all the ocean-treasury of the merits of buddha-nature be realized as equal to space within the signless;
may the mind of joyful wisdom realize that the nature of the mind is empty and free from thought.
Without arising, they constantly illuminate the nature that enters the samādhi of cessation;
they do not perceive any signs or any self-nature,
for their joyful and blissful equality of essence is eternally luminous.
To progressively realize and enter into permanence, bliss, self,
and purity is what is called the noble nature of the Tathāgata’s bodhi, nirvāṇa, and the Path;
this is the tenth, the crown of the head.
The Bodhisattva gives rise to a lofty and eminent mind to rescue all sentient beings;
constantly practicing acts of loving-kindness, they cultivate and maintain the supreme Buddha-wisdom.
Having extinguished the view of a self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being, and the view of a life-span, the Bodhisattva enters into meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
It extinguishes the wheel of views regarding selflessness, doubt, and the body;
it extinguishes all fundamental afflictions rooted in delusive conceptualization; and it eliminates greed, hatred, and ignorance.

Through the contemplative observation of the mind’s tranquil clarity, one perceives the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), which is called "realizing the summit of the mind. Like the summit of a mountain, this contemplation is continuous; like the summit of a mountain, it is continuous. At the summit of the mind, within the emptiness of the *dharmadhātu*, there is neither cause nor effect—only the single path of suchness, pure and most supreme, like the summit of a mountain.

Just as the crown of a person’s head is the most noble part, so too, within the sixty-two views and the five destinies of sentient beings, it is impossible to perceive a self-view that is not like the great void; therein, no such view can exist.
If a bodhisattva, abiding in the untainted mind, realizes the quiescence of intrinsic nature,
they do not perceive the existence of a mind; thus, the imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva) is extinguished,
and all characteristics such as the self, a master, movement, shifting, and contraction are extinguished.
Within the mind, the samādhi, and the true suchness (tathatā) of intrinsic purity, there is nothing to be obtained, nothing to be grasped, and nothing to be bound.
At that time, this person—the Bodhisattva—attains entry into the ten gates of emptiness.

They enter into internal and external emptiness, the emptiness of non-alteration, the emptiness of essential nature, the emptiness of specific characteristics, the emptiness of common characteristics, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of non-apprehensibility, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of intrinsic nature, and the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence.
At that time, the Bodhisattva constantly abides in the ten gates of emptiness. The Bodhisattva immediately penetrates the holy nature and the holy path;

with a direct mind of true emptiness, there is not a single sentient being-nature, and the deluded mind is extinguished. Not perceiving conditions and not perceiving non-conditions, the Bodhisattva dwells in the Samādhi of the Summit, illuminating stillness and realizing the mark of cessation. Distinguishing the seeing-part from the perceived-part, he enters the self-verifying part and realizes the part that verifies the self-verification. Thus he attains the meditative concentration of the mind of quiescent extinction and gives rise to the fundamental holy practices, proceeding toward the true nature of the Way.
The Bodhisattva, moreover, completely extinguishes without remainder the bonds of the views of self and person, the eight inversions, and their causal conditions through the gate of non-duality;
thus, they shall never again undergo the eight difficulties, whether in the mundane or supramundane realms.
Within the ocean of birth and death, they ultimately do not undergo the karmic results of illusory transformations.
The Bodhisattva gives rise to a mind of great loving-kindness and great compassion,
causing all sentient beings to go, come, sit, and stand.
One cultivates entry into the Tathāgata’s bodhi, the noble path, and the adamantine noble nature;
one extinguishes all karmic obstacles and hindrances,
eliminates the ten unwholesome actions, and gives rise to the ten paths of wholesome conduct.
Entering the correct nature of the Path, correct wisdom, and correct practice,
the Bodhisattva penetrates the true nature, and contemplative insight manifests before them;
they shall never again undergo the fruits of the six realms within the cycle of birth and death.
Ultimately never regressing from unsurpassed bodhi, they shall,
within the dharmas of bodhi,
give birth to the noble nature of the Buddha-seed in life after life and age after age.
Having been born into the family of the Buddhas and entered the stage of the Buddha-nature,
they attain the samādhi of noble wisdom characterized by the same right faith and right view as that of the Tathāgata’s bodhi; therefore,
after the Tathāgata had thus spoken, [he continued].
The assembly of bodhisattvas each, in turn, practiced, studied, believed, accepted, and carried out [the teachings].
*The Great Vehicle Yoga Sūtra of the Ocean of Vajra-Nature Mañjuśrī with a Thousand Arms and a Thousand Bowls*, Fascicle Seven.
*The Great Vehicle Yoga Sūtra of the Ocean of Vajra-Nature Mañjuśrī*...
The Great King of Teachings Sūtra of the Thousand Arms and Thousand Bowls, Scroll Eight.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master of Da Xingshan Monastery, the Śramaṇa Amoghavajra, by Imperial Decree. At that time, Vairocana Tathāgata...
Within the holy nature of all dharma-realms,
he manifests oceans of thousands of billions of worlds and enters the hundred-jeweled lotus-flower ocean-treasury dharma-nature samādhi, which is the vajra-samādhi of the holy wisdom of all Buddhas.
The World-Honored One arose calmly from samādhi and sat upon the Lotus King of a Thousand Rays throne.
Vairocana Tathāgata then addressed him.
All Buddhas and all Bodhisattvas, you should know and listen attentively, listen attentively.
Regarding that which you previously asked about the ten minds of cultivation,
within this great assembly—
I now do so for the sake of the questions posed by the Bodhisattvas of Great Wisdom and Supernatural Penetration;
from these ten minds of initial aspiration,
one cultivates entry into the stage of firm Dharma-patience.
One practices the ten ways of nurturing the mind directed toward the fruit of Bodhi.
For this reason, the Tathāgata shall now explain them.
What are the ten ways of nurturing the mind?
First is the mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
The bodhisattva, relying on the loving-kindness of the Tathāgata,
[directs it] toward all sentient beings.
One should not create the causal conditions for the ten non-virtuous actions;
constantly contemplating one's own nature, one gives rise to a compassionate and upright mind.
Practicing the path of the Bodhisattva, one should rescue all sentient beings.
Extensively guiding various classes of beings so that they do not create conditions for evil,
they constantly abide within the wisdom of non-self,
perceiving the purity of the nature of self and entering the dharma of noble wisdom.
One accords with the noble nature of purity, permanence, and bliss;
one realizes the emptiness of the five aggregates—the emptiness of form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—and the emptiness of non-apprehension.
Thus, one enters step by step into the Buddha’s great, quiescent nature.
There is no arising, no abiding, no characteristic of birth, and no characteristic of cessation.
Like an illusion, like a transformation, it is the single mark of suchness, being neither one nor two.
Therefore, the bodhisattva resolves upon great vows and gives rise to a mind of great compassion.
Within the ocean of birth and death across the six realms,
rescue and deliver all sentient beings,
swiftly causing them to leave suffering behind and reach the state of Bodhi.
For the sake of all sentient beings,
the bodhisattva guides them through successive eons in the practice of the bodhisattva path,
perceiving neither suffering nor affliction.
Having accomplished awakening,
the Bodhisattva shall turn the Tathāgata’s adamantine Dharma-wheel of all phenomena.
With great compassion, he delights in transforming and delivering all sentient beings,
causing them to give rise to right faith and attain the wisdom of benevolence and kindness.
Entering the ocean of sarvajñā (all-knowledge),
their great compassion and wisdom in emptiness do not follow the teachings of Māra;
they realize the fruit of compassionate bliss and enter the path of non-arising.
Within the true nature of the excellent compassion of the Vajra-wheel,
one perceives neither evil results nor good results;
nor does one perceive the fault of the cycle of birth and death within a self-nature.
Within the dharmatā of the noble wisdom of all Tathāgatas,
he realizes and practices emptiness, attains the nature of unimpeded noble wisdom,
and enters the samādhi of the empty intrinsic nature.
Because he has attained the Tathāgata’s Vajra Samādhi,
having spoken thus, he shall then proceed to expound it in due order;
that is what should now be explained.
Second is compassion.
The bodhisattva vows to rescue and deliver [beings],
practicing the compassion and wisdom of all Buddhas.
That which is compassionate mind is the Tathāgata’s original nature, the spontaneously present, true,
and pure great compassion. Within such great compassion,
within emptiness, it is empty of emptiness, quiescent emptiness, signless, and unarisen.
Within the noble path of the wisdom-nature of the fundamental compassion that takes emptiness as its object, one extinguishes all causes of suffering for oneself;
this is called the cessation of the truth of suffering.
Furthermore, one extinguishes the conditions for the suffering of all other sentient beings.
Regarding the immeasurable causes of suffering for all sentient beings,
the Bodhisattva gives rise to the wisdom of great compassion;
this is because they take the non-killing dharma as their object and do not cling to the object of a self.
Constantly practicing non-killing, non-stealing, and non-lust, one does not afflict or obstruct any sentient beings.

A Bodhisattva who has resolved for Bodhicitta carefully examines the path of seeing the emptiness of the pure mind-nature; through the contemplation of the fundamental seed-nature within the functioning of consciousness, they perceive all afflictive phenomena as they truly are. Realizing that the fundamental seed-nature is inherently pure, their wisdom-mind of the realized path accords with supreme bliss, compassion, and the wisdom of emptiness amidst the three grades of the six types of kin and the six types of enemies—regarding both kin and enemies equally. Seeing no evil therein, even amidst the nine grades of adverse conditions, they obtain the fruit of bliss which is empty and eternally present before them; thus, their own body and the bodies of others, and all sentient beings, are equal in a single bliss and a single nature.
Because of the arising of the samādhi of great compassion,
having spoken thus, he then expounded it in sequence;
that is what should now be explained.
Third is the mind of joy.
When a bodhisattva practices the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā),
they diligently cultivate all the paths to the enlightenment (bodhi) of all Buddhas.
In contemplating the Buddha-nature, there is no joy.
Why? Because its fundamental substance is pure;
within the characteristics of this pure nature, [there is no joy].
He clearly perceives the lineage, essence, and characteristics of all sentient beings, as well as their intrinsic nature.

He realizes and enters the pure Buddha-nature of the wisdom of the Path; with a mind of emptiness within emptiness and joy, he is unattached to the objects of his own perception. He possesses sovereign spiritual power regarding the arising and ceasing across the three periods of time, knowing all causes and all effects, as well as suffering, the origin of suffering, and the entire entry into the cessation of the cause of suffering. Thus he illuminates and penetrates the Buddha-nature, contemplating the true nature through the contemplation of emptiness.
Attaining equal joy and delight identical to the Bodhi of the Buddhas,
the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva gives rise to a heart of utmost sincerity,
causing all sentient beings to [attain this].
Realizing the joy of awakening,
they enter the nature of the Tathāgata’s noble wisdom-path;
they abandon evil associates and seek out virtuous friends.
Show me the good path so that all sentient beings may be born into the family of the Buddha-dharma,
enter into the Buddha-dharma and constantly give rise to joy,
and attain the rank of Dharma King.
Furthermore, they cause all sentient beings to enter into right faith and right wisdom,
and to abandon all evil and false views;
for the cycle of birth and death is the accumulation of suffering within the six realms of existence.
Because of having realized the Samādhi of Joyful Delight in Buddha-nature,
and in order to cause all sentient beings likewise to enter this Dharma and attain Bodhi—
having spoken thus, one should then expound it in successive order.
Fourth is the mind of equanimity.
The bodhisattva generates great vows and practices,
cultivating and maintaining the bodhisattva path throughout successive lifetimes.
To extensively deliver sentient beings,
one should constantly contemplate and observe the body and mind, training in the noble wisdom and noble insight of the Tathāgata; within the nature of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*),
all things are empty and non-existent, like the great void which possesses no marks whatsoever.
There is neither the mark of relinquishment nor any volitional construction.
Within the nature of the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi) of signless emptiness,
one perceives neither good nor evil, neither seeing nor non-seeing.
One contemplates both demerit and merit with equal equanimity,
clearly perceiving the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
Within the nature of suchness (*tathatā*), there is no mark of a self (*ātman*) and no mark of a person (*pudgala*).
Furthermore, there is neither the view of a self nor the bondage of grasping at "mine," for the essential nature of both self and other is entirely unapprehendable,
and even the true nature of suchness is unapprehendable.
Because it has no reckoning or attachment, it is like empty space;
this is called the characteristic of great emptiness as relinquishment (*mahā-śūnyatā-tyāga-lakṣaṇa*).
Within this characteristic of the great emptiness of relinquishment, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices for many eons.
Together with one's own body and the bodies of others,
may all sentient beings resolve to seek bodhi and give rise to vast,
great vows within the emptiness of suchness.
Practicing the bodhisattva path, one vows to relinquish body, flesh, hands, feet, sons, daughters, wife, children, kingdoms, cities, fields, and houses—
giving up all internal and external phenomena and all things as if they were illusions, transformations, flowing water, or the flame of a lamp. This is the great renunciation of all things.
That which is called unconditioned relinquishment is called signless relinquishment.
Within this unconditioned relinquishment,
there is neither cessation nor arising.
Within the nature of the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), one does not perceive any relinquishing;
this is called great equanimity (*mahopekṣā*).
By being equal to the non-relinquishing of all things, one attains the same noble nature as awakening (*bodhi*).
Because Bodhisattvas constantly cultivate true equanimity,
it is called the signless great relinquishment;
this is the fundamental self-nature of the Tathāgata.
Because the nature of bodhi is empty and fundamentally lacks the characteristic of relinquishment,
the Tathāgata, having thus spoken, should subsequently expound it in this sequence.
Fifth is the mind of giving.

When a bodhisattva seeks awakening, they practice giving by means of the body, giving by means of speech, giving by means of the mind, giving material wealth, giving the Dharma, and giving instruction.
As explained above, these six types of giving are condensed into three kinds. What are these three?
First, giving that arises from one's own spontaneous resolve;
second, giving when entreated by another;
third, giving through instruction.
If a bodhisattva gives with their own resolve,
they contemplate the original *tathatā* and its primordial self-nature;
because there is no [grasping] within the act of giving, it is called "signless giving" (*animitta-dāna*).
Next, when a bodhisattva is solicited by others for alms,
or if a bodhisattva solicits alms for the sake of all sentient beings,
this is called "giving with signs" (sanimitta-dāna).
Therefore, immediately thereafter, one should instruct the donor:
"The Bodhisattva has resolved his mind, vowing to deliver all sentient beings;
he shall provide offerings and practice generosity toward all living beings."
To have no rest, with a mind that never ceases,
and to cause all sentient beings to aspire toward and seek unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment in accordance with the dharma-realm—
this is what is called the unconditioned, untainted gift.
If a bodhisattva, for the sake of all sentient beings,
is universally able to personally resolve to practice giving,
this is called signless giving.
Thus, regarding one's own body, the bodies of others, cities, men, women, wives, children, fields, houses, and all conditioned things—
giving them all away completely is called attaining unimpeded, unconditioned giving.
Therefore, the bodhisattva penetrates the nature of the unconditioned;
contemplating the nature of suchness with clarity,
there is no thought of material wealth, nor is there any recipient.
That giving is like space, having neither interior nor exterior;
it is without conjunction or dispersion, and is devoid of mental activity.
The Bodhisattva contemplates the fundamental nature at the source of his own mind.
When one does not perceive the existence of a "giving" by virtue of penetrating the principle,
this is called giving that is wishless and signless.
A bodhisattva is one who constantly practices such signless giving.
Because the ever-abiding mind-source, the naturally pure land, manifests and proceeds before one.
Having spoken thus, it should now be explained in its proper sequence.
The sixth is the mind that delights in wholesome speech.
The Bodhisattva cultivates the essential nature of the Tathāgata’s skillful means,
constantly giving rise to benevolent intentions and speech that is truthful, real,
and the speech of the vajra-secret samādhi.
This is the method for accomplishing the Bodhi of the Three Mysteries of the Buddha.
How does one accomplish the Three Mysteries of the Tathāgata?
First, it causes one to realize the secret of the ground of mind of all sentient beings.
One attains the Bodhi of the essential nature of the Body-Secret (kāyaguhyaka),
because one achieves the Bodhi of the Prajñā of Words through the supreme ultimate truth of the Samādhi of Loving Speech.
Second, it causes one to cultivate the secret of the Mind-Ground (cittabhūmi).
One realizes the bodhi that is the essential nature of the secret of speech (*vāgguhya*).
One practices the secret contemplation of the meaning of the words of all the Tathāgata’s teachings contained within the three piṭakas,
and one authentically realizes and attains mastery in the eloquence of the secret of speech.
Because of the accomplishment of the great wisdom of the Vajra-Bodhi of Contemplative Prajñā;
third, it causes one to cultivate the secret of the mind-ground and realize the Bodhi that is the essential nature of the Secret of Intention (mantra).
Entering the noble practice of the samādhi of all Buddhas— the prajñā of the true mark of reality—
one contemplates and perceives the adamantine limit of the true word, the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), which is the essential nature of all Tathāgatas.
Because one achieves the realization of the vajra-bodhi of prajñā-pāramitā as the true mark, at that time,
the bodhisattva practices noble wisdom, noble nature, noble conduct, and the path to bodhi upon all sentient beings.
Always practicing truthful speech,
one correctly follows the single word that harmonizes all-knowledge,
causing sentient beings and all bodhisattvas [to attain it].
Free from anger and resentment, and devoid of the nature of contention, strife, or vexation,
one should constantly contemplate the nature of the mind within the prajñā of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*),
realizing the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmaśūnyatājñāna*) as the single characteristic of true reality.
The Bodhisattva, whose nature is pure because there is neither cause nor condition, constantly cultivates eloquence;
entering the samādhi of the nature of loving speech,
he gives rise to great kindness and great compassion for all sentient beings.
They constantly give rise to love and compliance;
every word and every phrase acts in accordance with the Buddha’s intent,
and they likewise extend this to all other beings.
Regarding "words of excellent meaning":
by means of the Dharma-speech through the power of noble wisdom, the Bodhisattva protects,
rescues, instructs, and guides all sentient beings.
Constantly practicing virtuous speech and maintaining a correct intention in accordance with suchness,
they give rise to roots of goodness to enter the wisdom of the unsurpassed path to bodhi;
by abiding in the Buddha’s pure land, they enter the vajra-samādhi.
At that time, after the Tathāgata had finished speaking, he expounded it in successive order:
"Seventh, the Bodhisattva of Beneficial Mind cultivates the conduct of a *sattva* and enters the *samādhi* of the Tathāgata’s Wisdom Body."
To bring benefit, peace, and happiness to all sentient beings, may they,
through the essential nature of true wisdom and noble insight, extensively practice the path of knowledge;
and by the power of noble conduct, may they accomplish the noble path, unsurpassed bodhi, and the vajra-samādhi.
This is the Dharma-gate of the Dhāraṇī of All Radiant Flames.
It is the noble practice of contemplating the essential nature of the seven riches,
intended to provide benefit to those who come before.
The Bodhisattva, having resolved upon the mind of great wisdom, extensively benefits all beings by offering his own and others' bodies and lives;
attaining the seven riches, noble conduct, and the fullness of merit and wisdom,
he enters the samādhi of benefiting others.
The Bodhisattva cultivates and realizes the sacred nature of the Buddha,
empowering the body, speech, and mind of all sentient beings,
and causing them to enter the lineage of the Tathāgata’s Dharma.
Having realized the lineage of emptiness and quiescence, the lineage of noble conduct, and the lineage of the realization of the Path,
he entered the Tathāgata-samādhi.
Having attained this samādhi, the great trichiliocosm suddenly shook in six ways.
The Bodhisattva enters into the six realms of existence to rescue and deliver all sentient beings,
enabling them to attain peace and happiness and swiftly realize Bodhi.
Yet the Bodhisattva enters the six realms of existence;
through common purpose and common Dharma, manifesting immeasurable forms, bodies, and physical characteristics,
they rescue and deliver sentient beings from suffering and affliction.
They do not regard this as a calamity; rather,
it only increases the benefit for others,
because the Bodhisattva constantly abides in the samādhi of benefiting others.
Having spoken thus, he expounded it in successive order.
Eighth is "sameness of mind":

the Bodhisattva causes all sentient beings equally to enter the samādhi of the emptiness of the same essence—the noble wisdom of self-realization that realizes the true nature of the Tathāgata’s body.
Entering into the dharma of non-arising,
one perceives that the wisdom of non-self is identical to the emptiness of the nature of non-arising;
they are equal and non-dual, sharing the same fundamental essence.
Regarding all sentient beings and all phenomena— the source and objects of self and other—
as being of one essence, their intrinsic nature is the very characteristic of suchness;
within the phases of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing, the bodhisattva...
Through the sovereign power and function of divine wisdom and noble insight,
one attains the realization of unimpeded, pure, great wisdom—
eternally arising, eternally abiding, eternally quiescent, and eternally extinguished.
With mastery over appearing and disappearing, they are identical in nature;
regarding phenomena of the past and future worlds,
their wisdom of prajñā flows on in continuous succession.
Throughout countless and immeasurable kalpas, without end or interruption,
the Bodhisattva shall once again give rise to great compassion,
with a mind of noble conduct and wisdom, providing great protection and great salvation.
He manifests the samādhi of infinite and boundless transformations of identical essence,
entering into the forms, bodies, colors, minds, and the activities of the six sense organs of all sentient beings.
Furthermore, when entering the various six realms of existence, he is identical to all things and categories therein;
by means of the power of his noble conduct and his spiritual efficacy,
the Bodhisattva empowers all sentient beings.
Being identical to emptiness and non-arising, empty and devoid of substance,
one realizes the secret Vajra-mind, the wisdom-function of the self-soul,
and thus manifests divided bodies and dispersed forms while abiding eternally in quiescent extinction.
They give rise to the resolve to rescue and protect,
extensively delivering all sentient beings and causing all living beings to enter the samādhi of the same Dharma.
Because he abides in the Tathāgata-vajra-samādhi,
at that time the Tathāgata, having already spoken, sequentially expounded it.
Ninth is the concentrated mind.

The Bodhisattva constantly enters the Tathāgata’s samādhi, the Vajra-like Samādhi; through the essence of noble wisdom, they contemplate all sentient beings—self and others—with their minds and hearts fundamentally tranquil, partially realizing nirvāṇa that is without object-condition and without cause.
Within the self-nature and intrinsic being of my own person,
the element of consciousness, the element of form, the realm of emptiness, the formless realm, and the realm of cessation are pure; the Bodhisattva,
by means of the wisdom of noble nature, [perceives this].
Reflecting back upon the source of the mind, one perceives that consciousness is the realm of emptiness;
awakening thoroughly to the ground of the mind, one realizes the nature of wisdom within the three realms.
Thus, one sees that the nature of reality is immovable amidst arising and ceasing, and amidst adversity and favor.
The divine power is sovereign and constantly enters into quiescence.
Abiding in the ten factors of dhyāna, by means of the wisdom of a single thought-moment, one clearly perceives the self,

the person, the master, and the mental attachments— the nature of pervasive conceptualization— whether internal or external, within the minds of all sentient beings, both one's own and those of others.
The seeds of noble wisdom are pure by nature;
they are non-apprehendable, neither conjoined nor dispersed.
The bodhisattva again contemplates all sentient beings.
The essential nature of the wisdom-mind is an accumulation and formation that cannot be apprehended;
the habitual tendencies and seeds of all sentient beings are likewise so.
If there are bodhisattvas among all sentient beings who cultivate and realize awakening and enter the nature of the noble path,
their ignorance and afflictions will then be eternally extinguished.
The Bodhisattva gives rise to great vows and constantly abides in samādhi;
entering and emerging with mastery, he manifests supernatural powers to guide all sentient beings throughout the three realms.
It is so that suffering sentient beings may cross the ocean of misery,
realize the Tathāgata’s vajra-bodhi, and enter the samādhi of the great wisdom of noble insight into the ocean of the nature of all Buddhas.
Having spoken thus, one should explain it by unfolding it in successive order.
Tenth is the mind of wisdom:
the Bodhisattva enters the Tathāgata’s adamantine secret bodhi-essence Buddha-samādhi and realizes the ocean-like samādhi of the light of wisdom.
Illuminately perceiving the minds of all sentient beings,
one understands, as they truly are, the afflictions of self and other— the nature of which is characterized by greed, hatred, delusion, false views, and the fetters—
and thus realizes that they possess no fixed nature.
Why is this? Because afflictions are the very nature of bodhi.
By cultivating the nature of afflictions through the advancement toward suchness, one attains bodhi.
For this reason, regarding all sentient beings, the bodhisattva...
They transform and inspire all sentient beings,
causing them to practice the Tathāgata’s true suchness (tathatā) and the patience that accords with reality (anulomikī kṣānti), because all things are empty.
Within the nature of all phenomena, they are neither aggregates (skandha) nor elements (dhātu).
Neither entering nor not entering;
neither a sentient being nor not a sentient being;
neither one nor two; neither self nor person.
Because they have realized the true nature of the causes and effects of the three periods of time,
Bodhisattvas constantly cultivate and realize quiescent Bodhi for the sake of all sentient beings within the Dharma-realm.
Entering into the noble contemplative practice of the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena,
one realizes the power of noble wisdom arising from the nature of one's own essence,
and universally radiates vajra-intelligence throughout all things.
The light illuminates the Buddha-body, identical in nature to the Tathāgata-samādhi;
it pervades the entire dharma-realm,
each ray of light shining as a single illumination, each flame brilliantly clear.
Clearly beholding all bodhisattvas and all sentient beings,
may they swiftly cultivate and enter the samādhi of the true nature of the ocean of wisdom of the dharma-realm,
and quickly attain the liberation of the samādhi of bodhi.
Its wisdom and skillful means nurture and develop the mind;
it penetrates the nature of all phenomena, causing the mind to realize emptiness.
Through the eye of wisdom that is empty of emptiness, it realizes entry into the emptiness of non-arising.
Because of the Tathāgata’s secret vajra-samādhi, the "Vajradharmadhātu-avatāra-sahasrasāgara-nayana-rāja-samādhi-śatadharma-vairocana-mukha," the Thus-Come One,
having thus spoken, expounded it in successive order.
At that time, Vairocana Tathāgata,
abiding within the ocean-treasury of the true nature of the *tathatā* dharma-realm,
manifested a world-system of the dharma-nature consisting of an ocean-treasury of hundreds of thousands of millions of lotuses.
There emerged from it hundreds of thousands of millions of all Buddhas and all Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas.
They manifested a thousand-light-king, hundred-jeweled lotus throne,
upon which Vairocana Tathāgata sat, seated on the thousand-light-king vajra-jewel throne.
He emitted the golden light of purple-vajra, which universally illumined the ocean-treasury of dharma-realms as numerous as atoms, making them all pure and entirely golden.
The Tathāgata then addressed them, saying: "All Buddhas and all Bodhisattvas, you should know this."
Listen attentively, listen attentively! You should first inquire about the seed-syllables of the ten vajra-minds;
I shall now explain them for the sake of this great assembly and in response to the questions of the Bodhisattvas of Great Wisdom and Penetration and the others.
From these ten stages of nurturing the mind, one enters into the firm cultivation of patience; herein it is explained that one enters the ten adamantine minds directed toward the fruit of bodhi.
How does the bodhisattva practice the contemplative wisdom?
Regarding the cultivation of entry into the ten adamantine minds, what are the ten?
First is the mind of faith:
the Bodhisattva cultivates and studies with utmost sincerity the secret samādhi teachings of the Mahāyāna sūtras of all Tathāgatas.
With profound wisdom and faith, one cultivates mindfulness and practices all the secret conduct of bodhisattvas, training in the vajra-secret teachings on enlightenment of all buddhas and tathāgatas,
and extensively delivering all sentient beings.
Taking faith as the foremost, one cultivates and accomplishes unsurpassed bodhi;
it is the root of noble virtue: right view and right meditative attainment.
They do not give rise to the thoughts of birth and death born of the heterodox views of external paths,
nor to the malevolent and resentful conduct of demons;
rather, Bodhisattvas constantly clarify their minds and illuminate their inherent nature.
One attains the vision of the fundamental afflictions that obscure and delude;
through the grasping of self-clinging, various views, and attachments, one becomes bound by existence.
Yet, having performed karma, one ultimately does not undergo [rebirth], but enters into the samādhi of the nature of emptiness.
Within unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), the bodhisattva cultivates entry into tranquility and does not perceive arising, abiding, change, or cessation.
Free from the three marks, there is neither non-existence nor non-arising;
there is no arising and no abiding.
Abiding in non-abiding abiding and ceasing in non-ceasing ceasing,
the bodhisattva partially realizes the wisdom of quiescence within the nature of the noble path of practice.
There is not a single dharma that possesses the characteristics of conditioned phenomena;
within the wisdom of the two truths— the conventional truth and the ultimate truth—
one realizes the practice of cessation.
When formations cease, ignorance ceases.
If a bodhisattva, within the fundamental nature of the mind— which is unconditioned and signless—
contemplates that phenomena possess no distinct characteristics and that their nature is identical to the dharma-nature.
The emptiness of emptiness and the emptiness of form are realized through the subtle mind.
Mind upon mind becomes subtle;
mind upon mind becomes empty.
Therefore, it is called "profound faith.
It enters deeply into the fundamental nature of quiescence;
it is without substance or characteristics, unified in a single nature, and without dependence.
However, the subject—the functions of self, person, and spirit—is bound by the three realms;
it is a provisional meeting, a provisional conjunction, and a provisional "self" and "mine.
There is nothing to be attained and nothing to be accumulated; all are entirely extinguished.
All marks enter into the suchness of the noble nature.
When a bodhisattva attains this, they are said to possess the mark of the unconditioned and the signless;
this is called profound faith.

At that time, the Tathāgata, having spoken this "Chapter on the Bodhisattva’s Cultivation and Realization of the Faith in Non-Existence," [taught] the entry into the Buddha-body through the sequential stages, the Samādhi of the Silent Nature, the Holy Practice of the Single Nature, and the Samādhi of the Single Characteristic.
Having spoken thus, the Tathāgata should explain it in successive order.
Second is mindfulness:
the bodhisattva’s resolve is diligent and energetic.
One cultivates and studies the Tathāgata’s samādhi of all dharmas of the Mahāyāna;
one contemplates the nature of the mind of the mental consciousness,
and maintains constant awareness through mindfulness of the six recollections and the cultivation of discernment.
Even for as long as a single thought arises, he gives with a mind constantly intent on giving.
The Bodhisattva cultivates all dharmas through the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) of emptiness,
remaining unattached, unstained, unbound, ungrasping, and undispersed.
When a bodhisattva realizes and enters the wisdom of quiescence,
they abide together within the characteristics of arising, abiding, changing,
and ceasing; they perceive neither movement nor non-movement.
One does not perceive the arrival of existence, nor does one perceive the arrival of non-existence;
yet, regarding the recipient of all past and future karmas, they constitute a unified mark.
All dharmas, all paths of practice, and all karmic deeds bring about the cultivation and perfection of merit and wisdom.
The Bodhisattva dedicates all of this toward entering the noble nature and noble wisdom of the vajra-dharmadhātu.
The Bodhisattva makes a vow to bring all sentient beings and his own body to fulfillment, entering the wisdom of signlessness.
The characteristics of wisdom ride upon the vehicle of the vehicle, reaching the stillness of cessation.
Flame upon flame illuminates the nature; the light shines forth, penetrating non-arising.
There is no arising, no shifting, and no differentiation within the path of emptiness.
The former transforms into the latter, and the latter transforms into the former.
Transformation follows transformation, and manifestation follows manifestation;
these transformations and manifestations shift and change, yet they abide together simultaneously.
The flames and their radiance, as a single characteristic and a single stillness, are empowered by the holy nature simultaneously.
That which has already transformed, that which has not yet transformed, and the process of transformation itself—all these transformations likewise perish and cease at one and the same time.
Attaining the realization of the single nature of the vajra,
the essence of each and every mind is free from thought;
that state of being free from thought is equal to the realm of empty space.
The dharma-realm is of a single characteristic and is all-pervasive,
for one enters the samādhi of the adamantine body of quiescence, which is the nature of suchness.
Having spoken thus, one should then explain it in its proper sequence.
Third is the mind of dedication.
The bodhisattva practices and maintains the Tathāgata’s secret samādhi,
giving rise to great vows to extensively deliver all sentient beings.
Within one's own profound mind, one should constantly practice the correct wisdom of bodhi for the benefit of both self and others,
causing all sentient beings to share the same aspirations and practices,
and cultivate the supreme truth of emptiness.
Within the samādhi of true knowledge regarding the true dharmas, one contemplates emptiness;
one progressively realizes the noble nature of the true truths,
and through the perfection of virtuous karma, the causes and fruits of bodhi are accomplished.
The supreme, uninterrupted, and sublime Noble Path is called the Ultimate Truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

Within the Truth of the Path, the convergence of all phenomena— which are conventionally designated by worldly names— along with their causes, effects, self, person, and master, is likewise termed the Ultimate Truth.
Regarding these two truths of existence— the truth of suffering and the truth of its origin—
the Bodhisattva should dedicate [their merit] toward entering the ocean of the Tathāgata’s vajra-like omniscience (*sarvajñatā*),
and thus deeply penetrate the *prajñāpāramitā*.
One realizes the nature of wisdom that is the emptiness of the dharmas of enlightenment;
yet there is no coming or going, for illusory transformations and karmic maturation are such that all categories of experienced karma are ultimately and eternally extinguished.
One does not enter the conventional reality of birth and death or the causal conditions of various karmas;
within the secret, holy nature of the Vajra-sage ground,
there is no self, person, or life-span, nor is there any mundane world.
This is called the Samādhi of Liberation through the Noble Wisdom of Bodhicitta that Profoundly Enters the Nature of Mind.
Therefore, after the Tathāgata has delivered this teaching,
one should next study it and put it into practice.
Fourth is the mind of penetration.
The bodhisattva penetrates the nature of the Buddha-dharma,
enters the vajra-bodhi-secret samādhi, and realizes the samādhi of the noble wisdom of the dharma-nature.
Within this samādhi, the true nature of noble wisdom,
one realizes the patience that accords with all the teachings of the noble ones regarding the nature of emptiness and illumination,
and thereby enters into the true nature of the Tathāgata’s noble wisdom.
Regarding all the bodhi-vajra noble wisdom:
within the dharmatā of all the noble wisdoms of bodhi,
the bodhisattva realizes the emptiness of the noble practice of the dharma-dhātu, being neither bound nor liberated.
They enter the unimpeded noble nature;
they penetrate meaning, penetrate expression, and penetrate the methods of transformation;
they penetrate the causes and effects of the three periods of time, and the faculties, practices, and actions of all sentient beings as being identical to the single suchness-nature.
When a bodhisattva arouses a mind of diligent effort,
they then contemplate the spiritual function of the noble nature as sovereign and free,
unobstructed and unhindered, neither conjoined nor dispersed.
Because the perfectly awakened true nature of suchness (*tathatā*) is bodhi without utility,
it employs non-utility as its utility;
it employs the nameless as its utility.
Because it functions without marks,
its function is to enter all emptiness through the wisdom of contemplation.
This emptiness of emptiness, which illuminates and penetrates emptiness, is called the noble nature (*ārya-dhātu*).
One penetrates the emptiness of all phenomena;
even emptiness, emptiness-as-emptiness, and the mark of suchness are ungraspable.
This is because one has accomplished the bodhi of the vajra-sacred wisdom.
At that time, having thus spoken, the Tathāgata proceeded to explain it in due order.
The fifth is the straightforward mind,
which constantly practices what is straight and upright.
"Upright" means that the dharma-nature of true suchness (tathatā) is free from crookedness and deviation.
When a bodhisattva contemplates the essence of the minds of both self and others,
they perceive the true nature of true suchness because it is devoid of any deviant nature.
This is called "direct illumination.
It is the seeing that the nature is unchanging and undifferentiated.
This refers to the Bodhisattva’s entry into the samādhi of the true nature of suchness.
Illuminatively perceiving the conventional truth of birth and death,
there is seeing, grasping, and attachment to delusive conditions;
yet the self-spirit (*ātman*) as sovereign is of one and the same purity.
Entering into the wisdom of non-arising within the true suchness of the essential nature,
one clarifies the mind and perceives the purity that extinguishes ignorance, the divine self, and the sovereign creator.
This principle of emptiness within emptiness resides in both existence and non-existence.
This is called the bodhi of the sacred nature of the secret vajra that realizes emptiness;
it does not destroy the vajra-seed of the sacred path.
Within this untainted sacred nature, the bodhisattva...
Entering the Tathāgata’s Vajra-Bodhi Samādhi through a single contemplation and a single illumination,
one teaches and transforms all sentient beings throughout the ten directions, as numerous as the atoms of dust.
They are all able to enter the ocean of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge),
realizing the true nature of the path of noble wisdom;
they proceed directly, with direct nature, through the direct nature, practicing emptiness within emptiness, emptiness, and emptiness.
There is no self (ātman) as a sovereign subject defiled by the three realms,
because the outflows, fetters, and bonds have been eternally extinguished and are no longer experienced.
At that time, it is called the samādhi of the Tathāgata’s adamantine secret holy nature and holy practice, characterized by direct mind and direct nature.
Having spoken thus, he explained it in successive order.
The sixth is the non-retrogressive mind;
herein, the bodhisattva arouses a spirit of diligent exertion.
May they cause their own minds and the minds of others to rescue and sustain all sentient beings;
may they extensively practice the bodhisattva path and cultivate ascetic disciplines;
and may they study and master the secret samādhi of the Buddhas’ noble treasury of wisdom.
Entering the stage of the three mysteries of the adamantine true limit— the samādhi of the Tathāgata’s true nature—
one attains the non-retrogressive mind and never again enters the stage of ordinary beings.
One does not commit various evils nor give rise to various views.
One does not further nourish the three karmas of the new mind that lead to the sins of birth and death,
nor does one again practice the causes of suffering such as the notions of "self" and "person."
One shall never again enter the ripening karmic fruits of the three realms;
one realizes, stage by stage, the vajra-bodhi and the emptiness of the three mysteries of conduct,
abiding neither advancing nor receding within the supreme Middle Way.
Because they enter the gate of liberation through the secret sacred nature by means of unified practice,
they likewise do not regress. Thus,
within the true limit of enlightenment (*bodhy-anta*) and the fundamental nature of reality, [they abide].
Because it possesses neither a single substantial nature nor dual characteristics,
there is not even a single thought-moment, nor is there any retreat or discouragement;
there is no shifting and no movement within the contemplation of the unconditioned and signless.
Entering the continuous flow of the mind that rides upon the vehicle of the vajra-nature of wisdom— the emptiness, quiescence, and luminous reflection of non-arising suchness—
one enters the emptiness of the two truths, the single path, the single pure nature, and the wisdom of nirvana.
One never again enters the cycle of birth and death within the three periods of time;
within the tranquil path of the noble ones,
one perceives neither regression nor progress.
This is because it is called the Samādhi of the Secret Bodhi of the Vajra Reality-limit of the Buddha’s Realization.
Having spoken thus, one should next expound it according to the teaching.
Seventh is the Mahāyāna mind.
This bodhisattva generates great vows and does not train in the minds of the two vehicles.
Thus they instruct the masses of sentient beings.
May they practice the Tathāgata’s supreme, most excellent, and foremost vehicle,
thereby guiding and delivering all sentient beings.
The Bodhisattva studies and practices the Mahāyāna secret Vajra Ground of the Mind,
cultivates the samādhi of the One Vehicle,
and instructs and guides sentient beings.
They cause [beings] to enter the supreme and extraordinary samādhi of the Tathāgata’s holy nature— the quiescent dharma-realm whose essence is emptiness—
and to progressively realize the emptiness of dharmas within the holy practices for awakening of all Buddhas.

The complete stillness of mind after mind is called the One Vehicle; it is the vehicle of the wisdom that realizes the single nature of emptiness, the vehicle of practice, and the vehicle of vehicles. This wisdom of mind carries and employs every sentient being across the great river of birth and death within the three realms.
What is this great river of the three realms?
First is the great river of birth and death, the ocean of suffering, wherein one sinks and drifts through the flow of afflictions in the desire realm.
Second, in the realm of form, there is the obstruction of attachment to the meditative concentrations seen through the cultivation of dhyāna;
clinging to stillness, one enters and emerges from dhyāna with sluggish stagnation, like being caught in a bottomless great river.
Third, in the formless realm, the measure of the retribution of lifespan comes to an end.
They cycle through the six realms of rebirth and the three existences of the six desires;
in the form realm and the four formless attainments, they are stained by attachment and habituated to meditative concentration;
though the devas practice dhyāna, they do not sever the arising and ceasing of birth and death.
The Great Bodhisattva of Non-conceptualization, who experiences bliss through the meditative concentration of love,
sits at the site of enlightenment within the great river of birth and death in the triple world.
The supreme, foremost vehicle is capable of carrying all and is employed for all purposes;
because the movement and penetration of noble wisdom lead one toward entry into the fruit of Buddhahood,
at that time the bodhisattva gives rise to a mind of great compassion.
If there are any sentient beings who have not yet reached the site of enlightenment,
may they realize the site of enlightenment through the samādhi of the One Vehicle.
If one has not yet attained the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) of the wisdom that realizes emptiness,
then regardless of how one practices or employs it, it is not called the Mahāyāna in its ultimate sense;
it is merely called a "vehicle" (yāna).
Therefore, these bodhisattvas and all sentient beings must first practice the supreme and foremost vehicle of the Tathāgata,
and advance toward the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).
Those who enter the Vajra Samādhi cross over the ocean of suffering; therefore,
it is called the Tathāgata’s Mahāyāna accomplishment, the supreme Vajra Bodhi of the One Vehicle.
Having spoken thus, one should explain it in successive order.
Eighth is the signless mind (*animitta-citta*).
The bodhisattva cultivates and maintains the signless mind of the Tathāgata.
The samādhi of the bodhi of all dharmas refers to the step-by-step realization of the true nature of suchness, the objectless and signless samādhi,
within the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi) of the mind’s essential nature, which is suchness itself.
With the clarity and purity of the mind’s eye, one perceives that the nature of greed, hatred, delusion, false conceptualization, and inversion is simultaneously extinguished;
there remains only the nature of liberation, bodhi, noble wisdom, and the prajñāpāramitā.
Because it is neither one nor two, it is non-extinguishing;
all phenomena of the three periods of time—whether they be fetters, karma, maturation, birth, or cessation—are entirely identical to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Thus, one enters into the suchness (*tathatā*), the single truth, the noble nature of all Buddhas, which is empty, wishless, and signless.
They attain the samādhi of the empty, true nature of the Tathāgata’s wisdom regarding the non-arising of phenomena;
because they know for themselves that they shall attain Buddhahood, all Buddhas are their equals.
"All worthy and holy ones are my fellow students,
for we all equally share the Tathāgata’s nature of reality— the adamantine bodhi of emptiness and non-arising.
Having spoken thus, one should then proceed to expound upon it in sequence.
Ninth is the mind of wisdom.
The bodhisattva constantly contemplates the noble wisdom of the Buddha,
cultivating and maintaining the Tathāgata’s vajra-bodhi secret samādhi for as many eons as there are atoms.
One attains entry into the noble wisdom of suchness, the vajra-nature of the noble ones, and the noble insight;
these penetrate and unify with a single object, being equal to true thusness, the boundless dharma-realm, and immeasurable divine powers.
The Samādhi of the Single Nature Vajra.
Within this noble ground of the Vajra-nature,
there is no accumulation, no experiencer, and no one who is born.
There is no non-existence and no arising.
Within the nature of non-arising,
there is no ignorance, no cessation of ignorance, and no nature of affliction.
Neither bound nor liberated,
all worthy ones and sages practice this path within all the dharma-gates of the Prajñāpāramitā.
All dharmas contemplated by the noble Bodhisattvas,
all aspects of enlightenment, and all noble paths are likewise the nature of suchness.
The Bodhisattva makes a vow that his own essence, wisdom, and the self-nature of noble insight shall be identical [to theirs].
All such methods of skillful means for the Buddha’s transformation of beings and his knowledge—
I have gathered them all within a single mind,
because they are identical with the samādhi of the noble nature of vajra-bodhi.
All the magical illusions produced by the efforts of externalists with their false views, false doctrines, and false concentrations;
all that is spoken by Māras and all that is spoken by Buddhas;
and the distinctions between the profound and shallow meanings of the Sāṃkhya school.
All enter into the single nature of the two truths, which is pure and devoid of all marks.
It is neither one nor two, and there are no aggregates, elements, or sense bases.
It is unconditioned, markless, and a single path of universal unity.
One realizes the light of the Tathāgata’s vajra wisdom.
This light illuminates the nature, which is by its very essence quiescent.
It is the single object, the single nature, the vajra samādhi.
Because one enters the vajra-bodhi of the samādhi of the noble nature of the Tathāgata regarding all phenomena.
Having thus expounded this, one should then explain it in its proper sequence.
Tenth is the indestructible mind. For one great asaṃkhyeya kalpa, as numerous as the atoms within it,
the bodhisattva practices and studies the Tathāgata’s adamantine bodhi— the profound, subtle, and secret noble wisdom, the three mysteries, the noble nature, and the samādhi.
Entering the stage of the noble ones (*āryabhūmi*), one approaches the state of liberation;
entering the realm of the Buddhas,
one attains the correct wisdom of the Path and clarifies the bodhicitta.
The patient acceptance of submission (伏忍) accords with emptiness and cannot be destroyed by the eight māras.
The various sages stroke one’s head, and all Buddhas exhort and inspire one.
One enters the sovereign spiritual power of the Tathāgata’s vajra-samādhi of stroking the head.
The Bodhisattva then emits light from his body;
this light illuminates all the pure lands of the Buddhas of the ten directions,
as well as all the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and worthy sages.
Because you have come to bear witness for me,
I shall vow to remain within the world of sentient beings for one great asaṃkhyeya kalpa.
He trains in the majestic deportment of the Buddhas and in the supernormal powers of appearing and disappearing.
He acts with sovereign mastery through the operation of holy power,
shaking the great trichiliocosm and bringing all sentient beings to maturity.
The sacred nature of bodhi and the stage of equality are of one essence;
they constitute the wisdom of vajra-intelligence,
non-dual, non-one, undifferentiated, and non-distinct.
There is neither entering nor exiting, yet this is not non-madhyamaka;
one enters into the noble nature via the path of noble wisdom by means of the power of samādhi.
Within the light, there appeared hundreds of thousands of billions of Buddha-worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
within transformed lands as countless as motes of dust,
Tathāgatas appeared in the world.
Manifesting now, he preaches the Dharma to instruct sentient beings.
At that time, the Bodhisattva gives rise to a mind of great compassion,
thereby realizing the *mūrdhan* samādhi and ascending to the stage of enlightenment within the space of the *dharmadhātu*.
The secret holy practices of the dhāraṇīs are fully perfected;
mind after mind, practice after practice, is emptiness.
This is the Middle Way within the wisdom of emptiness.
Unconditioned and signless, it is a single illumination and a single purity;
all conditioned phenomena and their marks are entirely extinguished.
One thus realizes entry into the gate of the Vajra Three Mysteries Bodhi Samādhi.
Because the bodhisattva simultaneously accomplishes all gateways of practice, all gateways of dharma, and all gateways of dhāraṇī,
and also realizes the vajra-secret samādhi of the Flower Ornament Ocean-Treasury— the noble nature of equality like space belonging to all Tathāgatas.
When the World-Honored One had thus expounded it,
all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas accordingly practiced,
studied, believed, accepted, and carried out its teachings.
The Mahāyāna Yoga Vajra-nature Ocean Mañjuśrī Thousand-Arms Thousand-Bowls Great Dharma-King Sūtra, Scroll Eight.
The Mahāyāna Yoga Vajra-nature Ocean Mañjuśrī Thousand-Arms Thousand-Bowls Great Dharma-King Sūtra, Scroll Nine.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Śramaṇa Amoghavajra of Great Xingshan Monastery, by Imperial Decree.
Chapter Five: What is the sequential entry into the gates of liberation?
First, one enters the contemplation of the syllable *na*, [realizing] the meaning that the fundamental is non-existent and that self-nature is devoid of intrinsic nature.
Amoghasiddhi Tathāgata expounds the gate of liberation for accomplishing adamantine bodhi.
Within this gate, there is one chapter.

The first is the ninth chapter, concerning the ten noble Bodhisattvas entering the stages (*bhūmi*) and the two sublime positions (*viśeṣa-mārga*), practicing and progressing upon the noble path to attain the bodhi of a Buddha.
At that time, Vairocana Tathāgata was in the secret samādhi of the pure ocean-nature of the dharma-realm of all Buddhas, numbering in the hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis;
the Tathāgata manifested worlds within a lotus-ocean treasury, as numerous as the atoms of hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of dust.
In each and every world, there further appeared as many transformation Śākyamuni Buddhas as there are atoms in a thousand billion worlds;
furthermore, as many transformation Bodhisattvas as there are atoms appeared within the world-realm of the Ocean Treasury.
Furthermore, a thousand-light-king hundred-jeweled lotus throne appeared;
thereupon, Vairocana Tathāgata sat upon the thousand-light-king vajra great jewel lotus throne.
The Tathāgata on the seat emitted the golden light of the purple-gold vajra from the ocean-seal samādhi (*sāgaramudrā-samādhi*),
which universally illuminated dharma-realms as numerous as motes of dust;
all were transformed into gold and became entirely pure.
The Tathāgata addressed all the Buddhas and all the Bodhisattvas, saying:
"O Buddhas, you should know: listen attentively, listen attentively!
I shall now inquire as to what the meaning and purpose of the ten holy stages (daśabhūmi) are."
I now, for the sake of this great assembly, first inquire of the Buddhas and the Bodhisattvas of Great Wisdom and Supernatural Powers.
From these ten adamantine minds, one cultivates entry into the firm and holy patience; herein I shall explain the entry into the ten holy stages of mind directed toward the fruit of Bodhi.
Having spoken thus, one should explain it in successive order.
How does one cultivate entry into the ten noble stages?
The first is the stage of the equality of essential nature (*dharmatā-samatā-bhūmi*).
Vairocana Tathāgata addressed them, saying:
"O thousand Buddhas, listen attentively, listen attentively!
Now, as for the one who first asks about the stages (bhūmi):"
What is the purpose of all Bodhisattvas cultivating and realizing bodhi?
If a noble son, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva,
in the past cultivated and maintained the Vairocana Five Wisdoms, the Tathatā Dharma-treasury, and the Vajra Secret Samyak-saṃbodhi.
Entering the ground of the essence of equanimous wisdom, the samādhi of the three secrets,
the bodhi-wisdom of the *tathatā* and *dharmadhātu* is the true Dharma;
it causes one’s own mind and the minds of others to extensively practice the conduct of a *sattva*.
He transforms all sentient beings endowed with omniscience,
practicing the bodhisattva path for the benefit of both self and others,
and fully perfects the vehicle of the four fruits of the Heavenly Light.
By means of the principle of unimpeded and spontaneous transformation, one exercises mastery over transformations;
through the power of such spontaneous transformation, one attains mastery over supernatural powers (ṛddhi),
the ten powers (daśabala), the ten epithets (daśa-nāmadheya), and the eighteen unique qualities (āveṇika-dharma).
Abiding in the Buddha’s pure land through immeasurable great vows,
I, a bodhisattva, have attained entry into eloquence, fearlessness, all dharmas, all wheels, and all gateways of practice.
Having given birth [to this state], one dwells within the Buddha-family and sits upon the stage of the Buddha-nature.
All afflictions and all obstacles of existence,
as well as the causes and effects of ordinary beings, are ultimately not experienced.
Greatly joyful and delighted,
the Bodhisattva at that time enters immeasurable Buddha-lands from a single Buddha-land,
and enters immeasurable eons from a single eon.
One cannot speak of the ineffable Dharma as if it were a speakable Dharma;
yet with a single wisdom one knows all-knowledge,
and through the insight of prajñā one contemplates and illuminates all phenomena.
They view all phenomena in their reverse aspect and view all phenomena in their direct aspect;
they constantly enter into the two truths while abiding within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
With a single wisdom, one knows the sequence of the ten stages,
their respective principles, and their respective phenomena,
manifesting them for all sentient beings.
Yet they cause them to abide eternally in the Middle Way of the mind within the mind,
knowing all the various qualities of Buddha-lands and the teachings spoken by Buddhas through a single wisdom,
while their body and mind remain unchanging and undifferentiated.
With a single wisdom, one knows the twelve links of dependent origination and the ten types of evil natures,
yet remains ever-abiding in the noble path of bodhi.
With a single wisdom, one perceives that there are no two distinct characteristics.
With a single wisdom, one knows and enters the ten factors of dhyāna and practices the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment;
yet, within the six realms of existence, one manifests all manner of physical forms with sovereign mastery over appearing and disappearing.
With a single wisdom, one knows that the various forms of the ten directions arise moment by moment;
one enters into the experience of the karmic retribution of form for all sentient beings,
yet mind and mind are neither bound nor obstructed.
One realizes the light of the samādhi of the emptiness of equal wisdom.
This light illuminates all the pure lands of the Buddhas;
therefore, the bodhisattva realizes the faith in the emptiness of the wisdom of non-arising.
Faith, patience, emptiness, and wisdom are constantly present before one,
