from the first stage and the second stage up to the stage of the Buddha-realm.
Within this interval, one enters all the dharma-gates of the Buddhas and Tathāgatas.
They are practiced simultaneously.
Therefore, I have briefly expounded this Dharma-door of the Ocean-Treasury Samādhi of the Equal Ground,
which is but a single drop from the ocean, or a mere hair-tip’s worth of the vastness of bodhicitta practices and vows.
Having spoken thus, one should explain it in successive order.
Second is the stage of the nature of virtuous wisdom (*svabhāva-prajñā-bhūmi*).
Vairocana Tathāgata addressed [the assembly], saying:
If a noble son, a bodhisattva mahāsattva,
practices the Vajra Bodhi Samādhi of the Three Mysteries— the Dharma-treasury of the Five Wisdoms of the World-Honored One Vairocana— then...
Entering the stage of the essence of excellent wisdom,
one attains pure and clear penetration of the reality-limit and the dharma-realm; thus,
one extensively practices the bodhisattva path for the benefit of both oneself and others.
They rescue and gather all sentient beings of diverse kinds who possess form;
through the perfection of their roots of goodness,
they cause them to enter the Four Noble Truths and reach the state of Bodhi.
The Bodhisattva gives rise to the mind of great aspiration.
First, they initiate the noble practices and cultivate entry into the four immeasurable wisdoms of non-conditioned compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.
The source of all merit is observed through the mind of *sattva*;
one enters into the wisdom of the path of skillful means within the great emptiness.
One sees that all sentient beings are nothing other than the Truth of Suffering.
Within the conditions of the three evil realms—the blades, staves, and all manner of afflictions—they possess a conscious mind;
the arising of consciousness therein is what is called the Truth of Suffering.
Regarding the three characteristics of suffering: as when the body first experiences sensation,
from the two conditions of the sword or staff and the bodily aggregate of form,
the arising of sensation serves as the condition for the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).
Next, the mental consciousness perceives the body as a heavy object of suffering;
because it encounters phenomena such as swords, staves, and bodily sores and swellings,
it perceives the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*).
Because the conditions for suffering are heavy, it is "suffering as suffering" (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*).
Next, there are two mental states that take feeling and formations as their objects;
because they give rise to the perception of suffering within the wound of the decay of the bodily aggregate of form.
This is called the condition for the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*).

Because the three types of perception arise sequentially as three kinds of mind, they constitute the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkha*) and the suffering of change; for if sentient beings who possess minds perceive all phenomena through these three perceptions, they give rise to immeasurable causes and conditions for suffering and affliction.
The Bodhisattva makes this vow: "Within all causes and conditions of suffering,
I shall enter the samādhi of transformative guidance and, through spiritual power,
manifest all forms of physical bodies."
Acting as a teacher within the six realms of existence,
they manifest to transform and deliver all sentient beings.
After the Bodhisattva had extensively made these great vows before the Tathāgata, [he continued...]
He realizes ten kinds of eloquent exposition regarding all the Buddha’s teachings on the Dharma-gates,
namely: the suffering of sentient beings, the consciousness of suffering, and the conditions of suffering.

When the conditions of weapons and staves are present, painful consciousness arises within the body as sores, swellings, and ulcers, whether internal or external, or both; or when these two conditions are incomplete, consciousness arises from their presence. This consciousness acts, and through its acting, it experiences contact; this consciousness is called "painful consciousness. Because it proceeds by way of these two conditions, the mind takes form as its object, and the mental contact brings about affliction. When one experiences the poison of vexation, this is called "suffering as suffering" (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*).

Regarding the consciousness that takes suffering as its object: when it first arises at the sense faculties, the awareness of the object of suffering is called the "feeling of suffering. When the mind acts upon the mind—that is, when the contact (*sparśa*) is experienced as feeling (*vedanā*)—and the consciousness perceives the contact before it has yet been afflicted by distress, this is called the "suffering of conditioned existence" (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).

When one experiences sensations of constriction as if sparks were struck from stone within the body and mind, arising and ceasing moment by moment, and when the body disintegrates and perishes, the evolving consciousness enters the consciousness of dissolution;

as conditions assemble, the mind gathers and scatters, becoming a mind of suffering, a mind of affliction, a mind of sensation, and a mind of thought. Following such thoughts, the mind clings to subsequent objects and does not let them go—this is the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*).
At that time, the Bodhisattva contemplates the truth of suffering throughout the entire triple world;
he further contemplates how ignorance accumulates immeasurable states of mind,
producing all karmic actions in a continuous and interconnected succession.
The causes of habituation and the causes of accumulation are called the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*).

When a bodhisattva possesses right view and right reception regarding the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*), and attains liberation through the wisdom of the path of emptiness within emptiness—moment by moment—this is termed the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*).
All possess karmic retribution; all possess the untainted (anāsrava).
All possess subtle and wondrous merit, as well as pure prajñā and profound wisdom.
The Bodhisattva contemplates with precision, illuminating the essential nature of all things.
Sublime wisdom and quiescence are called the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*).
The faculty (*indriya*) is the perfection of the category of wisdom regarding this single truth.
All the nature of bodhi-wisdom realizes emptiness.
Entering into contemplation, the first is the initial root of virtue;
the second is the Bodhisattva’s contemplation of equanimity (*upekṣā*),
which relinquishes all fetters and bonds of conditioned phenomena, such as greed, hatred, and delusion.
Entering into the emptiness of universal equality,
one contemplates all phenomena within the emptiness of great equanimity, which is without cause and without condition.
In reality, the nature of emptiness is of one essence and one mark.
When I contemplate all the earth and soil of the ten directions,
I see that they were all my own bodies in former lives and the very soil I utilized.
The waters of the four great oceans are the water used by me in the past;
all the fires of the kalpas are the fire used by my former bodies;
and all the wind-circles are the breath used by me.
I now enter this ground;
the Dharma-body being fulfilled, I cast off my former body and shall never again receive an impure body composed of the four elements and subject to segmentation.
This is called being fully endowed with the perfection of relinquishment.
Third, the bodhisattva next contemplates those to be converted, instructing all sentient beings so that they may all abide in peace and happiness,
and be granted the bliss of humans and devas.
The joy of the fruit of the ten stages;
the joy of being free from the fear of the ten unwholesome actions;
and the joy of attaining the wondrous flower samādhi.
Up to and including the bliss of the Buddha’s awakening and nirvāṇa—those who contemplate in this manner are said to be fully endowed with the category of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
At that time, the bodhisattva dwells within this stage.
Exhaustively free from obstacles, without attachment, without hatred, and without delusion,
the bodhisattva contemplates and enters the equal essence, the single truth, the true nature, and the treasury of the *tathatā* (suchness) of phenomena.
They enter the source of all noble paths— the noble nature— and,
through noble wisdom, noble power, and sovereign spiritual penetrations,
they travel throughout the Buddha-lands and worlds as numerous as the atoms within the pure lands of the dharma-nature of all Buddhas across the ten directions.
In each and every world, he manifests immeasurable dharma-bodies and immeasurable form-bodies,
appearing in various forms to teach and transform all sentient beings,
so that they may all abide in peace and happiness and swiftly attain the fruit of Buddhahood.
The Tathāgata’s secret teaching on unsurpassed bodhi—
such a dharma instruction as this— is expounded in the "Chapter on the Radiance of Heavenly Flowers."
Therefore, the Tathāgata has said that one should explain it in successive order.
Third is the Stage of the Radiant Essential Nature (*prakṛtiprabhāsvarabhūmi*).
Vairocana Tathāgata addressed [the assembly], saying:
If a noble son, a bodhisattva mahāsattva,
practices and studies the Vairocana Tathāgata’s samādhi of contemplation— the ocean-treasury of the five Buddhas’ five wisdoms, the vajra-bodhi of the three secrets— then...
Entering the Samādhi of the Reality-Limit and Dharma-Domain, which is the Ground of the Essence of Radiance,
one extensively practices the bodhisattva path for the benefit of oneself and others within all the teachings and practices of the noble ones.
By means of the wisdom that understands the noble nature through the power of samādhi,
one knows the meanings, principles, and categories of the Dharma-gates and the twelve divisions of the scriptures of all Buddhas of the three periods of time:
the prose, verses, mixed prose and verse, expositions, parables, stanzas, utterances, expressions, birth stories, past deeds, marvelous events, and discourses on the Vinaya precepts.
The intrinsic nature of these phenomena is termed "one" while their meanings are distinct;
this is explained within the section on names, phrases,
and syllables as referring to all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*).
Receiving birth part by part, consciousness first enters the womb;
the growth of the four great elements and the emergence of form and mind are called the six stages of abiding (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*).
Within the sense faculties, the arising of actual cognition before the differentiation of suffering and pleasure is called contact (*sparśa*).
Furthermore, consciousness perceives suffering and pleasure; this consciousness is called the three types of sensation (*vedanā*).

One continuously and repeatedly perceives and clings to these sensations—suffering within suffering, and suffering as suffering—such that the consciousness of existence through desire, self-view, and grasping at merit and demerit is inexhaustible.
That which begins with the consciousness of birth and ends with the consciousness of death is called the ten categories of the present suffering of suffering and its causal conditions and fruits.
Because I have long since departed from the middle way within these modes of activity, [I am liberated].
The Bodhisattva has long since cultivated mindfulness and attained tranquil illumination, seeing that all things lack intrinsic nature.
Having entered the Samādhi of Radiance, he possesses mastery over supernormal powers, dhāraṇīs, and eloquence; in every thought and every mental activity, he dwells in emptiness.
Furthermore, within the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, they manifest the transformation of kalpas;
they transform hundreds and thousands of kalpas,
nurturing the divine way within those lands.
Having realized the noble nature and paid homage to the Tathāgata,
they received the words of the Dharma from the presence of the Buddha, the World-Honored One,
and further manifested bodies throughout all six realms of existence.
Within a single sound, he expounds immeasurable categories of Dharma,
thereby delivering all sentient beings; each,
according to their respective capacities, hears the Dharma desired by their own hearts.
The sounds of the single truth— suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self—
are manifested differently according to the distinct bodies and minds of various lands;
this is called the Ground of Wondrous Flower Radiance.
The Tathāgata has briefly revealed a dharma the size of a single hair-tip.
This chapter on the Dharma, the Gate of Contemplative Understanding of Dharmas,
is spoken in the "Chapter on the Samādhi of the Buddha’s Threefold Samādhi of the Vajra Thousand-Ocean Treasury."
The Bodhisattva practices the path of the profound and subtle meaning of the secret Dharma of Bodhi.
Having spoken thus, one should explain it in its proper sequence.
Fourth is the stage of the nature of *jñeya* (the knowable).
Vairocana Tathāgata declared:
"If a noble son, a bodhisattva mahāsattva,
practices the Vajra Bodhi Samādhi— the Dharma-treasury of the essential nature of the five wisdoms of the World-Honored One Vairocana— [he shall attain the three secrets]."
Contemplating and entering the true suchness (tathatā) and dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) of the stage of the essence of the knowable (jñeya),
one employs all dharmas and teachings through noble conduct to deliver all sentient beings.
Because the ultimate and conventional truths, as well as the ultimate and conventional realities within the sphere of objects (*jñeya*),
are non-dual, there is neither annihilation nor permanence; it is simultaneously arising and abiding,
and simultaneously changing and ceasing, throughout a single eon and a single lifetime.
Within a single moment and a single thought, there are various differences,
because different transformations and different manifestations occur.
Thus, the Middle Way of causes and conditions is neither one nor two.
It is neither good nor evil, neither ordinary nor holy.
It is neither Buddha, nor is it not-Buddha.
It includes the realm of Buddhas, the realm of ordinary beings, and all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) consisting of the dual practices of both ordinary beings and sages.
Therefore, this is collectively termed the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
By means of the power of wisdom and the sovereign mastery of their noble nature,
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas enter into the fundamental source and essential nature of all sentient beings and give rise to roots of goodness.
From the fundamental nature of their own self-nature, Bodhisattvas enter the Tathatā-dharmadhātu, the essential nature of Vairocana Tathāgata;
they realize and enter into the Buddha-nature of sentient beings as being of one and the same essence.
Therefore, this is called the same conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
The Bodhisattva contemplates and illuminates the secret practice, the noble conduct, the noble path, and the noble nature of the Tathāgata;
he clearly observes and perceives the noble wisdom of the essential nature.
Within the noble practice of the quiescent noble path,
there is neither one nor two; one realizes the single nature of purity and enters the category of profound and penetrating noble meditative concentration.
This refers to what is called the Buddha’s noble nature, noble wisdom,
and the mental activities [of those who] train in the initial awakening and meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

At that time, by means of faith, one awakens to the thought of awakening, the awakening of stillness, the superior awakening, the awakening of mindfulness, the awakening of wisdom, the awakening of contemplation, the awakening of pliancy, the awakening of bliss, and the awakening of equanimity.
This is called the fruit of entering meditative absorption through each successive stage of the path of wisdom regarding skillful means;
such a person abides within meditative concentration.
As each momentary flame perceives the nature of phenomena, the practice of the Dharma becomes empty and void.
If one gives rise to the thought of concentration, one enters the meditative absorption of mental emptiness,
giving birth to love that accords with the Noble Path, Noble Wisdom, and the Noble Nature.
All phenomena are signless; by nature they are fundamentally unarisen.
This is called the acceptance of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), the joy of the Dharma, the endurance of patience, the realization of patience, and the patience of cessation.
Through these five patiences, Bodhisattvas enter the pure lands of all Buddhas.
Within the Samādhi of the Radiance of Radiant Flowers,
he manifests immeasurable Buddhas who stroke his head with their hands.
The Tathāgata, by means of a single sound of the Dharma,
proclaims hundreds of thousands of inspired teachings of the holy doctrine,
yet he does not emerge from meditative concentration.
Abiding in the flavor of meditative concentration, attached to concentration, greedy for concentration, and correctly established in concentration,
they remain in concentration for one kalpa, a hundred kalpas, a thousand kalpas, or many kalpas. Within that samādhi,
they behold the Tathāgata upon the Vajra-seat of Bodhi within the Lotus Assembly.
This discourse on the "Entrance to the Illumination of the Hundred Dharmas" has been honored by this person for immeasurable kalpas;
likewise, having heard this Dharma, he remains in meditative concentration for a hundred kalpas.
At that time, within the light of all Buddhas, the Bodhisattva had his head stroked,
whereby he was inspired to give rise to the category of meditative concentration (*samādhi*),
because of the emergence of signs, the advancement of signs, and the movement toward signs.
Neither sinking nor emerging, neither regressing nor falling, neither declining nor perishing,
they abide within the Buddha-nature and the holy dharmas of the Samādhi of the Summit,
attaining the supreme patience of bliss, forever extinguished without remainder.
The Bodhisattva’s contemplative illumination immediately enters the pure lands of all Buddhas;
they cultivate and maintain immeasurable meritorious practices and conduct,
and through the radiance of their path, they enter into skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*).
They transform and guide all sentient beings,
enabling them to realize and witness the Buddha-nature’s permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
For this reason, Bodhisattvas are born and abide within this stage.
Through the gateways of the Dharma for practicing and cultivating the path of teaching and transformation,
one gradually enters deeply into the wisdom of the sublime flower contemplation.
One then enters the samādhi gateway of all phenomena within the middle way of the essential nature of the three mysteries.
The category of dharmas is fully perfected, like the brilliance of a hundred thousand vajras and the shining of the sun and moon;
for the Tathāgata has taught and accomplished the hundred thousand vajra-samādhis and Buddha-samādhis of the noble nature of the path-category.
The meaning of this has already been clarified in the "Chapter on the Gate of Bodhi-Wisdom.
Having spoken thus, it should now be explained in its proper sequence.
Fifth is the Ground of Essential Nature and Wisdom-Illumination.
Vairocana Tathāgata declared:
"If a noble son, a bodhisattva mahāsattva,
practices and advances in the Vairocana World-Honored One’s samādhi of the five wisdoms, the precious vajra-treasury, and the three secrets of bodhi."
One contemplates the ground of the essence of wisdom that enters [the dharmas],
the true emptiness of the dharma-realm,
through the power of the noble path and the qualities of omniscience.
Benefiting oneself and others to extensively save all sentient beings,
one attains the ground of the mind of all Bodhisattvas through the ten dharma-power contemplation gates of the Tathāgata’s noble conduct.
May they be led into the stages of noble conduct,
and may all sentient beings swiftly transcend toward Bodhi within the path-factors of the noble wisdom of the Ten Powers.
The Bodhisattva enters the stages through contemplative practice,
giving rise to all meritorious qualities;
from the practice of the Buddha-dharmas, there arises the contemplation of the ten powers.
The power of omniscience and all-encompassing wisdom through skillful means;
the category of power for knowing the distinct spheres of activity of the two types of karma—wholesome and unwholesome;
and the category of power for knowing the performance of actions, namely, performing what is unwholesome as wholesome and performing what is wholesome as unwholesome.
To perform all manner of wholesome deeds with the desire for their karmic fruition, seeking excellent and great vows,
and to manifest transformations throughout the six realms of existence to cultivate wholesome births and the fruits of virtue— this is called the Chapter on the Power of Desire.
Within these six realms of existence, the distinctions among virtuous natures, non-virtuous natures, good natures,
and differing natures are categorized as the Chapter on the Power of Nature (*dhātu-bala*).
Because each of the powers of all roots of virtue and non-virtue is distinct, they are named the Chapter on the Power of the Faculties (*indriya-bala*).
That which consists of wrong concentration, deluded concentration, right concentration, and non-concentration is called the category of the power of concentration.
By means of all causes and effects, the result is multiplied by the cause and the cause is multiplied by the result;
thus, evil results lead to evil results, and good results lead to good results.

The vehicle of the fruit, the vehicle of the stage, the vehicle of power, the causal vehicle, the resultant vehicle, the noble vehicle, and the vehicle of the path constitute the Chapter on the Power of the Path.
Because one knows all phenomena through the five eyes and perceives all births,
it is called the Chapter on the Power of the Divine Eye.
To know, one by one, the events of hundreds and thousands of kalpas,
including the names of each successive life in past existences, is the category of power of world-knowledge;
for it is through this that all sentient beings cultivate the bodhisattva practices.
The Tathāgata, through the empowerment of the power of the noble path,
brings to an end all afflictions, ignorance, and birth-and-death;
this is called the Chapter on the Power of Liberation.
Therefore, this is called the "Chapter on the Ten Powers of Contemplation.
By means of his own power of wisdom,
the bodhisattva knows the causes and effects of his own cultivation.
Furthermore, knowing the causes and effects of all sentient beings is called "distinguishing categories.
The noble wisdom of a bodhisattva discriminates between good and evil.
Yet, by means of the power of their wisdom, they exercise mastery over body, speech, and mind through discrimination,
such that they can transform a pure land into an evil land,
and an evil land into a land of sublime bliss.
One can transform good into evil and transform evil into good;
one can transform form into non-form and non-form into form.
Transforming male into female and female into male;
transforming the six realms of existence into that which is not the six realms,
and transforming that which is not the six realms into the six realms.
This applies even to all phenomena and the elements of earth, water, fire, and wind;
they are not earth, water, fire, or wind, and all things are likewise so.
Therefore, by means of the power of wisdom and great skillful means, the Bodhisattva...
He bestows empowerment upon the body, speech, and mind of all sentient beings.
Through his noble nature and noble power, he advances them toward enlightenment;
his immeasurable merit is beyond comparison and inconceivable.
This is not something that can be known or perceived by all bodhisattvas of the lower stages;
it is the noble path for every single step of lifting and setting down the foot.
Therefore, this is the contemplative practice of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
Entering into great luminous wisdom,
they gradually advance upon the path, part by part attaining entry into noble wisdom and bodhi;
they realize a hundred samādhis, with radiant light shining forth everywhere.
Throughout the immeasurable and boundless pure lands of all Buddhas within the *dharmadhātu*,
Bodhisattvas transform and guide unspeakably unspeakable numbers of sentient beings by means of the Dharma of the Great Wisdom *Prajñāpāramitā*.
Because it is always present before one.
Having spoken thus, one should explain it in its proper sequence.
The sixth is the stage of the Flower-Light of Essential Nature (*svabhāva-puṣpa-prabhā-bhūmi*).
Vairocana Tathāgata addressed them,
saying: "If a noble son, a bodhisattva mahāsattva,
practices and realizes the Vajra Samādhi of the Three Mysteries— the treasury of the wisdom of the fivefold enlightenment of the World-Honored One Vairocana— "

Contemplating and entering the essential nature of the Flower-Light Stage (Puṣpalocanā-bhūmi), the perfectly pure Dharma-realm, and the ten kinds of supernatural powers and noble wisdom of the Tathāgata’s Bodhisattva Vehicle,
he guides all sentient beings toward self-benefit and the benefit of others.
By means of inexhaustible vows and practices, they gather and deliver sentient beings, attaining the path of supreme enlightenment.
The Bodhisattva then raised a question: "How is it that within all worlds..."
In the "Chapter on Supernatural Powers and Clear Wisdom," the Tathāgata instructs all bodhisattvas and points out the way for all sentient beings to cultivate awakening.
Therefore, the Tathāgata replied:
"The bodhisattva on this stage enters the ground of the essence of Flower Radiance through the practice of contemplation,
by means of the ten types of supernormal knowledge."
They know the various sovereign transformations of the noble powers through the clear wisdom of the divine eye,
perceiving all material forms as numerous as the atoms within the lands of the three periods of time.
They are divided into the bodies of the six classes of sentient beings.
Each individual body’s subtle form is analyzed into its constituent gross elements.
These divisions are known through wisdom, observed with the clear insight of the divine ear.

One knows that the sounds of suffering and joy of sentient beings in the six realms of existence— numbering as many as the atoms of the ten directions and the three periods of time— are neither non-sounds nor non-voices,
as well as the sounds of all phenomena;
this is through the clear wisdom of contemplating the celestial body.
They know all forms, both form and non-form,
neither male nor female in appearance.
Within a single thought-moment, they universally know the measure of lands, kalpas, and time throughout the ten directions and the three periods of existence.
With the wisdom that perceives the minds of others in the heavens,
they know the mental activities of all sentient beings throughout the three periods of time, as numerous as the atoms within all large and small lands.
They fully know all subtle and coarse activities and divine transformations through the number of atoms,
using the holy wisdom that contemplates the heavens to know all sentient beings within the six realms of the ten directions.
They perceive all things— the mind and mental factors, such as suffering, pleasure, good, and evil—
as well as all conditioned and unconditioned phenomena,
knowing them completely through the clear wisdom that observes devas and humans.
He knows, within all lands throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time,
the causes and effects of the past lives of all sentient beings— their suffering and happiness, their lifespans,
whether their lives are long or short, and the continuous succession of their births and deaths.
Having passed through hundreds and thousands of kalpas, he fully knows each and every one.
Through the clear wisdom that observes the liberation of the devas,
he knows all sentient beings of the ten directions and the three periods of time.
Liberation consists in severing all veils of ignorance, whether numerous or few, which are as subtle as atoms;
this is accomplished through cultivation and realization from the first stage up to the tenth stage,
the stage of Equal Enlightenment, and the stage of Wondrous Enlightenment.
It extinguishes the extinction of extinction— the subtle outflows and afflictions—
and causes all conditioned phenomena with characteristics within the knowable to be utterly eliminated.
It brings about their total cessation without remainder, such that they are entirely stilled.
They attain the noble path of liberation, the Vajra Bodhi of the Tathāgatas.
With the clear wisdom of the mind in the *dhyāna* of Contemplating Devas,
they know the sentient beings within the lands of the ten directions and the three periods of time.
Whether the mind is concentrated or unconcentrated, it is not that concentration exists independently;
rather, concentration arises from what is neither concentrated nor unconcentrated.
This is achieved through methods, skillful means, and that which is embraced.
Entering the Vajra Samādhi of the nature of the Tathāgata’s three secrets,
and because of realizing this samādhi-samāpatti,
one employs the clear wisdom of celestial awakening through contemplation.
He knows the number of kalpas as numerous as the atoms of all sentient beings,
and whether they have already attained Buddhahood or have not yet attained it through their sequential cultivation and entry into the stages (bhūmis);
he even knows all beings of the six destinies throughout the three periods of time.
They distinguish the various differences in the divisions of mind, as well as lifespans, births, and deaths,
both great and small; they are also able to fully know all the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, of the three periods of time,
and completely understand all the profound and wondrous teachings they have expounded.
By means of the wisdom arising from the contemplation of celestial realms,
one knows all sentient beings and the masses throughout the past, present, and future— across three, ten,
and a hundred thousand kalpas, and within all great and small kalpas.
Regarding the quantity and duration— whether long or short— of the lifespan of those with merit and those without merit,
the Bodhisattva generates the power of a great vow and observes it with the wisdom of great aspirations.
They know the small and great vows of all sentient beings;

they seek to accomplish the vow for the realization of Bodhi, and they vow to study and practice all the Buddha-dharmas of the Tathāgata, entering the stages of the sages and worthies, including the thirty minds, the ten bhūmis, the stage of Equal Enlightenment, and the stage of Sublime Enlightenment.
Within each and every state of mind, the practices and vows performed reach as far as the stage of Buddhahood.
Whether it be suffering or pleasure, whether it be the Dharma or non-Dharma,
the Bodhisattva makes a great vow to enter into them all completely.
He shall rescue and deliver all sentient beings so that they may attain Buddhahood in the future,
causing all beings to share his ten great vows and become fully endowed with the hundreds of thousands of great vows of a bodhisattva.
When this Bodhisattva dwells within this stage, through the clear wisdom of the ten supernormal powers,
they manifest immeasurable bodies, speech, and minds like those of a Tathāgata, and proclaim the qualities and measures of the stages.
For unspeakably unspeakable hundreds and thousands of eons,
one could not exhaustively describe the subtle and excellent dharmas of this stage through noble wisdom.
At that time, Vairocana Tathāgata—
A brief exposition on the chapter "Knowing the Noble Grounds through Supernatural Powers and Clear Wisdom" is inexhaustible and inconceivable;
likewise, it is so within the chapter "Contemplating the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination through Noble Practice."
The Tathāgata has thus spoken of matters as small as a single atom;
therefore, they should now be explained in their proper sequence.
Seventh is the Stage of Perfecting the Essential Nature through Contemplative Insight.
Vairocana Tathāgata addressed them, saying:
"If a noble son, a bodhisattva mahāsattva,
practices and enters the Vairocana World-Honored One’s Samādhi of the Secret Vajra of the Dharmadhātu, the True Treasury of the Five Wisdoms."
Entering into this Dharma, within the true nature of the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) of the stage of fulfillment,
the bodhisattva’s contemplative practice employs the wisdom of intrinsic nature,
which is equivalent to the power of the wisdom of the Tathāgatas.
They advance in the cultivation of all sentient beings,
causing them to enter the noble practices of the teachings of Bodhi,
and cultivating entry into the eighteen categories of the noble ones' wisdom.
It is not shared with any bodhisattvas of the lower stages.
The body realized by the bodhisattva is free from outflows and faults;
the mouth is free from verbal transgressions.
The mind is free from loss of mindfulness;
detached from the eight worldly dharmas, it abides eternally in the nature of equanimity and emptiness regarding all phenomena.
It constantly enters the three secrets within samādhi.
This is called the completion of the six categories for entering the stages.
Furthermore, from this wisdom,
the bodhisattva gives rise to the wisdom of the six bases and initiates the contemplative practices of the six gates.
Because they will ultimately never again experience the fetters, bonds, perfumations, or habitual tendencies of the three realms,
they possess the power of desire.
Because they fulfill all virtues, all dharma-gates, and all that is sought in merit and wisdom, they are fully endowed with power.
This is called the perfection of the mind of diligence.
It encompasses all phenomena of the three periods of time, the various marks and causes and effects throughout all kalpas,
as well as all conditioned activities of sentient beings.
Because one knows [all things] within a single mind, in a single thought-moment, and at a single time,
it is called the "sufficiency of mindfulness.
Therefore, these are the dharmas of the two truths and the mental dharmas of sentient beings in the six realms.
Because one knows all phenomena through a single wisdom,
it is called the "perfection of wisdom.
Because one knows the ten stages of departure for the worthy and benevolent through a single wisdom.
Up to the ten stages of the noble ones and the stage of Buddhahood— the two sublime stages of awakening—
one knows through a single wisdom that the nature of the samādhis of all Tathāgatas is free from fetters and habitual tendencies, and that their three bodies are pure.
This is called the "Understanding of the Feet.
By means of the Tathāgata’s adamantine holy nature and holy wisdom,
through a single wisdom, one knows and perceives the number of kalpas as numerous as atoms, as well as all sentient beings throughout the three periods of time.
The cycle of birth and death with its causes and effects of good and evil;
the nature of delusions as numerous as motes of dust;
and the false imaginings of attachment to the views of self and person.
The habitual tendencies of defilement and the notion of self,
as well as the seeds of the wholesome, the unwholesome, the out-flowing,
and the non-out-flowing, all become perfect enlightenment.
Therefore, this is called the "foot of liberation through knowing the minds of others.
You, O Benevolent One, are said to have entered the six perfections.
The Bodhisattva contemplates and perceives with clear and wise knowledge.
He then gives rise to the wisdom-body, manifesting transformations that accord with the thoughts, aspirations, and practices of sentient beings throughout the six realms.
With eloquence of speech, he expounds immeasurable categories of Dharma-doors,
instructing and manifesting for the sake of all sentient beings.
While abiding in the samādhi of the eternally constant nature of the mental activities of all sentient beings,
he manifests the quaking of the great earth throughout the ten directions,
because he has realized the samādhi of the radiant nature of the Flower-Light.
It enables all sentient beings to enter,
heart after heart, into the perfection of great clear wisdom,
thereby beholding all the Buddhas who appeared in the world throughout immeasurable kalpas of the past.
They also cause them to attain the holy wisdom of non-attachment in the minds of all sentient beings, which is perfectly penetrating;
they also see the teachings and the preaching of the Dharma by all Buddhas within all lands throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time.
May all sentient beings, in every thought-moment,
advance in their practice by means of the path of supernatural powers and noble wisdom,
seeing all Buddhas appearing in the world throughout all future eons.
He instructs and guides all sentient beings;
because they rely on this Tathāgata to receive instruction and listen to the Dharma,
he causes them to realize and enter the eighteen stages of the noble sages.
The noble mind enters the Tathāgata-samādhi of the nature of the noble mind.
The Bodhisattva should then again carefully contemplate and observe that the forms within the three realms, as numerous as motes of dust, are his own former bodies.
This body, in its cycles of transmigration, arising and passing away,
is like the infinite sentient beings throughout the three periods of time, within space, atoms, and the dharma-realm;
all of them have been my parents, brothers, sisters, and so forth.
Now, entering this stage,
one internally realizes all merits, all supernormal powers, all samādhis, radiant light, and the power of blessings,
through the instructions and teachings practiced by all Buddhas.
Up to and including the eighth, ninth, and tenth stages, as well as the stage of Equal Enlightenment and the stage of Sublime Enlightenment—
because I have already attained entry into all the categories of the Dharma-gates of all Tathāgatas.
Within Buddha-lands as numerous as the atoms of those very atoms,
he manifests the attainment of Buddhahood, the turning of the wheel of Dharma, and the mastery of supernatural powers, abiding in the adamantine nature of a Tathāgata.
Though unborn and undying, eternally abiding in the Dharma-realm,
they shall likewise manifest entry into nirvana and parinirvana,
transforming others throughout the past, future, and present.
He constantly enters as many buddha-fields as there are atoms,
teaching and transforming all sentient beings;
in each instance, he likewise attains unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Therefore, after the World-Honored One has spoken,
the Tathāgata shall subsequently expound it in sequence.
The eighth is the stage of the essential nature of the Buddha’s roar of contemplative illumination.
Vairocana Tathāgata addressed them,
saying: "If a noble son, a bodhisattva mahāsattva,

practices and realizes the Vairocana World-Honored One’s five wisdoms, the true treasury of the limit of reality, the holy nature of the dharma-dhātu, and the subtle, fine, and wondrous samādhi of the secret adamantine ground."
Through contemplative practice, one enters the stage of the Buddha’s roar,
which is the essence of reality as it truly is; thus,
the bodhisattva attains entry into the rank of the Dharma King.
Having realized the samādhi of the bliss of the essential nature,
their wisdom is like that of a Buddha and is therefore called the Buddha’s Roar Samādhi;
thus they enter the ten stages of great, clear, and wise knowledge.
The gate of the concentration of empty stillness is constantly present before him;
he has entered the samādhi of the Flower-Light-Sound Entering the Mind.
As for the wisdom of emptiness,
it refers to entering the gateway of the wisdom of internal emptiness, the gateway of the wisdom of external emptiness,
the gateway of the wisdom of conditioned emptiness, and the gateway of the wisdom of unconditioned emptiness.
The gate of wisdom of the emptiness of nature; the gate of wisdom of beginningless emptiness;
the gate of wisdom of the emptiness of the ultimate truth; the gate of wisdom of the emptiness of emptiness;
the gate of wisdom of the emptiness of the emptiness of emptiness; and the gate of wisdom of the great emptiness of the emptiness of the emptiness of the emptiness of emptiness.
These ten gates of the Tathāgata’s adamantine nature, emptiness,
and wisdom are such that all bodhisattvas of the lower stages cannot know them. Therefore,
this is the lion’s roar of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva.
One enters the gate of wisdom-emptiness, the vajra-noble nature, the equality of the ten emptinesses,
the ground of the nature of space that is indestructible and unchanging.
Therein, the Bodhisattva contemplates and perceives all noble natures and noble wisdoms through gnosis.
Possessing the power of knowledge of the spiritual faculties (*abhijñā-jñāna-bala*) that is as vast as space and beyond description,
one knows all Buddha-dharmas with a single moment of wisdom, along with their distinct,
exquisite, and profoundly deep meanings and principles.
They enter into buddha-fields as numerous as infinite atoms of dust,
and before each and every Tathāgata, they inquire for and receive the medicinal teachings of the Dharma,
successively instructing and transforming all sentient beings.
He causes all bodhisattvas to transmit the Dharma and deliver sentient beings,
bestowing it upon all living beings and extensively applying the medicine of the Dharma to them.
This one is called a Great Dharma Master;
they may also be called a Great Guide.
They destroy the four Māras and, through the transformation of the Dharma-body, enter the realm of the Buddha.
This is the number of all Buddhas.
Entering into equal enlightenment and wondrous enlightenment, one completes the number of the Bodhi of all Buddhas.
Entering into the body of essential wisdom, one realizes the Dharma-body of adamantine sacred insight.
They accomplish one hundred thousand dharani-doors,
realize one hundred thousand samadhi-doors,
and enter one hundred thousand vajra-doors.
They enter a hundred thousand gateways of supernormal powers;
they enter a hundred thousand gateways of liberation;
they enter a hundred thousand gateways of the equality of space.
Entering the gateway of the Tathāgata’s non-empty vajra-bodhi-accomplishment,
through the majestic power of the sublime wisdom of Mahesvara,
all ordinary and holy practices are realized in a single thought-moment.
At one time, he entered the Buddha’s adamantine bodhi-sacred-nature-tathatā samādhi.
He fully knew the profound essentials and various categories of all dharmas, and preached various sublime paths:
he spoke of kalpas as non-kalpas and non-kalpas as kalpas.
To speak of the path as non-path and non-path as path;
to speak of the six classes of sentient beings as non-six-classes and non-six-classes as sentient beings.
It is not that sentient beings speak of the six realms;
it is not that Buddhas speak of Buddhas, for Buddhas speak of non-Buddhas.
Yet, they exercise mastery in entering and emerging through divine power and sagely nature.
He realizes the samādhi of the noble wisdom of Vairocana;
his entry into the samādhi of the essential nature of all Buddhas is likewise so.
The bodhisattva’s contemplative practice employs the noble wisdom of intrinsic nature.
Using wisdom, one reflects back, reflecting in accordance with the flow, reflecting against the flow;
reflecting before and reflecting after, reflecting on the cause and reflecting on the fruit;
reflecting on emptiness, reflecting on non-emptiness, and reflecting on the supreme Middle Way.
The Samādhi of the Illumination of the Meaning-Truth, the Illumination of Quiescence, and the Illumination of Space;
therefore, this Bodhi-Sage-Wisdom Samādhi is realized only from the eighth stage upward.
All Bodhisattvas of the stages below cannot reach it.
Therefore, the Vajra-Bodhi of the Noble Ground is immovable and unshakable;
it neither enters nor exits.
Neither arising nor ceasing, neither perishing nor exhausting—
such are the immeasurable and boundless, most excellent and wondrous principles contained within this chapter on the Dharma-gate of this stage.
The Buddha said: "Such a Dharma-gate as this could not be fully expounded even in eons as numerous as motes of dust; it is unspeakable, even unspeakably unspeakable.
Now, the Tathāgata shall briefly proclaim and reveal a small portion of the secret, holy nature, and the subtle, wondrous merits of the vajra."
To speak of even a single hair-tip’s worth of matters through a portion as vast as hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of atoms—
this has already been clearly explained in the "Chapter on the Noble Conduct and Noble Path of Mahāyāna Bodhisattvas and Arhats. Thus it has been said.
One should expound this in successive order.
Ninth is the Flower Ornament Stage of the Essential Nature of Contemplative Illumination.
Vairocana Tathāgata addressed them, saying:
If a noble son, a bodhisattva mahāsattva,

cultivates and realizes the samādhi of the subtle, wondrous wisdom of the adamantine secret traces of the firm nature— the ocean of the path of the fivefold holy nature of the World-Honored One Vairocana— then...
Through the practice of contemplation, one realizes the essential nature of the Avataṃsaka stage,
enabling all bodhisattvas to enter the Buddha-nature of the Tathāgata’s dharma-realm and become of one essence,
thereby accomplishing the noble wisdom of vajra-bodhi.
He entered the Tathāgata-vajra-samādhi-īśvararāja-samādhi, a state of meditative concentration in which there is no fixed time for entering or emerging,
throughout the ocean-like realms of the ten directions within the trichiliocosm.
There are ten billion suns and moons, ten billion Sumeru mountains,
and four hundred billion sets of four continents;
therein, all bodhisattvas practice for enlightenment.
At one time, they attain Buddhahood and turn the Great Dharma Wheel;
even unto their parinirvāṇa, all Buddha-activities are accomplished because of the realization of Bodhi.
Thus, the Bodhisattva contemplates and illuminates with a single mind.
In a single thought-moment and at a single time,
he manifests to all sentient beings the Vajra-Spiritual-Power Samādhi,
the Secret Nature-Wisdom Body and Dharma Body of the Three Mysteries of Bodhi.
Manifesting a body of wondrous form with the primary marks and secondary characteristics—
namely, the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor signs—
and abiding by the sovereign power of a sage in the indestructible diamond-like stage of a Buddha.
The Samādhi of Sovereign Freedom illuminates the joy of emptiness,
equal to the immeasurable great compassion and the light of the thousand samādhis of the Tathāgata; it is adorned with the marks and characteristics of light upon light,
and is neither deva, nor human, nor of the mundane world, nor of the six realms of existence.
It is likewise for that which transcends all phenomena of the dharma-realm throughout the three periods of time.
The bodhisattva-mahāsattva constantly practices such contemplation:
entering the six realms of existence, he manifests immeasurable bodies, manifests immeasurable speech, manifests immeasurable minds, and expounds immeasurable dharma-gates.
They are able to transform the realm of Māra into the realm of the Buddhas, and transform the realm of the Buddhas into the realm of Māra;
furthermore, they transform all the dogmatic views of non-Buddhists,
causing them to enter the correct view of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas.
He transforms the views of all Buddhas,
enters into the views of all non-Buddhists,
and further perceives the Buddha-nature as transforming into the nature of sentient beings.
Seeing the nature of sentient beings transform into the Buddha-nature,
that nature of noble wisdom shines radiantly;
light illumines light, and wisdom illumines wisdom.
The radiant flames, the radiant flames, illuminate the quiescent holy nature,
the indestructible vajra qualities,
the ten powers, and the eighteen unique dharmas of practice.
Liberation and nirvana are unconditioned and signless;
they are the single path of purity.
The bodhisattva contemplates and enters the realm of sentient beings to rescue and gather them all.
Furthermore, regarding all sentient beings,
they have been one's parents and brothers in every lifetime; thus,
it is said that their teaching of the Dharma continues throughout all kalpas.
And they attain the fruits of the Path.
Furthermore, they manifest all lands throughout the three periods of time for all sentient beings.
They regard one another as fathers and cherish one another with thoughts like those toward a mother;
likewise, they regard even the celestial Māras and non-Buddhists as fathers and love them as mothers.
Thus, when a bodhisattva dwells in this stage,
from the limit of saṃsāra up to the adamantine limit,
they are able, within a single moment of mind, to enter into the realms of immeasurable sentient beings.
He likewise manifested such events.
At that time, within the *Puṣpasaṃcaya* chapter,
the Tathāgata briefly explained matters as vast as the ocean, yet as small as a single drop or a single mote of dust.
It is ineffable and cannot be fully described.
Having spoken thus, one should explain it in successive order.
The tenth is the contemplation of the essential nature and entry into the stage of the Buddha-realm.
Vairocana Tathāgata addressed him,
saying: "If a noble son, a bodhisattva mahāsattva,

cultivates and realizes the Samādhi-Ocean of the Five Noble Wisdoms of King Flower-Light of Vairocana World-Honored One, and becomes one with the holy nature— the subtle, firm, and profound wisdom of the Three Mysteries of the Vajra Samādhi— "
Entering the nature of Vajra-wisdom,
he realized a thousand billion samādhis and entered the Vajra-samādhi of the essential nature of the Buddha-realm.
And [he is] identical with the vajra-prajñā-dharmatā-jñāna-kāya and dharma-kāya of all buddhas and tathāgatas,
by means of the bodhi of the Buddha and all the dharmas of the pāramitās.
They have accomplished the great Mahāsattvas and entered the noble stage of the emptiness of great wisdom; their nature is empty,
and that emptiness is further emptied, such that even the noble wisdom is empty.
The wisdom that is equal to the nature of space is the realization by the Bodhisattva of the ten titles of the Tathāgata, the adamantine *dharmatā* of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
It possesses ten kinds of sublime qualities.
They are fully endowed with the emptiness of all phenomena;
they are of one nature, one characteristic, and an unconditioned essence.
Their spirit is void, their substance is one, and their dharmas are identical to the dharma-nature.
This is called the Tathāgata’s conformity with the Four Truths and the Two Truths;
for he has exhausted the limits of the cycle of birth and death throughout the entire dharma-realm,
and because the Dharma-nourishment and the Dharma-body are non-dual.
This is called the Tathāgata Arhat;
there is not a single sentient being who does not respond to his influence,
as he pervades all sentient beings throughout all worlds of atoms.
Practicing the bodhisattva path and the noble conduct of the Tathāgatas,
they enter the noble liberation of correct nature and correct wisdom,
knowing that all phenomena are neither existent nor non-existent.
Furthermore, because one knows the distinctions in the faculties and natures of all sentient beings through noble wisdom,
this is called "Perfect Complete Enlightenment" (Samyak-saṃbodhi).
It is so named because it is fully perfected at the time of attaining the fruit of Buddhahood through the practice of clear, luminous, and manifest conduct.
He is named the One Perfected in Knowledge and Conduct (Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna).
As for the term "Well-Gone" (Sugata), the dharmas of the Buddha’s teachings throughout the three periods of time are identical to those of previous Buddhas;
by his noble nature, the Buddha departs well and arrives well.
This is called the Sugata.
This person practices the noble conduct of the Buddha;
this is called the supreme superior practice.
With noble virtue fully perfected, he enters the world to teach and transform sentient beings,
causing the power of the sages to permeate subtly;
he realizes liberation and enters the gate of the Buddha’s great tranquility.
Knowing that all fetters of ignorance have been completely extinguished without remainder,
this is called being a knower of the world.
This person has realized the supreme noble understanding of all Tathāgatas, which stands above all phenomena.
They enter into the Buddha’s majestic deportment, supernormal powers, and physical forms;
their essence is of one single nature, no different from that of the Buddha.
Like the Buddha, the Great Man, the Tathāgata, and the Mahāsattva, they abide in the sphere of practice where noble virtues are perfectly complete.
He is named the Unsurpassed One (*anuttara-puruṣa*).
As one who disciplines through the Dharma, he disciplines all sentient beings;
thus, he attains the full perfection of the Dharma.
This is called the "Tamer of Men," who instructs all sentient beings among devas and humans by receiving and accepting their inquiries regarding the words of the Dharma.
This is called the Teacher of Gods and Humans.
The Dharma is fundamentally one; its wondrous essence is fundamentally twoless.
The Buddha-nature is profound and subtle, mysteriously penetrating the path of awakening.
Permanence, bliss, self, and purity are the great fulfillment and absolute purity.
Because all sentient beings pay him homage and revere him,
he is therefore named the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
All Bodhisattvas of the three realms, all worthy sages, all devas, all nāgas and spirits,
and all sentient beings of the human world, rely upon the Tathāgata’s teachings to believe, accept, and practice them.
One attains entry into the stage of the Tathāgata.
Thus, within this Buddha-stage,
it is the locus entered by all noble beings.
It is called the stage of the Buddha-realm;
it is the stage that accomplishes the two positions of Equal Enlightenment and Sublime Enlightenment,
attaining the indestructible diamond of the Buddha’s Bodhi.
In order to realize *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*,
at that time, Vairocana Tathāgata,
within the great Flower Treasury World-Ocean of the Samādhi of the Boundless Ocean of the Nature of a Thousand × Hundred × Ten Million Vajra Secrets, [resided].
Seated upon a great lotus throne of a hundred jewels,
the World-Honored One sat upon that throne and emitted a golden radiance, brilliant with purple-gold vajra light.
Like hundreds of thousands of suns,
the Samādhi of Radiant Golden Light blazes intensely,
illuminating the trichiliocosm so that there is nowhere it does not pervade.
Within each of those lights, countless atoms transformed into Śākyamuni Buddhas and countless great Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas,
all of whom came together for this assembly.
Together with them, their minds were all granted the prediction of enlightenment;
they were filled with joy and happiness as the Tathāgata,
with his body of manifest wisdom, extended his golden hand.
He stroked the crown of that bodhisattva’s head. All Buddhas and all bodhisattvas—
those who see alike, study alike, practice alike,
and follow the same path— are likewise [present].
With one voice and in unison, they praised [the Buddha] without duality;
entering the Tathāgata’s sublime and wondrous Dharma,
they rejoiced incessantly, all finding complete satisfaction.
Furthermore, there were all the Buddhas and all the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, numbering as many as the atoms within hundreds of thousands of billions of worlds from other directions,
who came together at the appointed time to appear and serve as witnesses.
At one time, they gathered like clouds and requested that he turn the wheel of the Dharma.
The Wheel of the Holy Path is a dharma that cannot be spoken;
yet it is a dharma that can be spoken.
The Buddha taught that the noble nature (*āryadhātu*) is like empty space and identical to the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Therefore,
this dharma possesses an ineffable, wondrous, and sublime gateway to the teaching.
The gate of the wondrous and extraordinary samādhis and the three vidyās;
the gate of the wondrous and extraordinary dhāraṇīs and total-holdings; the gate of all vajras;
and the gate of all supernormal powers.
The gateway of the equality of all space;
the gateway of all liberations.
Such is this supreme dharma-gateway as described above.
It is that which all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of the lower stages cannot know or comprehend,
as well as the mental consciousnesses of all the devas.
Nor can they know it; it is known only by the Buddha,
the World-Honored One, through his supreme and holy nature of body, speech, and mind,
within the inconceivable Dharma-gate wherein the source of all phenomena can be exhausted yet remains ineffable.
The Tathāgata spoke of this in the "Flower Chapter of the Immeasurable Samādhi Light of the Gods" within the *Vajrasamādhi-sūtra* of all Buddhas,
stating that the ten inexhaustible fearlessnesses of the noble nature are identical to the Buddha-way.
Therefore, as the Buddha has taught above regarding the ten stages of the sages,
one subsequently enters the stage of Equal Enlightenment and the stage of Wondrous Enlightenment;
all Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas should study and practice these in successive order through contemplative observation.
Entering the vajra-bodhi of the Tathāgata stage,
they attain the fruit of Buddhahood.
At that time, all the great Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas...
Having heard the World-Honored One’s exposition of the ten holy stages, such as the *Viśeṣabhūmi* and others,
they revered the Tathāgata deeply, accepted it with faith, and practiced accordingly.
At that time, Vairocana Tathāgata...
Having entered the hundred-thousandfold Samādhi of the Holy Nature of the Vajra,
and having entered the hundred-thousandfold Gateways of the Samādhi of the Equality of Emptiness,

he causes all Bodhisattvas to contemplate and penetrate the True Suchness and the Limit of Reality (bhūtakoṭi), and to realize the Stage of Holy Wisdom— unbreakable due to the holy nature of subtle and wondrous wisdom that is as firm and dense as a vajra— and to enter the Stage of the Sublime Enlightenment Equal to a Vajra.

In the space of a single thought-moment, one swiftly enters the Vajropama-samādhi; through the realization of the nature of the three secrets of bodhicitta, one attains the stage of wondrous enlightenment.
Having attained the samādhi of the noble vajra-nature, one achieves the fruit of the Dharmakāya Buddha-Tathāgata.
In this way, all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who practice and maintain the Tathāgata-samādhi of contemplative cultivation enter entirely into this indestructible ground of the vajra-sage-wisdom—
the true suchness and ultimate nature of the Buddha’s vajra-bodhi and the three secrets of the holy path.
This establishes the attainment of the fruit of Buddhahood, which is unsurpassed, perfect,
and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*), because one has accomplished *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, the Tathāgata Vairocana addressed [the assembly], saying:
"O Buddhas, you should know: listen attentively, listen attentively!
When I was formerly practicing as a bodhisattva, I cultivated and entered the Vajra Secret Bodhi Samādhi as taught by the Tathāgata."
The root and source of the fruit of Buddhahood is as follows:

all sentient beings who cultivate and attain Buddhahood must all practice and enter the ten stages of departure, the ten stages of nurturing, the ten adamantine stages, and the stages of Equal Enlightenment and Sublime Enlightenment.
Upon entering the Mountain of Non-arising,
one realizes the noble path of liberation of the Tathāgata Vajrabodhi;
one shall then attain the Buddha-body, identical to bodhi, unconditioned, signless, great fulfillment, and eternally abiding.
The ten powers, the eighteen unique qualities, and the wisdom-body and dharma-body are fully perfected.
Therefore, the essence of the heart of Vairocana Tathāgata is the fundamental bodhi-vajra, the holy nature.
Possessing the power of great vows, may I be born together with all sentient beings in the nature of the noble ones;
may I now eternally abide in the Dharma-body.
It resides within the nature of all sentient beings,
dwells within the minds of all bodhisattvas,
and takes the equal dharma-realm as its body and mind-essence.

Furthermore, it is because they are empowered by the holy power [of the Buddha] so that all bodhisattvas and all sentient beings may realize the buddha-nature of nirvana— characterized by permanence, bliss, self, and purity—
and swiftly attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Therefore, all the great Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, having heard what the Tathāgata had spoken,
each deeply revered it, accepted it with faith, and put it into practice.

Translated by the Tripiṭaka Śramaṇa of Daxingshan Monastery, Da Guangzhi.
Translated by Amoghavajra by Imperial Decree. At that time,
Śākyamuni Tathāgata again descended from the palace of the Heavenly King Maheśvara and arrived in Jambudvīpa in the south.
He came and went, preaching the Dharma at the Great Assembly Site of the Jeta Grove Monastery in Śrāvastī,
where the Tathāgata sat upon a pedestal of a hundred-jeweled lotus flower.
Upon the jeweled throne, he entered the Lion’s Vigorous Display Vajra Samādhi.
Arising from this samādhi,
his radiance shone universally throughout thousands of billions of Buddha-lands and pure realms, as numerous as motes of dust.
All dharmas of the three periods of time throughout the dharma-realm, up to the Peak of Existence and the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception;

all sentient beings, including the Great Brahmās, the various devas, Śakra Devānām Indra Lord of the Six Desire Heavens, the various devas of the Four Heavenly Kings, the great deities, the four noble wheel-turning kings, and the hundreds of millions of minor kings, ministers, military commanders, and executive officials of Jambudvīpa, as well as all the people they govern.
The World-Honored One emits a great light of compassion,
which shines universally and pervasively everywhere,
so that all bodhisattvas and all sentient beings are gathered and drawn into the ocean of Dharma.
May they cause [beings] to cultivate the noble nature and noble conduct of bodhi;
may wholesome dharmas increase and calamities and obstacles not invade them;
and may all transgressions as well as icchantikas [be purified].
All those who slander the Vaipulya sutras shall be completely extinguished.
At that time, the Tathāgata arose from samādhi and addressed the great assembly of bodhisattvas.
The two great beings, Samantabhadra and Mañjuśrī, as leaders of the assembly,
along with all the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and others—
I now see them in future ages.
At the time when the holy Dharma of the Buddhas is about to reach the end of the kalpa and is disturbed by the turbidity,
and when spirits and deities are in chaos within this world—
what do you think? Now is precisely that time.
If there are kings, ministers, rulers, or officials who do not believe in the Buddha-dharma and do not respect their teachers and elders,
they will cause the benevolent deities of the realm to be displeased and the dragon kings to be unhappy.
The five grains will not ripen and wind and rain will be untimely.
Such people who do not revere the Buddha-dharma do not believe in creating merit nor do they cultivate the path of practice.
Those who experience pleasure born of greed without awareness or knowledge will have their minds disturbed by various evil spirits and ghosts.
Such persons will find that their craving for desire becomes intensely fierce, accumulating wealth and treasures without ever knowing contentment.
Therefore, one should know that such persons as these ought to reflect upon themselves with urgency, feel remorse and reproach,
resolve to attain bodhicitta, and extensively cultivate merit.
One should rescue one's own body.
Furthermore, there are worldly ordinary people who do not revere the Triple Gem and do not believe in the Buddha-dharma.
Furthermore, they will be deluded and distracted by ghosts and spirits who enter their hearts;
such demonic persons, possessed by ghosts, will engage in strife and competition to afflict and harm the virtuous and good.
They are able to produce heterodox views, evil attachments, and disputes over right and wrong;
they devise secret plots and strategies to destroy the virtuous and good,
including kings, ministers, and military commanders.
Do not allow the deluded and distracted mind to cause what is perceived to prevail as a state of pervasive perversion and rebellious disorder. Why is this?
Therefore, people of the world should know this.
One must by all means remain vigilant and give rise to faith;
thus, one should cultivate various meritorious virtues.
Therefore, O son of good family, if you wish to turn your mind toward reverence and cultivate merit, [you should do so].
There are three kinds of Dharma. What are the three?
First is the Jewel of the Buddha, second is the Jewel of the Dharma, and third is the Jewel of the Saṃgha.
How does one rely upon these Three Jewels, and how does one practice their retention so as to bring about merit or demerit?
If one makes offerings to the Sangha, the merit is a hundredfold;
if one makes offerings to the Dharma, the merit is a thousandfold;
if one makes offerings to the Buddha, the merit is ten thousandfold.
This is the infinite merit of taking refuge in the Triple Gem of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha. Therefore,
you sons of good family should know that if one harms the Saṅgha-gem,
spirits will enter one's heart, causing one to lose their human form and the rank of a high minister.
They will enter hell forever, with no time of release.
If they destroy the Jewel of the Dharma, spirits and deities will enter their hearts to diminish their merit and fortune,
and they will suffer the retribution of blindness, deafness, muteness, and folly.
They constantly fall among the animals as camels, donkeys, pigs, or dogs.
Even if they encounter the Jewel of the Buddha, demons and spirits enter their minds;
they are full of lust and desire, full of anger, and lack joy. Their minds are perpetually obscured and deluded by others.
Having lost the royal throne, this human body so difficult to obtain will perish;
one will fall into the Avīci hell and fail to be reborn in heaven,
sinking forever into the ocean of suffering.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the sons of good family and all sentient beings,
earnestly exhorting them:
"I can no longer bear to behold the sentient beings in the hells who have committed evil karma."
Lacking faith in the Triple Gem, one's merit and fortune are exhausted;

they cultivate self-starvation, enduring hunger and abstaining from food; they speak to others with external words, claiming for themselves that they have attained the Way and are neither hungry nor thirsty. This is called the method of non-eating among the self-starving non-Buddhists.

I said that I am able to know reality.

When these signs are present, that person is dull-witted;

Reflecting upon this, one must awaken;

If such a person has passed away from the realm of hungry ghosts and is reborn in this world, they will possess these characteristics:

They are stingy, greedy, envious, and jealous; they fear government officials;

All Buddhas as numerous as the atoms of the universe,
all great Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas,
and all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
All the Great Brahmā devas, those of the four dhyānas and eight samādhis, the emperors of the six heavens of desire,
the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, the four great heavenly kings,
the four types of wheel-turning monarchs, and all the nāgas, ghosts, and spirits.
The assembly of the twenty-eight classes of yakṣas;
and all the great and small kingdoms throughout the four continents of Jambudvīpa,
including the kings of great and small realms, who are like grains scattered about.
The fourfold assembly of disciples— bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās— as well as sons and daughters of good family,
have deeply given rise to a sense of shame and trepidation, looking up to the Tathāgata with reverence.
He expounded the sublime Dharma and praised its unprecedented nature.
All were filled with joy, received it with faith, and practiced accordingly.
In the future, they shall all attain Buddhahood and swiftly transcend to the other shore.
To realize and perfect *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
